News.title: Andy Burnham meets Trump live: US President praises our leader after showdown talks on Falklands and Chagos
News.content:
Donald Trump, the US leader, has engaged in crunch talks with Andy Burnham today, but these follow a rambling address to the UN Assembly in New York City in which he talked about artificial intelligence

Donald Trump today praised Andy Burnham — but branded the Chagos Islands deal "terrible".

Following the showdown talks on various other topics, including trade and immigration, the US President said he felt the US and UK are "doing very well" when he answered questions from the media today. Mr Trump and Mr Burnham's meeting was the first face-to-face encounter since Mr Burnham became Prime Minister.

Their crunch talks happened, though, moments after Mr Trump had said — during his speech at the UN General Assembly — he planned to rename artificial intelligence. Our US Political Editor described the bizarre address as "one of the darkest, angriest speeches" he's seen Mr Trump make.

Speaking about the Chagos Islands deal, Mr Trump bluntly told reporters: “I don't support it. I think it's terrible. It was a terrible deal. They all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it's ridiculous.”

The sovereignty of the British-controlled archipelago in the Indian Ocean has been the subject of ongoing discussion between the UK government and Mauritius, with a deal to cede sovereignty put on hold earlier this year after the US withdrew its support. The islands are home to Diego Garcia, a joint UK-US military base that hosts "super-secret" facilities in a region under strategic threat from China.

Follow Trump and Burnham's meeting using our live blog below...

News.title: Tributes pour in for woman and three children killed in Bootle house fire
News.content:
Tributes have poured in for a woman and three children believed to have died in a house fire in Bootle, Merseyside.

Tributes pour in for woman and three children killed in Bootle house fire

Tributes have poured in for a woman and three children believed to have died in a devastating house fire in Bootle, Merseyside.

Emergency services were called to the semi-detached house at around 3.40am on September 22. Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said firefighters arrived within seven minutes to find the property "well alight".

The Liverpool ECHO understands the four victims were a woman and three children. Their next of kin have been informed, but formal identification has yet to take place.

Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle described the blaze as an "intense fire which spread very rapidly". A fifth person was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

Tearful neighbours told how a man smashed the property's windows as he desperately tried to save those inside, but was beaten back by the flames. Another neighbour said he tried to use his ladder to reach the property but was "just too late" as the fire was already out of control.

One neighbour said she was haunted by hearing a woman screaming at around 3.30am. "I heard a commotion and went outside. I heard screaming, the lady was shouting," she said.

Neighbours have gathered near the scene to pay their respects, with dozens of tributes left in memory of the victims. The main fire has been extinguished, and Merseyside Police and Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service are carrying out a joint investigation to establish its cause.

News.title: 'Andy Burnham navigated minefield of tensions and avoided drive-by with Donald Trump'
News.content:
The Prime Minister and his team will be pleased with how his first meeting with Donald Trump played out, despite being fraught with risk.

Burnham appeared to navigate the minefield of tensions, including the Falklands, Ukraine and immigration, in his closed-doors meeting with the US President.

Speaking to the media afterwards, Trump said Burnham was a "natural businessman" - high praise in his book - when asked if he was a man he could do business with.

Trump didn't bite on a question about the UK's decision to slap trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which could have been a serious point of tension. But he did return to his criticism of the "terrible deal" to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, which Burnham said he was looking at.

‌



Andy Burnham doesn't rule out rejoining EU in next Labour election manifesto READ MORE :

Andy Burnham braces for first high-stakes talks with unpredictable Donald Trump READ MORE :

View 2 Images Trump said Burnham was a 'natural businessman' (Image: Toby Melville/PA Wire)

Trump couldn't resist a swipe at Keir Starmer, saying the relationship was "more up" than down under Burnham. His resentment stems from a bitter grudge against the last PM for refusing to let the US use British bases to bomb Iran.

But he said things were on the up under Prime Minister "Andy". In all, the meeting can definitely be chalked up to a win for Burnham.

He avoided one of Trump's televised drive-bys, and the US President's outburst on the Chagos islands was predictable.

‌



It wasn't as chummy as Starmer's first meeting with Trump in the Oval Office, which turned into a love-in once the-then PM handed over an invitation for a second state visit. But that early bonhomie didn't stop Trump from turning on Starmer once he refused to do what he wanted.

Burnham looked slightly uncomfortable at times but he also decided to gently mock Trump for calling Manchester "some town" - a braver move than it might appear.

The pair have started to build a rapport, which is the only way to deal with Trump. But it's not clear yet whether Burnham was able to get any tangible wins from the meeting.

His big push on AI safety is going nowhere with Trump, and efforts to get more air defence support for Ukraine are yet to bear fruit. Then there's the disastrous Iran war that is putting an economic squeeze on the PM's plans - but Trump has so far failed to extract his country from.

‌



The US President appeared to draw a line under his battles with Starmer - and to suggest things between the UK and the US are on the up.

So the question is whether Burnham can turn good vibes into real action.

News.title: Pain of NHS whistleblowers as call for Lucy Letby retrial grows louder
News.content:
Pain of NHS whistleblowers as call for Lucy Letby retrial grows louder

As Dr John Gibbs, who gave crucial evidence against Lucy Letby, suggests a retrial could be "the most appropriate thing for everyone", the Mirror hears from Dr Susan Gilby, who successfully sued the Countess of Chester for unfair dismissal

View 8 Images Dr John Gibbs has suggested that a retrial in the Lucy Letby case could be 'the most appropriate thing for everyone' (Image: Cheshire Constabulary/AFP via Ge)

On the morning of July 3, 2018, Lucy Letby was arrested at her Chester home on suspicion of eight counts of murder and six counts of attempted murder of vulnerable newborns.

‌



Suspicions had been raised over the neonatal nurse as early as September 2015, when Countess of Chester Hospital staff began to notice a disturbing correlation between infant deaths and Letby's shift patterns.

‌



As the death toll rose, the connection became impossible to ignore. For months, dread filled the hospital corridors, but, as the Thirwall Inquiry would later determine, senior managers were slow to react, delaying urgent meetings for which medics pleaded.

‌



Had Letby been removed from her duties in October 2015, when concerns were first raised, twin babies O and P may not have died in June 2016. It wasn't until June 29, 2016, that Letby was finally removed from frontline duties.

Hospital boss altered baby deaths review to make two Lucy Letby victims appear to have died naturally, inquiry finds READ MORE :

View 8 Images The Thirwall Inquiry determined senior managers had been slow to react, delaying urgent meetings medics had pleaded for. (Image: The Thirlwall Inquiry via Getty Images)

Mere weeks after Letby's first arrest, Dr Susan Gilby joined the Countess of Chester as medical director and deputy chief executive. As Dr Gilby would later testify during the inquiry, having reviewed the June 2016 CQC report, she'd expected to "go into a high-performing organisation".

‌



Ahead of her start date, Dr Gilby was "brought up to speed" on some of the unfolding issues. She told the Mirror: "I was aware that there had been many unexplained and unexpected deaths and collapses on the unit in 2015/16, and I was aware that there were some relationship problems between the paediatrician consultants and the executive team, and that the chair was trying to improve relations between those two groups."

The Thirwall Inquiry would later refer to this division as a "gulf". Consultants were forced to apologise to Letby, and management even threatened to report whistleblowers to the General Medical Council (GMC).

View 8 Images It took three arrests before Letby was charged (Image: Netflix)

‌



Dr Gilby, appointed following the retirement of Mr Ian Harvey, was informed of Letby's arrest shortly before the announcement. The staff reaction was unexpected. She recalled: "I thought I would find a team who were very distressed by this turn of events, as I said in my Thirwall statement. But in fact, I found that three weeks after the arrest, they were very entrenched in their view that nothing would come of this."

Considering why this might have been case, Dr Gilby reflected: "I've no idea why they thought that. It seemed that they'd just not been professionally curious enough about why babies were collapsing and dying unexpectedly and in an unexplained manner on their unit.

"[...] If you have repeated cardiovascular collapses and death, and you can't explain them, and they weren't expected, that just doesn't happen in clinical practice."

‌



View 8 Images Concerns grew after a correlation was noted between baby deaths and Letby's shift patterns (Image: Countess of Chester Hospital)

Dr Gilby spent three hours, alongside Dr Brearey, analysing the timeline of each incident. She also read consultant questions submitted to Mr Chambers, telling the inquiry how she could “see the anguish coming off the page", and how she'd noticed her predecessor's "very defensive" response.

She continued: "It was important that I listened to the paediatricians and looked at all of the documents I had at my disposal myself, because I was being asked to deal with the paediatricians, and also to arrange the mediation. I met with Dr Brearey, and it was minutes into that conversation that I realised that the executive team had got this very wrong. I absolutely did expect at some point that there would be charges. I didn't know when that would be."

‌



It was, as Dr Gilby emphasised, a "complicated case", with each incident requiring a separate investigation. Three days after her first arrest, Letby was released. She was rearrested and rereleased on June 10, 2019, at her parents' Hereford home. The third time, on November 10, 2020, Letby was charged with eight counts of murder plus 10 counts of attempted murder, and denied bail.

View 8 Images Ian Harvey was the medical director at the time of Letby's killing spree (Image: Cheshire Live/MEN MEDIA)

By this point, Dr Gilby explained, "virtually all of the previous senior leadership team had moved on", but she was able to inform them "out of courtesy". Dr Gilby said: "Those who were still in the organisation were devastated. There was nobody in the senior leadership team who believed that this was the wrong thing to happen.

‌



"They were distressed, and absolutely were looking at themselves in terms of, 'Could we have known about this? Should we have known, and did we actually know?' There was also a lot of concern about supporting the staff who were witnesses, and who had to be interviewed multiple times by the police, and were now going to have to give evidence as witnesses in a criminal court.

"There was a lot of horror for the parents in particular, and just wondering what they were going through. It's unimaginable, really. There was nobody that I spoke to, including very senior people, board members, who felt that there was any issue with the charges that had been brought, other than could they have done something sooner to prevent this."

View 8 Images Dr Susan Gilby took over Dr Harvey's role mere weeks after Letby's first arrest (Image: PUBLICITY PIC)

‌



Letby, now 36, was convicted of killing seven babies and attempting to murder seven more, and was given 15 whole-life orders. Since 2015-16, there has been just one death at the neonatal unit, in September 2019. For her colleagues, the long-term impact has been profound. Some have reported suffering post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), as well as severe depression and anxiety.

In December 2022, Dr Gilby resigned, filing a claim for constructive unfair dismissal, after she'd made allegations of bullying and harassment against the trust's chairman, Ian Haythornthwaite. Dr Gilby told a tribunal how one Trust director, Ros Fallon, had taken her to the pub that October, telling her it was “time for you to go”, adding, “If you don’t agree to go, we will start a process against you.”

While Dr Gilby was offered a payoff to walk away, this was under the condition that she drop any allegations. Having previously raised concerns at work without issue, Dr Gilby told us: "It was a shock to me, to be honest, to find that in Chester there was not a history of openness when listening to people who were raising concerns.

‌



View 8 Images Dr Gilby successfully filed an unfair dismissal lawsuit against the Countess of Chester (Image: LIVERPOOL ECHO)

"It was an even bigger shock to me when, as a chief executive who was medically qualified with a background of being a medical director in three organisations and a consultant in critical care and anesthesia, that when I raised concerns that the behaviors of the chair and others on the board were putting patients at risk and were putting staff, including myself, at risk, that... it wasn't just that we weren't listened to. I was asked to keep quiet and offered a bribe to do so."

Dr Gilby was awarded £1.4 million in damages after it was ruled she'd been wrongly dismissed, and Haythornthwaite resigned. Looking back at her time on the Countess, Dr Gilby's thoughts remain with the families of the victims, some of whom have been left with lifelong injuries. The money, she notes, could have been better spent on patient care.

‌



She remarked: "I really am concerned that in the higher echelons of the NHS, right at the very top, there isn't necessarily always the openness and willingness to accept that there might be a problem that we would expect, and then that cascades its way down into some organisations."

View 8 Images Dr John Gibbs says he holds 'a very small concern that there may not have been any deliberate harm done' (Image: ITV News)

This comes as Dr John Gibbs, one of three consultants whose evidence helped convict Letby, told The Sun he holds "a very small concern that there may not have been any deliberate harm done", arguing that a retrial could be “the most appropriate thing for everyone”.

Article continues below

Regarding this suggested retrial, Dr Gilby commented: "The convictions are sound, in my view. There are other cases that she could have been convicted of. The appeal, she's been convicted by two juries. The people who are best placed to investigate unexplained, unexpected deaths are the police, and they did that. The people who are best placed to present the evidence are the Prosecution Service, and the people best placed to make a judgment are the jury and the judge. And then the appeal court. And as far as I'm concerned, that's what's happened, and I'm not in a position, and neither is anybody else, to go behind that."

Do you have a story to share? Email me at julia.banim@reachplc.com

News.title: Brooding Donald Trump brags about war crimes and seeks to rebrand AI as an American superweapon
News.content:
Brooding Donald Trump brags about war crimes and seeks to rebrand AI as an American superweapon

OPINION: Trump's annual address to the UN General Assembly quickly turned from American greatness to American might and power - and his willingness to use it to get what he wants

View 2 Images Donald Trump gave an angry, brooding speech to the UN (Image: MICK TSIKAS/EPA/Shutterstock)

Donald Trump gave a dark, angry speech to the United Nations, seeking to rebrand AI as an American super weapon and bragging about the US committing a string of apparent war crimes.

‌



The embattled President opened his address to the UN's General Assembly by bragging about his perceived achievements.

‌



But the address quickly turned from American greatness to American might and power - and his willingness to use it to get what he wants.

‌



"While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace," he claimed, implausibly.

"While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them. While others have talked of courage. America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world."

In a lengthy section about Iran, Trump said he needed to decide whether to make a deal - or "annihilate the Islamic Republic."

‌



He mused about whether he should "drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations", which would be a war crime.

He went on to boast about how America is extracting millions of barrels of oil from Venezuela after America's invasion of the country in January - which he's now calling a war. He even declared "to the victor belong the spoils" as he bragged about pillaging the state - which is also a war crime.

‌



He talked about how he's going to plant two massive military bases on Greenland, which Denmark has signed up to despite many observers still warning that it could be a prelude to him annexing the island by force.

The delegation from Cuba walked out in protest when Trump bragged about his economic and energy embargo against the island, which only falls short of the war crime of "collective punishment" because America and Cuba are not technically at war.

It probably didn't help that he described Cuba as a "failed state" and a "haven" for America's adversaries.

‌



He declared America won't be doing very much to regulate AI, despite increasing warnings that the technology could cause the destruction of the human race.

View 2 Images If Marvel made a movie where a supervillain did this, people would say it was too on the nose (Image: Brendan Smialowski/Pool AFP via)

Instead, Trump sought to rebrand it "Super Intelligence" - and making the case for an AI arms race with China. Because if there's a dangerous, destructive power in the world, Donald Trump wants to own it.

‌



In a moment almost buried in the speech, Trump sought to engineer the collapse of the International Criminal Court, which he said was a "rogue organisation", before urging all member states to resign from it.

One of the International Criminal Court's primary functions is to prosecute people for war crimes.

Trump's UN speech last year was the easily mockable rambling of a freewheeling elderly man hurling insults at his favourite targets for sport.

Article continues below

This year his approval rating is in the 20s. He's seven months into America's most disastrous war since Iraq - a war that is incredibly unpopular and making his voters poorer. And he's staring down the barrel of a midterm election that is widely expected to be a bloodbath for the Republican Party. Trump is not in the mood for fun.

He's banning journalists from the White House because they won't write propaganda about him, bragging about the war crimes he's got away with and threatening to commit a few new ones. And he's doing so from the podium of the United Nations.

Forget acting like a dictator - if Marvel made a movie with a supervillain who did this, critics would say it was a bit on the nose.

News.title: Harry and Meghan issue 'totally unnecessary' warning to school parents about photographing Archie and Lilibet
News.content:
Harry and Meghan issue 'totally unnecessary' warning to school parents about photographing Archie and Lilibet

EXCLUSIVE: Parents visiting Archie and Lilibet's school have been sent letters of warning over photographing children, with one parent calling the measure 'complete overkill'

View 4 Images Harry and Meghan have prioritized their family's safety since moving back to the UK (Image: John Angelillo/UPI/Shutterstock)

Parents visiting the school where Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have moved their children to have received warnings over taking photos of pupils.

‌



Guidance has been issued over the expected conduct of parents and care-givers of students at the village prep-school, after the Duchess of Sussex’s phone number was shared from a parents' WhatsApp chat.

‌



Parents at neighbouring schools, which play sport against each other, have been reminded to only take photos of their own children when supporting the team. In a letter sent to parents this week, one school stressed “the importance of only taking photos of your own children”.

‌



Meghan Markle spotted for first time since return to the UK with Hollywood A-lister READ MORE :

Prince William ignores awkward question about Earl Spencer’s book and smiling Charles shrugs off row READ MORE :

View 4 Images Harry and Meghan have sent a warning to parents about taking photos at Archie and Lilibet's school (Image: AP)

One parent told The Mirror : “It can't be a coincidence that these notices are going out now just after Harry and Meghan have moved their children into the local area.

"It's complete overkill, everyone knows the boundaries, and could you imagine the uproar from other parents if someone was discovered purposely taking pictures of children that weren't theirs. I hope this isn't a sign of things to come because it's totally unnecessary.”

‌



Harry and Meghan last week moved their children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, to a new school closer to their temporary home, citing security fears over a school 30 minutes away.

View 4 Images Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

The family moved back to the UK last last month after spending six years in the United States. However, their private security team did not do a recce of the first school which was located in the centre of Oxford.

‌



A source close to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said the city traffic left the family like "sitting ducks" when they got stuck between cars on the school run.

The family’s security team advised on pulling the children out over fears of the heavy term-time traffic, having only tested the route during the summer holidays.

View 4 Images The Duke and Duchess moved their children to a new school closer to their home (Image: AP)

‌



Unexpected congestion on the route from where they are living to the school meant a 30-minute journey turned into an hour’s journey at rush hour.

The children’s new school is just a short drive from their temporary home, avoiding built up areas. The Mirror is not identifying the schools or the family’s location.

One parents at Archie and Lilibet’s new school described two 4x4 cars “rushing” down the country lane near to the school, before Harry and Meghan exited with their security team and children outside the school entrance on their first day.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

The parent said: “Everyone is very down to earth and normal here. We all help each other and help out whenever we can with school events. We would hope all new parents want to get involved and immerse themselves in school life and the wider community.”

Prince Harry has shared his intense security fears for his family, taking the British government to court twice over the decision to strip him of taxpayer funded security.

Article continues below

The prince was handed new hope of getting the government to foot the estimated £5million a year bill for his security when the Home Office confirmed it would carry out a new review into the threat against him and wife Meghan, following the family's return to the UK.

News.title: Man arrested twice and released from custody - then he killed three pensioners
News.content:
Man arrested twice and released from custody - then he killed three pensioners

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell had 'delusions about paedophiles and being kidnapped' before he killed Anthony Payne and twins Roger and Dick Carter in Exeter

View 3 Images Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested twice shortly before he killed three men (Image: Devon and Cornwall Police)

A triple killer was arrested and released twice in the days leading up to his fatal attacks on three elderly men, their inquest has heard.

‌



Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was suffering from delusions about kidnappings and paedophiles before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and twins Roger and Dick Carter, 84. Mr Payne was attacked with a hammer, while the Carter brothers were bludgeoned to death with a shovel.

‌



The deadly attacks took place three hours apart at two houses located a mile and a half away from each other in Exeter, Devon, on February 10, 2019. More than seven years later, a jury inquest is now taking place into the three men's deaths at County Hall in Exeter.

‌



View 3 Images Anthony Payne (Image: Payne family/SWNS)

The court was told today that Lewis-Ranwell, now 35, was initially arrested at a farm in Combe Martin on suspicion of burglary on the morning of February 8 and taken to Barnstaple police station. He was released the day after but was back in a cell seven hours later.

He was arrested again after attacking farmer John Ellis with a 4ft saw and stick. It was Mr Ellis' wife, Maureen Ellis, who called the police, with Lewis-Ranwell heard in the background as he was making allegations about paedophiles.

‌



Body-worn camera footage seen by the jury shows the man resisting officers during his arrest, as he was then warned he would be Tasered if he didn't stop. He then tells the armed officers: "Why are you f****** me? Why are you f****** me? Why are you f****** me? Why are you f****** me?

"Get off. Why are you f****** me? Get off, please. You are f****** me in the head. You raped me."

View 3 Images Police outside the house where the Carter twins were killed (Image: SWNS)

‌



Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and taken back to Barnstaple police station, less than 24 hours after his first detention. After another almost 24 hours in custody, he was released on the morning of February 10, just hours before his three attacks.

Today's proceedings heard Lewis-Ranwell got a taxi from Barnstaple and planned to go to Exeter but the driver left him at Copplestone railway station as he was scared Lewis-Ranwell would hurt him. He then got a bus to Exeter.

Driver Johnson Joseph said: "I felt there was something suspicious about his behaviour, as he immediately made me feel uncomfortable. He sounded psychotic, as he kept on talking to himself and mumbling, and I couldn’t understand everything he was saying.

‌



"He was talking about the trees, and came across as some kind of mental health patient. His behaviour just wasn’t normal, but I can’t put it into words.

"He was acting erratically, and kept on telling me to drive faster, and to overtake all of the cars. I just knew he was going to harm me."

At Exeter St David's station, Lewis-Ranwell got into a dispute about a woman who he believed was being held against her will by a taxi driver. Detective Sergeant Martin Sutcliffe, who was part of the investigation team, told the hearing that Lewis-Ranwell told doctors after the killings he was having "delusions about people being either trapped, kidnapped, held against their will, and that he was feeling a compulsion to try and help in some way".

‌



From the train station, he went towards the nearby Bonhay Road, where Mr Payne lived. CCTV from a neighbouring property shows Leiws-Ranwell entering Mr Payne's home and leaving just six minutes later.

Mr Payne was found dead in an upstairs bedroom having suffered blunt force head injuries when he was attacked with a hammer. Asked about the motivation for the attack, Det Sgt Sutcliffe replied: "Only through other experts and I mentioned before about him having a delusion.

"It was assessed by others that he was looking to free people, or they might have been trapped in some way. And my understanding is when that was examined by the experts, he expressed that when he saw the birth certificate on the side that he thought that perhaps Mr Payne was involved in something and keeping people against their will at the property."

Article continues below

The hearing was also told that several members of the public had interactions with Lewis-Ranwell in Exeter after Mr Payne had been attacked, who observed his unusual behaviour.

The inquest continues.

News.title: F-16 fighter jet crashes near Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany as pilot injured
News.content:
F-16 fighter jet crashes near Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany as pilot injured

A plane has crashed near the United States' Spangdahlem air base in Germany with one person injured, and reports say the aircraft went down on a golf course

View 2 Images An F-16 fighter jet has crashed at a US airbase in Germany (Image: x.com/eabajema)

An F-16 fighter jet has crashed at a US airbase in Germany, leaving its pilot injured after ejecting from the aircraft, the American military has confirmed.

‌



The jet, assigned to Spangdahlem Air Base in western Germany, crashed on Tuesday, September 22. The pilot ejected safely and is receiving medical care, according to a US military statement but no details have been given on how serious is his condition.

‌



Emergency services rushed to the scene following the crash. The Eifelkreis Bitburg-Prüm local authority confirmed that one person had been injured and said its emergency response had since concluded.

‌



View 2 Images An F-16 fighter jet has crashed at a US airbase in Germany (Image: x.com/eabajema)

The statement from the US Air Base Spangdahlem said the plane, which was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing, which crashed around 2:30 p.m. local time, and that the cause of the crash was being investigated.

Local newspaper Trierischer Volksfreund reported that the aircraft came down on a golf course near the B50 road between Binsfeld and Spangdahlem.

‌



In a statement, the Eifelkreis Bitburg-Prüm local authority said: “Following a plane crash near Spangdahlem Air Base, fire and disaster relief services from the Bitburg-Prüm district were deployed.

“According to current information, one person was injured. The emergency response has since concluded. The Bitburg-Prüm district is currently unable to provide any information regarding the cause of the accident or further details of the incident.”

Spangdahlem is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron with about 20 aircraft. The squadron, which supports US Air Force and NATO missions worldwide, is the centrrpiece of the air base.

‌



The base has about 5,000 military and civilian employees, plus their family members, according to the latest figures. The U.S. air base also employs between 700 and 800 Germans.

The US Air Force has maintained a presence in Spangdahlem since the mid-1950s. Along with Ramstein near Kaiserslautern in southwestern Germany, Spangdahlem Air Base is considered one of the most important airfields for the US military in the region.

This incident follows the crash of a US Air Force F-16 jet crashed in Zemmer-Rodt, not far from Spangdahlem, in October 2019. On that occasion there was a power failure on board. The pilot lost control of the aircraft and ejected, suffering only minor injuries.

News.title: Plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community disrupted, say police
News.content:
Two men have been arrested over a suspected terrorist plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester, police have said.

The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on Sunday on the eve of Yom Kippur - considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar - when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues already guarded with a heavy security and police presence.

The men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, according to the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation.

Sources have told the BBC the suspected plot was "fairly imminent" and in the later stages of planning.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the government would "continue to do all in our power to address threats against our Jewish community".

She added: "We cannot expect our Jewish community to live behind higher walls.

"We must also tackle antisemitism at its source and root it out wherever it rears its head."

News.title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
News.content:
Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.

The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004.

These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape.

Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December.

Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support.

"Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line."

Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said.

A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027.

Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood.

"Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women.

"These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women.

"Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings.

"The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial."

News.title: Earl Spencer should pull Diana book from shelves, Piers Morgan says
News.content:
Piers Morgan has called for Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana to be pulled from the shelves over a factual error.

Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, apologised to Morgan for incorrectly describing him in the memoir as the editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group published "highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym" in 1993.

Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said he accepted the apology but that his lawyers would be "laying out that we want the offending pages to be removed from this book. And if that means they pulp the first edition, so be it".

The BBC understands Penguin, the publishers of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, will be amending this one point in future editions of the book.

The photographs of Princess Diana mentioned in relation to Morgan in Earl Spencer's book were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993.

At the time, Morgan was working at The Sun and did not join the Mirror as its editor until 1995.

Earl Spencer admitted "his assumption was incorrect" and "apologises to Mr Morgan for this error", a statement said.

News.title: Father admits causing death of his son in hotel fall
News.content:
Foster was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week for the plea hearing to take place.

His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.

Paphos District Court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.

Foster decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.

A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing.

"The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.

The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.

In a statement given to the BBC, Alexandrou, said: "This was a momentary lapse of attention, without any intention to cause harm, which had the most devastating and unimaginable consequences.

"We will now present to the court the relevant mitigating evidence and circumstances for consideration ahead of sentencing."

The family have suffered "unimaginable grief" since the "horrific events" and have asked for privacy during this time, added the lawyer.

News.title: Booker Prize judges reveal shortlisted novels after selection 'tussle'
News.content:
The End of Everything by M John Harrison

An unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81.

The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud."

The Disappearers by Marlon James

This epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far".

The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour."

Black Bag by Luke Kennard

An out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life.

The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here."

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry

A modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist.

The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth."

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Strout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices.

The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events."

John of John by Douglas Stuart

The third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John.

The judges said: "A rich and moving novel about a father and son who live on a remote Scottish island in the 1990s, where small-town secrets and buried shame reverberate to surprising, devastating and even joyous effect."

News.title: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message
News.content:
By putting the European Union at the heart of how he would fund his tax cut, the Lib Dems couldn't be drawing a starker contrast with the Brexit-backing Reform UK and a Conservative Party also committed to cutting welfare.

But the plan is speculative. The Lib Dems insist a deal with the EU could be negotiated within a year if the party was in government after the next election.

Plenty of economic experts, including the official budget forecaster the OBR, believe the UK's economy could grow if the UK was in the Single Market.

But as recent political history teaches us, negotiating a deal with the European Union is often more difficult than party leaders hope.

And basing a tax cut on potential future economic growth is a risky business.

There is also uncertainty over whether the Lib Dems' sums add up. The independent think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the policy as set out in the press release would cost "much more" than the Â£17bn the Lib Dems have budgeted for.

The party says the tax cut wouldn't come in until the fifth year after the next election. So even if the party got into power and successfully negotiated an EU deal, the tax cut could be eight years away.

But the Lib Dem MPs I spoke to afterwards were less focused on these details than the message it sent to voters.

Davey came into this conference facing criticism over his leadership from some MPs in private and others in his party in public worrying about the party's ambition and direction.

For now those concerns have been dampened. "That was the speech a lot of us have been waiting for him to give," one Davey-sceptic MP told me afterwards.

A small number are uncomfortable with the main policy from the party's conference being a tax cut that would most benefit the better off.

One told me they would rather the focus had been wooing younger voters by tackling the amount graduates repay in student loans, an old bruise for the Lib Dems.

But overall this speech, and this conference, was well received by the Lib Dem faithful.

They are a party honing their messaging before the next general election. The strategy is primarily on those 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024. Most of them are held by the Conservatives and Davey's tax cuts are aimed at appealing to those voters.

But already the attack from the Tories has been that the Lib Dems are "Labour's lapdog". That attack is in part because Davey has given his most explicit answer this week on not going into a coalition government with the Conservatives after the next general election. He's done the same for Reform UK.

But he hasn't ruled out a pact with Labour.

So that attack from the Conservatives will come again and again before the next election.

But the Lib Dems leave their Brighton conference buoyed, with sights not just on retaining their record 72 seats won at the last election, but on winning some more.

And then?

"I've got no ceiling on our ambitions," Davey said this week.

He has already served in government once, in coalition with David Cameron's Conservatives. His eyes are on another stint in office.

News.title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Burnham
News.content:
Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.

The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and would raise the subject with von der Leyen when he meets her during a UN summit in New York.

Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".

He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy.

The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains.

Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.

Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us.

"We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain.

"We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies hereâ¦ we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem.

"We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."

News.title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.

The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.

The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".

"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."

Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".

Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).

He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."

The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".

He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.

His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.

News.title: Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market
News.content:
The Liberal Democrats will fight the next general election on a promise to cut taxes for millions of workers, Sir Ed Davey has said in a speech to his party conference.

The Lib Dem leader said that if he gained power, he would raise the annual tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000.

He would also raise the 40p income tax threshold from Â£50,270 to Â£56,000, in a Â£17bn package funded by the economic boost he says would come from the UK rejoining the EU single market and customs union.

He claimed the plan would mean a Â£680 cut for "most taxpayers" but it would not come into full effect until the fifth year of a Lib Dem government - potentially up to eight years away.

The announcement was greeted with sustained applause by Lib Dem MPs and activists in the Brighton conference centre.

The Â£12,570 income tax allowance was frozen by the Conservatives in 2021, resulting in more people being dragged into paying the tax, and Labour has so far resisted calls from trade unions and some of its MPs to unfreeze it.

The Lib Dems said they would raise the threshold to Â£15,000 a year, and increase the starting point for paying employee National Insurance (NI) to the same level.

At their conference earlier this month, Reform UK promised to increase the income tax personal allowance to Â£15,000 within 100 days if they won power.

Sir Ed told the Lib Dem faithful "the difference between us and Reform" is that "their tax cut is paid for through cruelty."

He said "Reform's figures show they'd pay for it by ripping Â£22bn of crucial support away from disabled people."

Explaining his pledge to raise the 40p income tax threshold, Sir Ed argued that more and more people were being dragged into a tax bracket that had originally been intended for higher earners.

"A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses" he said, adding: "That's not fair, it's not right."

Under the Lib Dem plan, based on research by think tank Frontier Economics, external, the economic boost from rejoining the single market would allow the party to spend Â£17bn on tax cuts by the end of the next Parliament.

The party says it would unfreeze personal allowances in the second year of a Lib Dem government, allowing them to rise with inflation, before bringing in big tax cuts in year five when the economic benefits of closer trading with the EU had kicked in.

However, the move would depend on the party being able to negotiate a closer trading arrangement with the EU in just 12 months.

Stuart Adam, of the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, told BBC Verify the Lib Dem package would cost "much more" than the Â£17bn quoted by the party.

Reform has estimated that its policy, to raise the starting threshold to Â£15,000 just for income tax, would cost Â£21bn by the fifth year.

The Lib Dems say their policy would be funded by an extra Â£27bn from its plans for a "growth and defence pact" with the EU.

News.title: Mum and three children die in Bootle house fire
News.content:
A mother and three children have died in a house fire on Merseyside.

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, at 03:45 BST.

Eight firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom who were showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

Another casualty, who was outside the property when crews arrived, was taken to hospital.

Officers from Merseyside Police were at the scene and a joint investigation with the fire service into the cause of the blaze is under way.

The North West Ambulance Service's hazardous area response team also attended the scene of the fire and confirmed the four fatalities.

Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle confirmed the "intense fire [had] spread very rapidly".

News.title: Reform MSPs walk out of parliament in protest against Scottish independence debate
News.content:
Michael Marra, the new leader of Scottish Labour, was among those backing the motion although he said it was more about SNP internal politics and less about practical action to make people's lives better.

His amendment, which was passed, retained Swinney's statement but added that efforts should be stepped up to tackle child poverty.

During the debate, Marra said there had "always been a route to another referendum".

That route was to "build a consensus â the settled will of the Scottish people â and make it overwhelming".

But he said he believed Scotland "can be a fairer and stronger nation without being a separate state".

He added: "I don't believe we have to risk our currency, our defence, our markets and our budgets to deliver a more equal and just Scotland."

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the SNP should accept the result of the "once in a generation" 2014 referendum - which saw Scotland vote by 55% to 45% to remain part of the UK.

"The SNP say that Scotland should decide. We did decide, more than two million Scots said no, and thank goodness for that," he said.

Swinney insisted that a simple majority of pro-independence MSPs represented a mandate for a referendum.

"My party believes it is for the people of Scotland to decide when there is an independence referendum."

Saying that Scotland needs the "fresh start" of independence, he told MSPs the "fundamental right to decide our nation's future remains".

Swinney also raised the demographic change in Scotland since the last independence referendum.

He claimed that by 2029 there would be more than one million people in Scotland who did not have the opportunity to vote because of their age, and by 2030 the youngest voters would not even have been born in 2014.

He added that Scotland's place in the UK and the world "had changed beyond recognition" after Brexit.

News.title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies aged 67
News.content:
British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness.

After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later.

As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict.

Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter".

The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster.

In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC."

In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle.

Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said.

In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia.

He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015.

News.title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
News.content:
The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek a rapid review of their care if they want.

It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule.

Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being taken on board.

The nationwide expansion should be complete by March 2028, after a trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out in all inpatient wards.

Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern.

News.title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe suspends production at key UK plants blaming high gas prices
News.content:
Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe's industrial giant Ineos is pausing production at its three plants in Hull, blaming high UK gas prices.

The firm said gas prices in the UK are twelve times higher than in the US, and eight times more expensive than the coal-based processes used by Chinese competitors.

Sir Jim said: "We are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe, but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete."

Ineos Acetyls, part of the Ineos Group, is the only European producer of key chemicals used in a wide range of products from food and medicines to explosives. Gas is a key ingredient in production.

Ineos said the move will affect up to 1,000 of its staff, of whom 245 work directly at the site.

But the BBC understands workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from the US at lower prices - which could take up to a year - or waits for gas prices to go down.

Ineos is asking governments in the UK and the EU - where most of its products are exported to - to put in tariff protections against Chinese products.

Two plants on the site have already been turned off, and the third will follow in coming days.

One plant makes acetic acid, which is used in vinegar, paint and glue. Another makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin, and the third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and for decaffeinating tea and coffee.

The disruption of supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran has pushed up prices around the world.

The wholesale price of natural gas â used for heating homes and generating electricity â has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

Sir Jim said the current government's energy policy was "economic vandalism on an industrial scale".

Ineos says that its plants in Humberside are "among the most efficient in the world", producing materials with half the carbon footprint of US rivals, and only one eighth the footprint of Chinese equivalents.

It's the second time in less than a week that Sir Jim, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, has heavily criticised government policy.

He told BBC News last week that he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide", which he blamed on high taxes and high immigration.

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said it would be a "concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families".

A spokesperson said: "We've taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including Â£350 million for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis.

"We've also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our Supercharger and British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive."

Ineos Acetyls company cut a fifth of its workforce last year, citing high energy costs and "dirt-cheap" competition from China. It called for tariffs - or taxes on imports - to protect the industry.

News.title: Inquest opens into 'Putney Pusher' suspect's death
News.content:
A man suspected of knocking a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge was found dead by his brother-in-law after missing a family meal, his inquest has heard.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick on 15 September, West London Coroner's Court was told.

He had been arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident of May 2017, when a woman was shoved into the road by a jogger. His family say he was not involved.

Opening and adjourning the inquest, West London coroner Melanie Lee said she had been told of a referral to the Independent Office of Police Conduct and was suspending the hearing pending the outcome of its inquiry.

News.title: US is no longer the world’s ‘anchor’ but countries can still make a difference, David Miliband tells The Independent’s Climate 100 event
News.content:

America is no longer the “anchor” of the global system following its “severe” foreign aid cuts - but improving the lives of the world’s most vulnerable people is still “a solvable problem,” David Miliband, CEO of the International Rescue Committee, told The Independent Tuesday.

Miliband, the former U.K. foreign secretary who has led one of the world’s largest humanitarian groups for more than a decade, is among one hundred leaders, business titans, scientists and activists, and others, honored on The Independent’s third annual Climate 100 List.

The list, celebrating a diverse group tackling the climate crisis, was launched Tuesday during New York Climate Week, which coincides with the gathering of the United Nations General Assembly in the city. Others who made the list include environmental lawyer and activist Erin Brockovich, Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson, Swedish campaigner Greta Thunberg and Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist Bill Gates.

“I was brought up to believe if you can make a difference, you should, and if you don't, it's a waste. Who wants to waste our time here? It's a short time, so let's make the most of it,” Miliband, who gave the keynote address, later told The Independent’s Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig during a Q&A session.

Miliband oversees the IRC’s $1.1 billion-operations in more than 40 countries which have been shattered by conflict, hunger crises and climate impacts such as drought and flooding. The organization was co-founded by Albert Einstein during the Second World War to help refugees fleeing Nazi Germany.

open image in gallery David Miliband was the keynote speaker at The Independent’s third annual Climate 100 event, which celebrates diverse leaders tackling the climate crisis ( Juan M Soria )

Greig praised Miliband’s “personal, practical and political antennae, and dedication to public service” and noted his background as the son and grandson of Holocaust survivors.

Miliband addressed the crowd for around 30 minutes on the IRC’s work, saying the twin and overlapping perils of war and climate change are breaking records. And while the world has more resources and is more connected than ever, political will, financial investment and media attention have “vanished.”

He highlighted the Trump administration’s removal of $60 billion funding for the U.S. Agency for International Development last year - 1 percent of the U.S. budget - and how it had cost 700,000 lives as a direct result. A separate analysis, from The Rockefeller Foundation, has projected millions more could die by 2030, he noted.

“The U.S. was the anchor of the global aid system. It paid about a third of total contribution,” Miliband said, noting that the U.K., Germany, and France also cut their foreign aid but the European Union had not.

He continued: “There's an argument for more burden sharing, for more responsibility sharing ... but the consequences of the reductions are very severe.”

Miliband also spoke of “design failure” in the global aid system where funding often arrives too late.

open image in gallery The Independent’s Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig, left, listens as International Rescue Committee chief executive David Miliband speaks on September 22, 2026, in New York City ( Juan M Soria )

“The system waits for livestock to rot, children to starve, societies to collapse before launching a single emergency appeal. It's horrifying to me,” he said. In 2010 in Somalia, around a quarter of a million people died before famine was even declared, he noted.

“Even 24 hours of warning before a storm or a heatwave can reduce lost lives and resources by around 30 percent,” Miliband said.

Also writing today in The Independent, Miliband said there had previously been a fear that discussing adapting to the effects of climate change meant going soft on preventing it.

“But today, the failures and limits of mitigation mean we have no choice but to seek urgent mitigation and adaptation at the same time,” he wrote.

Even with current efforts, climate change is altering the environment in which politics, economics and conflict operate, Miliband told attendees. That’s been the case in drought-ravaged Somalia, too, where armed militias restrict access to water to control communities, he explained.

open image in gallery Miliband speaks to Climate 100 event attendees on September 22, 2026, in New York City. He said that the countries in need for climate adaptation receive the least support ( Juan M Soria )

Still, media coverage on the climate crisis in recent months has focused on the need for air conditioning during soaring European heatwaves rather than food insecurity in Somalia, or drought in Afghanistan, he said.

“The countries with the greatest need for adaptation, receive the least support for adaptation,” said Miliband. “In that way, the international system is rigged against them.”

Miliband pointed out that 65 wars are happening around the world right now, with the “top humanitarian crisis” in Sudan.

“The danger that we fear is that we're going into a syndrome of forever wars, because the number of wars that finish is much smaller than the number of wars that start,” he said.

open image in gallery A mother weighs her malnourished child in a nutrition center run by the International Rescue Committee in Panthau, South Sudan, in May 2017. Sudan is where Miliband says the ‘top humanitarian crisis’ in the world is underway ( AFP/Getty )

Later in the event, Bel Trew, The Independent’s award-winning Chief International Correspondent, spoke to the U.S.’s ongoing war with Iran and what would be its lasting impacts.

“We will have a food crisis off the back of that fact that there was interruption to fertilizers right now,” Trew, who recently reported from Sudan, said during a conversation with David Callaway, founder of analysis group Callaway Climate Insights. “We are not seeing the impact on our lives in the full amount. That won’t happen for another year.”

When asked by an audience member how he remained hopeful in the face of such steep challenges, Miliband shared words of wisdom he had heard recently from former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern.

“She said, ‘In New Zealand, we say nothing's too small,’” he said. “I thought that was really quite inspiring in the way that it says, ‘Look, stop moaning, do something.’”

Kat Dennings has recalled pushing back on an uncomfortable 2 Broke Girls scene in which she was meant to wear only a bra.

The actor looked back on the scene in a new TikTok video, explaining that she approached showrunner Michael Patrick King and asked if they could wear clothes in the scene instead.

“At the beginning of 2 Broke Girls, this must have been season 1 or 2, we had a table read,” Dennings recalled in a TikTok shared with her 1.5 million followers.

She explained: “In one of those episodes, there was a scene where Max (Dennings) and Caroline (Beth Behrs) are just wearing bras. They were just wearing bras and they were running around in the apartment set. The scene was just us wearing bras.”

Dennings, who starred in the sitcom during its run from 2011 to 2017, said she decided to push back despite not having much “pull” to make decisions on set at that time.

open image in gallery Kat Dennings has recalled pushing back on an uncomfortable ‘2 Broke Girls’ scene in which she was meant to wear only a bra ( CBS/Warner Bros. )

“After the table read, I went over to showrunner Michael Patrick King and said, ‘I’m gonna need you to take out the bra scene, or have us wearing clothes during the scene,’” Dennings claimed.

The actor claimed King initially pushed back, telling her, “‘No, I mean, this is the scene.’ And I said, ‘You don’t pay me enough for a bra scene.’ And sure enough the bra scene was gone. Never underestimate yourself, is the moral of the story.”

She concluded: “They weren’t paying me enough... although I don’t think anyone could.”

The Independent has reached out to representatives for King, Warner Bros. Television and CBS for comment.

2 Broke Girls was co-created by King and comedian Whitney Cummings. It followed two waitresses from different backgrounds working in a diner.

Dennings has previously spoken about the challenges she has faced in her career, particularly the criticism she faced for her appearance as a child actor.

Last year, she reflected on the “extremely negative feedback” she received from casting directors via her agent when she was a child actor.

open image in gallery Kat Dennings starred in the sitcom during its run from 2011 to 2017 ( Getty )

Speaking to People, the Shifting Gears actor said she remembered being told she wasn’t pretty enough and “fat” when she was 12.

“It was pretty crazy thinking about it. I’m like: "How can anyone say that about a little kid? This is insane.”

She explained: “I was 12. I’d go into an audition and I’d do it, and my manager would call me and I’d be like: “How’d it go?" And they’d be like: ‘Well, they thought you weren’t pretty enough and you’re fat.’”

At 14, she landed a role in an episode of Sex and The City called “Hot Child in the City” in 2000, in which she played a wealthy kid who hires Samantha Jones (Kim Cattrall) to plan her bat mitzvah party.

She had previously told The View about how the role changed her career, saying that although she didn’t know what it was about, she knew how huge the show was.

“I auditioned for it. I was like, ‘What a weird show. What a weird title. And then on the way home, on the train, we saw a building — like, a Sex and The City billboard across the whole building,” she said on the talk show.

CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss’ overhaul of 60 Minutes continues to face challenges as the revamped show saw a big drop in viewers for its second week.

The revered news program had 6.5 million total viewers Sunday, an 18 percent drop from the first episode of the season, which had about 7.94 million viewers, according to preliminary Nielsen numbers, cited by the Daily Beast.

Of those viewers, only 1.1 million were in the key 25-54 demographic, marking a 30 percent drop-off from the season premiere.

The most recent episode, which featured a heavily promoted interview with Patrick Clancy, reportedly performed slightly better than last season’s second episode however.

The Independent has reached out to Nielsen and CBS News for comment.

open image in gallery The most recent episode of 60 Minutes garnered 6.5 million viewers — an 18 percent drop from the first episode of the season ( Getty )

The show’s fall in ratings follows a tumultuous few months at CBS News, after billionaire David Ellison acquired Paramount — CBS News’s parent company — and appointed Weiss, a conservative columnist, as editor-in-chief last October.

After taking the job, Weiss promptly ousted several veteran 60 Minutes correspondents, including Scott Pelley and Cecilia Vega. Another, Sharyn Alfonsi, left after her contract expired.

Weiss, who came into the role with no prior broadcast experience, has also been accused by critics of dictating that the network’s news coverage be more favorable toward the Trump administration and Israel, claims that she has denied.

In July, CBS News announced a slate of new hires to fill the vacancies created by those departures.

“An exceptional lineup of journalists will be joining 60 Minutes, carrying on its tradition of fearless, independent and impartial reporting,” Nick Bilton, the show’s new executive producer, wrote in a July 28 memo shared on X. “I can't wait for them to get started.”

open image in gallery CBS News has seen a staffing shakeup since Bari Weiss was appointed as editor-in-chief last October ( Getty )

The appointments included Ross Douthat, a conservative New York Times opinion columnist and podcaster, and Norah O’Donnell, a CBS News senior correspondent.

For Sunday’s episode, Clancy was interviewed by Douthat, while O’Donnell reported on tensions in Texas over the creation of AI data centers.

Ahead of the premiere, Weiss was reportedly given a “blank check” to promote the revamped program, according to Puck News.

“Sources familiar with the plans say that CBS will blanket the airwaves and major markets with a multipronged, cross-platform campaign to emphasize the show’s new look and feel and commitment to its 60-year legacy,” the outlet reported in August.

News.content:
