Sports.title: Arteta agrees new Arsenal contract
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has agreed a new deal to extend his stay at Arsenal.

The 44-year-old's existing contract with the Premier League champions, signed in September 2024, was due to expire next summer.

But the Spaniard, who was appointed in 2019, has committed his future to the club and confirmation of his new agreement is expected during this international break.

When asked about his contract situation ahead of Arsenal's trip to Brighton on Saturday, Arteta said: "I think we are all very much aligned; whenever the time is right, we'll get that done. There is nothing to be concerned about.

"I think we both have the same ambition and the same will. So whenever we have time, we'll get that resolved."

Arteta has transformed Arsenal's fortunes during his tenure and guided the club to their first Premier League title in 22 years last season following three straight second-place finishes.

He also led the Gunners to only their second Champions League final, which they lost on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain. He has previously won an FA Cup and three Community Shields.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says he and the club are very much aligned when it comes to signing a new contract with the club.

'Arteta's new deal agreed but not signed'

Analysis by Sky Sports News' Gary Cotterill:

"It's not signed yet. Officially, the club are not saying it has been agreed, but our understanding is that an agreement has been in place for a couple of weeks.

"Mikel Arteta alluded to that on Friday when I asked him about it. He said they are aligned and in agreement.

"So, I believe the deal is agreed. It's now a case of sorting the formalities, sitting down and signing the contract.

"I expect that to happen during the next international break, potentially within the next two weeks.

"When he signed his current contract two years ago, that was also completed during the international break, on September 12.

"He tends to compartmentalise things. He has a break, then turns his attention to his future.

"The agreement has been in place for weeks. The only thing left now is to get the contract signed and make the announcement. The full details of the deal should follow in the coming weeks."

Sports.title: Jacks stars as England beat Sri Lanka in first ODI
Sports.content:
England continued their white-ball dominance over Sri Lanka as an 89-run victory in the first ODI in Durham saw them take a 1-0 lead in the three-match series.

Will Jacks starred with bat and ball, hitting an handy 46 not out off 47 balls before completing a career-best 5-22 to wrap up the Sri Lankan tail.

Captain Harry Brook (67 off 69 balls) top-scored after electing to bat at the toss but a middle order wobble inspired by debutant Sachindu Colombage (3-44) restricted England to 265 in 48.1 overs.

England took steady wickets to hamper Sri Lanka's pursuit of 266 before Jacks struck three times in the final over as the tourists were bowled out for 176 in 37 overs.

Score summary - England vs Sri Lanka, first ODI, Durham England 265 in 48.1 overs (elected to bat): Harry Brook (67 off 69 balls), Will Jacks (46 off 47), Joe Root (44 off 52); Sachindu Colombage (3-44), Asitha Fernando (3-53) Sri Lanka 176 all out in 37 overs (chasing 266):Dunith Wellalage (45 off 36 balls), Kusal Mendis (42 off 60), Pathum Nissanka (27 off 37); Will Jacks (5-22), Jamie Overton (2-21)

England take ODI series lead over Sri Lanka

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sri Lankan bowler Avishka Fernando took the first wicket of the ODI match against England.

England's decision to bat first after winning the toss was immediately tested when Tom Banton fell to a jaffa from Asitha Fernando, the delivery nipping back to clip the bail on top of off stump.

The hosts weathered the early setback, with Joe Root sharing 50-run partnerships with Ben Duckett and Harry Brook to steer England to 135-2 after Duckett was trapped lbw by Dunith Wellalage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Joe Root was bowled out by Sachindu Colombage on his debut during the ODI match between England and Sri Lanka.

Root's 68-run stand with Brook was ended when he was deceived and bowled by the mystery spin of debutant Colombage, six runs short of his half-century.

The dismissal of England captain Brook, caught off the bowling of Dushmantha Chameera after reaching a seventh ODI century in 49 balls, sparked a middle-order collapse.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rehan Ahmed was run out after a fantastic piece of fielding by Sri Lanka during their ODI match against England.

Jos Buttler was trapped lbw before Rehan Ahmed was run out by a superb direct hit from Charith Asalanka, while Jamie Overton, Gus Atkinson and Jofra Archer were all bowled by Colombage, Dilshan Madushanka and Fernando respectively, as England lost six wickets for 65 runs in 15.5 overs.

Will Jacks led England's resistance with a handy unbeaten 46 from 47 balls, including an explosive 18 in the 48th over as the hosts passed the 250-run mark. But the late salvo was cut short when Fernando produced a reverse-swinging yorker to clean up Josh Tongue.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sachindu Colombage took three wickets for Sri Lanka during their ODI match against England.

Sri Lanka negotiated the first five overs of their chase of 266 without alarm before Kamindu Mendis holed out to Duckett at short midwicket off Atkinson.

Tongue then accounted for Sri Lanka's other opener, inducing an edge through to wicketkeeper Buttler as the tourists slipped to 51-2.

Banton produced a stunning, sharp catch at extra cover to dismiss the driving Pavan Rathnayake, before Jacks trapped a sweeping Asalanka lbw three balls later to leave Sri Lanka 85-4 and in deep trouble.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Overton took a fantastic wicket during the England and Sri Lanka ODI.

Overton struck again three overs later, luring Janith Liyanage into a waft outside off as he edged behind to leave Sri Lanka 100-5.

The writing was on the wall when captain Kusal Mendis was trapped lbw by Jacks, leaving Sri Lanka floundering at 105-6, before their plight was compounded when Colombage suffered the same fate against Rehan Ahmed.

Wellalage led the Sri Lanka fightback, plundering 17 from an Ahmed over, and his 42-run partnership with Chameera revived hopes at 133-7.

However, Jacks extinguished those hopes by removing Wellalage, Fernando and Madushanka in a decisive final over.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Will Jacks took five wickets during England's win against Sri Lanka in the first ODI.

Jacks: A great all-round game

Player of the match Will Jacks (46no off 47) and 5-22 in 7 overs:

"It was a really good all-round performance from the team there.

"I am getting used to this role now. It is more about playing the situation and playing what is out there.

"Having batted on it and what it was like, I knew I was going to play a decent role.

"No matter the time, you have got to do your best."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England's Will Jacks reflected on a brilliant bowling display during the first ODI against Sri Lanka

Brook: Our communication was on point

England captain Harry Brook:

"It wasn't the easiest of surfaces but we want to be a team that can adapt to conditions. We did that well today.

"We knew exactly what we were going to do with the ball out there and we did that beautifully.

"I think the clarity we went out into the field with was outstanding. We communicated very well."

Sports.title: Celtic CEO backs O’Neill despite 'painful' week
Sports.content:
Celtic chief executive Michael Nicholson has backed manager Martin O’Neill despite a "painful" week.

The Parkhead club lost twice to Rangers - in the League Cup quarter-finals and Scottish Premiership - plus at home to Ferencvaros in their Europa League opener.

It follows last month's collapse against LASK in their Champions League play-off, losing the tie on aggregate despite leading 4-0 at one stage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Celtic's defeat at home to Rangers in the Scottish Premiership

Following the second of those Old Firm defeats, O'Neill said he was going to reflect on his future and admitted "it might be time to wrap it up".

While Nicholson has admitted "the losses in the last week have been painful for us all", he insists the club "will now come together and support Martin and the players, as we focus our efforts on achieving success domestically and in the Europa League."

Image: Celtic chief executive Michael Nicholson (centre) admits it has been a "painful" week for the club

O'Neill's return to Celtic last October - 20 years after his first spell as manager - came following the resignation of Brendan Rodgers.

Another spell as interim boss followed weeks later as Wilfried Nancy was sacked after a dismal 33-day tenure.

Nicholson added that the club "owe a debt of gratitude" to O'Neill and his management team for stepping in twice last season, and says the club were "delighted" he agreed to return on a permanent basis this summer.

Celtic loss revealed amid transfer revelation

Image: Celtic spent around £17m on Camilo Duran (left) and Kasper Hogh

The Celtic board have faced criticism from supporters over its recruitment strategy.

Figures in the report reveal £31.7m was spent on the likes of record signing Kasper Hogh, plus Camilo Duran, Mika Baur, Haïssem Hassan and others, with Nicholson adding the club worked with O'Neill over transfers.

However, that period is not covered in the report that highlights a post-tax loss of £4.8m, a stark contrast to the £33.9m profit 12 months prior.

Chairman Brian Wilson's statement highlighted a lack of Champions League football, increased wages and a smaller profit in player trading as some of the reasons why.

Celtic did end the year until June 2026 with £66.4m in the bank.

The longer international break - with four Nations League matches - gives the new boss more time with his squad as he looks to make an impact as Steve Clarke's successor.

"We have plenty of experience in the team, there are some new faces and young lads, and I think we have a good mix," Pocognoli told Sky Sports News.

"We need to make sure that the balance stays right, and to keep what makes the Scotland team really strong, it was the cohesion and really proper DNA in the team, and this needs to stay.

"The needed change was at this moment, because we follow the timelines, and the change is just about the things that we want to create on the pitch.

The squad then fly to North Macedonia on October 3 before returning to Glasgow to face Slovenia again on October 6.

Scotland were demoted from Nations League A after a play-off defeat by Greece last year and return to the second tier for this year's competition.

"There are many ways to be successful," the 39-year-old added.

"For me, in the Nations League, it's to stay competitive and try to be as much as possible higher in the ranking to go to League A.

"But just to recognise some principles on the pitch, recognise who are the leaders on the pitch, see some young lads playing, see team cohesion on the pitch.

Sports.title: Dual Champion Hurdle winner Hurricane Fly dies aged 22
Sports.content:
Hurricane Fly, the Willie Mullins-trained dual Champion Hurdle winner, has died at the age of 22.

The son of Montjeu proved himself one of the greats of recent National Hunt history, winning the Champion Hurdle at Cheltenham in 2011 and 2013 and the Irish Champion Hurdle five times on the spin between 2011 and 2015.

In total Hurricane Fly won a record breaking 22 Grade One races. He was retired in 2015 after a nine-year career to spend his days alongside other equine greats such as Faugheen, Hardy Eustace and Beef Or Salmon at the Irish National Stud.

Mullins described the superstar hurdler as "awesome" and "one of the biggest legends" to pass through his Closutton yard. Regular jockey Ruby Walsh simply labelled him "the perfect horse" and the best jumper of a hurdle he ever rode.

Image: Ruby Walsh and trainer Willie Mullins with Hurricane Fly in the parade ring after winning the Stanjames.com Morgiana Hurdle

"He won a record-breaking 22 Grade One races, which was remarkable," Mullins told www.sportinglife.com. "He's one of the greatest horses to ever come through our stable. He was a horse who loved a battle and was so brave.

"Ruby was able to stand back anywhere on him and he'd answer. He just put his rivals into trouble. He was such a proper horse. He was awesome, one of the biggest legends ever to come through Closutton."

Walsh, who twice scaled the heights at the Festival on his former partner, said: "Hurricane Fly was a brilliant racehorse but was without doubt the best jumper of a hurdle I ever rode.

"He was incredible, his accuracy, his bravery, the speed at which he could move his feet. He was bombproof, you could ride him down to hurdles like they weren't there because he was going to do the right thing every time.

"He had the engine to go with it. He had speed, class, he stayed and was in my eyes, for a little horse, the perfect horse."

Mullins admitted he paid a visit to see his former stable star and had a chance to say his goodbyes.

"I was lucky enough to visit him today just before the end and met Gail (Carlisle, stable lass) who had popped over to see him as well as she'd heard the news. It was very poignant and we were able to say our goodbyes.

"It's especially poignant following so shortly after the passing of his co-owner Frank Boyd and I'm thinking of his family and George Creighton's family too at this time. Hurricane Fly provided us all with so many wonderful days and memories."

The owners issued a statement which read: "The Boyd and Creighton families are deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Hurricane Fly. He provided us with so many great days and long lasting memories.

"We would like to thank Willie Mullins, Gail Carlisle, Harold Kirk and all the staff at Closutton, as well as the National Stud who provided him with such a happy retirement."

Sports.title: Wamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern Munich
Sports.content:
Manchester City produced a gutsy performance to fight back from 2-0 down and earn a draw away to Bayern Munich. A tough first half saw José Barcala’s side take the lead through Giulia Gwinn before a Kerstin Casparij own goal doubled their lead. But goals from Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser saw the visitors take home a hard-earned point.

It was always going to be a challenging start for the English champions against a Bayern team who have historically thrived in the league phase of this competition. Barcala’s side came into this encounter unbeaten in their last 15 group-stage matches and having made a run to the semi-finals last season that, according to Gwinn, had left them “even hungrier and eager for more”. Not only that but the German outfit have kicked off the defence of their Frauen-Bundesliga title in stunning fashion, with five wins from five leaving them two points clear at the top of the table.

Andrée Jeglertz’s side themselves had arrived in Germany full of confidence after an equally impressive start to their domestic campaign. Their 4-2 win over Liverpool on Friday night had been a sign of their mettle, finding a way to win despite not being at their best. European football, however, presents a different test altogether and they came into the competition with plenty of unknowns. How would they measure up against seasoned participants after a year out of the competition? Could their relatively small squad juggle the load of European football and domestic challenges despite the absence of the likes of Vivianne Miedema and Rebecca Knaak through injury?

Reality hit in a first half that saw a refreshed Bayern take control of proceedings. Barcala had been able to make five changes to his starting XI, having completely rested Klara Bühl and Gwinn against Köln on Saturday, and they looked full of energy.

Ballon d’Or nominee Bühl immediately stretched every sinew of City’s fragile-looking defence with her pace and guile. The 25-year-old was at the heart of everything Bayern created early on, firing a volley wide before setting up the equally prolific Pernille Harder for a half chance.

It did not come as a surprise, therefore, that the hosts broke the deadlock with just 11 minutes on the clock. It was a move that cut through the heart of Manchester City as Linda Dallmann broke through central midfield to send Gwinn on her way down the right. The full-back saw the pitch open up in front of her, dispatching a cool finish past Ayaka Yamashita in the City goal.

View image in fullscreen Giulia Gwinn reacts after opening the scoring. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP

It was moment that saw the 4,291-strong crowd raise the decibel level, energised by the domination of their team and, perhaps also, the Oktoberfest celebrations. This was Bayern’s first outing at Sportpark Unterhaching and the raucous crowd seemed to settle in straight away at their new home.

The pressure on City continued as the game progressed. Struggling to find any space in possession, they were guilty of playing into Bayern’s hands, channelling their play centrally rather than allowing Lauren Hemp and Aoba Fujino to try to exploit the width. Things got worse when an unwitting Casparij diverted a dangerous Harder cross into her own net to double the score.

This City side are made of stern stuff, however, and Jeglertz’s side were handed a lifeline just before the break, albeit in controversial fashion. As a blue smoke flare blazed on the pitch, the referee allowed play to continue as Casparij burst forward down the right. Her ball in eventually fell to a free Mead to tap home.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Bayern Munich and Manchester City try to stay focused despite a flare on the pitch. Photograph: Michaela Stache/AFP/Getty Images

The visitors’ comeback continued in the second half as the game ebbed and flowed in a much more even affair. They should have had an equaliser when Fujino was felled in the box by Ena Mahmutovic only for the goalkeeper to step up to save the subsequent spot kick from Khadija Shaw.

Jeglertz rang the changes with Mary Fowler replacing a struggling Shaw and Laura Blindkilde Brown coming into central midfield. Despite the hosts still looking potent going forward, City could sense that the tide was shifting and found an equaliser with four minutes to play. Wamser, signed from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer, arrived on the edge of the box to rifle home a finish on her return to Germany.

The substitute Edna Imade had two big chances to win it for the hosts late on but the visitors held strong to head back home with a valuable point. With one of their most difficult games out of the way, they face Real Madrid next week in Manchester with a chance of making another statement on the European stage.

Sports.title: Will anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacle
Sports.content:
For Gianni Infantino there is no international break. The Fifa president is widely expected to make an appearance at the United Nations general assembly this week in New York, where he will lobby heads of state for their federations’ support as he continues his campaign to be re-elected next year.

Infantino has not been idle during the lull since Fifa abandoned its World Cup sell-off plan last month, instead crisscrossing the globe on a private jet provided by Qatar Airways as part of its sponsorship deal with world football’s governing body.

From his strongholds in Doha, Rabat and Miami, Infantino has also visited Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Kyrgyzstan and various other countries, his trips often coinciding with the approval of funding for development projects worth millions of dollars. His would-be opponents have been conspicuous by their silence.

Whether Qatar Airways facilitating Infantino’s re-election campaign should be considered legitimate Fifa presidential business is a moot point, which neatly encapsulates the huge incumbency bias that will benefit Infantino if a vote takes place at the Fifa congress in March. That ballot appears to be in doubt, with multiple sources involved in the push to remove Infantino telling the Guardian they are running out of hope of finding a candidate to beat him.

Although dozens of the 200 member associations that had submitted letters of endorsement for Infantino withdrew them after the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise sale plan in July, the prevailing view is that the silent majority remain steadfastly behind him.

A meeting with the Caribbean Football Union, where funding projects were approved, may have splintered the vote at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and there are increasing concerns that the European alliance may not be watertight.

“As long as Gianni is running, I don’t think anyone else will raise their hand,” one source said. “They would effectively be running against Fifa the institution. Fifa declared his candidacy, provides staff, aeroplanes and cars, even a personal video team.

“If he doesn’t step down before March, the election will not be contested. Uefa and others could stage a boycott so the victory would be tainted, but Gianni will win a clear majority of whoever shows up.”

Infantino first declared at the April congress in Vancouver his intention to seek a fourth and final term of office. Fifa statutes limit presidents to three full terms but under a recent change he will be permitted a fourth because his first term lasted three years, rather than the usual four, after his 2016 election to replace the disgraced Sepp Blatter.

The 56-year-old reasserted his intention to stand after attending the first match of the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland a fortnight ago. That came via a statement issued by Fifa’s media team.

As it stands Infantino does not have an opponent, despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to go. Beyond the obvious difficulties of taking on an incumbent who controls the machinery of office and funding budgets – the last Fifa president beaten at the ballot box was Sir Stanley Rous in 1974 – there are specific reasons why none of the would-be candidates have declared.

The most credible challenger is regarded as Concacaf’s president, Victor Montagliani, but the Canadian is committed to standing for re-election at his confederation, and the vote is due to take place in February. Standing in both elections is not regarded as feasible, and Montagliani is understandably reluctant to walk away from Concacaf in favour of fighting a potentially losing battle against Infantino.

View image in fullscreen Victor Montagliani (right), president of Concacaf, is reluctant to walk away from his current role but would be the most credible challenger to Infantino. Photograph: Elizabeth Ruiz Ruiz/Getty Images

The AFC president, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, was beaten by Infantino in the 2016 election, the only time Infantino has faced an electoral opponent, and is further hamstrung by the fact that his confederation’s main powers, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are backing Infantino. Qatar’s position would also appear to rule out a challenge from Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, and an openly European move led by Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin, would have no chance of success. Ceferin, in any case, has his own presidential contest in March to focus on.

To compound the difficulties for Infantino’s would-be challengers, any election would be a secret ballot, making any promises from member associations during the campaign period all but worthless. As a result, Uefa is focusing most of its efforts on legal avenues to remove Infantino, accusing him of “criminal mismanagement” in a 56-page document lodged with US state courts in New York, Miami and Colorado last month seeking the disclosure of all documents relating to FFE.

Fifa responded strongly the week after Uefa made its legal complaint, filing a response in New York in which it sought to block the discovery process. Its submission accused Uefa of mounting a smear campaign against Infantino in the absence of any evidence of wrongdoing.

Fifa’s submission said: “Uefa’s application suffers from a fundamental defect: Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate.

“While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of Uefa’s smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership.”

Although there is widespread confidence that at least one of the three jurisdictions will grant discovery, the process grants Fifa the right of appeal, so there is little prospect of new material being made public before the 18 November deadline for presidential candidates to come forward.

An initial decision from the courts is expected next month, but an appeal from the losing party appears inevitable whatever the outcome.

“The issue with discovery is that it takes a long time,” a source said. “It’s likely to run beyond the date of the election in March. If the process is under way by then, Fifa congress could decide to wait until we find out what the courts discover and postpone the election. But there would still have to be a vote on that.”

Uefa’s not-so-secret hope is that the discovery process finds evidence that FFE was deliberately undervalued at $20bn (£15bn) to provide a guaranteed future windfall for Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, which had seemingly agreed to pay $4.2bn for 21% of the new commercial venture, giving it a significant share of future Fifa revenues.

Thrive subsequently bought 20% of the LA Lakers last month as part of a larger transaction with the former Disney chief executive Bob Iger that valued the NBA franchise at $12.5bn, a deal that has further highlighted Infantino’s valuation of the World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Fifa’s revenues for the four years to 2026 were $15bn, a figure projected to grow to $18bn over the next four-year cycle owing to larger broadcast deals, without accounting for any expansion of the World Cup and Club World Cup, which remains on the agenda.

A corporate fraud lawyer said that undervaluing FFE could potentially constitute a criminal offence by Fifa, a case Uefa would take to the Swiss courts. “If you’re doing a deal that is way off market then you are deceiving the stakeholders, in this case the member associations,” the legal source said. “That is criminal. If Uefa has a criminal case that’s where it will be. It’s about how the valuation was done, by whom, and what conflicts were there.

“All of that should come out during disclosure. If beyond that there were personal deals being struck on the side, that could also be criminal. All those details should be disclosed.”

Beyond the $20bn valuation, the identity of the would-be investors and Fifa’s claim that it would retain control over governance, very little has been made public about the development of FFE, with a sales deck produced by the US bank JP Morgan containing no details of a tender process, voting rights or future exit terms. A senior investment banker who has been involved in similar deals said it is inconceivable such details were not agreed before Thrive agreed to commit $4bn, albeit much of the funding was due from other investors.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino before the World Cup final. Photograph: Pablo Morano/BSR Agency/Getty Images

“I don’t think Thrive was going to be involved with Fifa for the next 25 years,” they said. “This looks like a quick in-and-out play. The plan would have been to buy it low and sell it high. I think the investors saw an amazing deal.”

There is no evidence of any wrongdoing or criminality on the part of the any of the parties involved in the proposed FFE deal.

Thrive has revealed little about its intentions beyond a statement issued last month in which it presented FFE as a proposal to be voted on by Fifa’s members, rather than a done deal.

Significantly, however, it also expressed an element of regret at getting involved given the political backlash, which many within football have interpreted as an attempt to distance the firm from Infantino.

“It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination,” Thrive said. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved.”

Uefa and Concacaf, in particular, appear prepared to dig in for the long haul, despite concerns that Infantino will be re-elected. The two confederations are continuing to work together to develop a unified Nations League competition, revealed by the Guardian last month, and last week wrote a joint letter to Fifa demanding that it release funds from its $6bn reserves to fund an additional payment of at least $10m to each of its 211 member associations during the next four-year cycle.

Some sort of payment appears inevitable given Infantino promised to provide $20m more to the member associations via FFE, but Uefa and Concacaf are hoping Infantino does not accrue political and electoral credit for it.

Ceferin and Montagliani are expected to meet at next week’s general assembly of the European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, where Infantino may also make an appearance. Infantino addressed the EFC’s 900 members at last year’s EFC meeting in Rome, where his suggestion that more international tournaments should take place during European winters to accommodate the global south caused controversy, although that pales compared with his pronouncements and plans since.

Uefa has made one accommodation with Fifa by withdrawing its threat to boycott the Under-20 Women’s World Cup that finishes on Sunday, and Infantino has agreed to its demand to commission an external governance review, which he communicated in a letter to the member associations this week. Suggestions that this move could lead to a truce with Uefa are given short shrift by those close to the leadership.

Despite the electoral gloom, those agitating for change are also clinging to memories of the fate of Infantino’s predecessor, Blatter, who was forced to resign in 2015 amid an FBI corruption investigation days after winning a fifth term against Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan. Blatter himself has never been charged in relation to the investigation.

For those looking to remove Infantino, the presidential election is not necessarily the end of the process. “This is a fight to the death now and we have to keep going,” one source said.

“The fact that Gianni is the only guy running at the moment does not mean it’s over. Look what happened to Blatter. He was re-elected in May 2015, but was gone in June. Eventually the truth will come out.”

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta agrees contract extension expected to keep him at Arsenal until 2030
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season and could take his reign as the manager beyond a decade.

The three-year deal he signed in September 2024 expires at the end of this season and talks have been ongoing since May when Arsenal ended their long wait to be champions. Negotiations were put on hold during the summer transfer window but the Spaniard has reached a ­verbal agreement to extend his stay for a second time.

The length of the contract is unknown but it is understood Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, will commit his future for at least another three years. The 44-year-old is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City at the end of last season.

Arsenal have been keen to reward Arteta for transforming the club. His current contract is believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal will cement his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world.

As well as leading Arsenal to a first Premier League title since 2004, Arteta last season guided them to the Champions League final, which they lost to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout in Budapest. The club started this season with seven straight wins in all competitions before Saturday’s surprise 3-0 defeat at Brighton.

Arteta reiterated before that game that he was relaxed about his contract situation. “I think we are all very much aligned,” he said. “Whenever the time is right, we’ll get that done. There is nothing to be concerned about. I think we both have the same ambition and the same will.”

Arsenal are also keen to extend Declan Rice’s contract, the England midfielder having entered the final two years of his deal. It is understood the club have an option to extend it by 12 months but would like to agree new terms in line with their policy of securing Arteta’s most important players on long-term contracts.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Klopp, Xavi, Zidane, Mancini: big nations ready to unleash bigger dogs
Sports.content:
INTERNATIONAL SUPERSTARS

While Thomas Tuchel continues to gaslight his employers at the FA into believing he was in no way responsible for England’s comically shambolic semi-final exit at the hands of Argentina, not every head coach who underperformed at the Geopolitics World Cup is still in their job. A total of 17 different managers who took teams to North America have since left their roles, with safety-first’s Steve Clarke, failing-up’s Roberto Martínez and tyranny’s Marcelo Bielsa among them. In Europe, teams such as Portugal (Jorge Jesus), Croatia (Slaven Bilic), Scotland (Sébastien Pocognoli), Czechia (Santi Denia) and Belgium (Mark van Bommel) will go into the Nations League under new management, but it is towards the bigger dogs of the football pack where Football Daily wishes to turn today’s beady gaze.

Germany: Having been accused of using his role as a TV pundit to undermine Julian Nagelsmann during the GWC, it was no great shock to see Jürgen Klopp take over from the 39-year-old when he stepped down. Klopp immediately fired a volley across the bows of the German press pack and will begin his first role in international management with a trip to the Netherlands. Unlike his predecessor, the former Liverpool boss is unlikely to rock up to training on a skateboard and it will be intriguing to see how successfully he instils his ethos of heavy-metal football in a group of players he only gets into the rehearsal room three or four times a season. “This is the pinnacle, the absolute high point of my footballing career as coach,” he parped, raising sceptical eyebrows on Merseyside. “I will give everything I have got.”

Netherlands: Upon replacing Ronald Koeman, Xavi Hernández was eager to emphasise his deep connection with the Dutch. While it remains to be seen if the former Spanish midfield maestro is a bike-riding windmill enthusiast with a capacity for extreme bluntness, he was handed his Barcelona debut by Louis van Gaal and name-dropped club legends Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels during his unveiling. Third choice on a shortlist of four behind Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot, Xavi can at least sleep safe in the knowledge the Dutch FA considered him a slightly more glamorous candidate than Michael Reiziger, and will begin his international reign with a match against a fellow newbie. “I feel motivated because we are playing against Germany,” he cheered, before his opening game in Amsterdam. “So yeah, it’s a big challenge from the beginning, but I think we will be ready.”

Italy: Having suffered the indignity of failing to qualify for their third successive World Cup, Italian football suits didn’t so much go back to the drawing board, as back in time when it came to replacing Gennaro Gattuso. Roberto Mancini is back for his second spell in charge, having previously masterminded victory in the European Championship in 2021 and subsequent failure to get to the HRWC in 2022. “I believed that the best person to become head coach was ‌Roberto Mancini,” tooted FIGC top brass Giovanni Malagò, shortly after his organisation’s plot to install Andrea Pirlo in the role was foiled by the former midfielder’s commercial ties to a Russian betting firm. A famously patient people when it comes to their national football team, fans of the Azzurri are surely unlikely to get upset if early results against Belgium and Turkey don’t go their team’s way …

France: It was a matter of when, not if Zinedine Zidane took over the national team and despite his pedigree as a three-time Bigger Cup-winning coach of Real Madrid, he has extremely big boots to fill. After taking over from his former French water carrier, Didier Deschamps, Zizou played all the right notes. “I’ve been looking forward to this moment,” he cheered. “It’s a dream come true. The France national team has been the most beautiful thing that has ever happened to me. It’s a great adventure that I hope is just beginning.” Kylian Mbappé has already described the prospect of working under Zizou as being “like a film”. Its box-office success will almost certainly stand or fall on the chemistry – or lack of it – between two of French football’s most iconic leading men.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Will Unwin at 5.45pm (BST) for Women’s Bigger Cup updates on Bayern Munich 2-2 Manchester City.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Every time I see it, I’m cringing, I’m in disbelief. It’s horrible to watch back and to see what could have been. Thankfully I was fortunate I did manage to fall on to the floor at the right time, so nothing snapped as the roller went over me … I was able to get my left arm up and relieve some of the pressure, and then I was able to get my teammates around me who were able to lift it, and I was able to squeeze out but at that moment where it was crushing my left leg, it was quite terrifying, I must say” – Andros Townsend explains what it was like to be run over by that pitch roller in Thailand and just how much he thanks his lucky stars for not coming to more harm than suffering a few cuts and bruises.

RECOMMENDED LOOKING

It’s our man David Squires on … Big Sir Jim lamenting the decline of once-mighty empires.

View image in fullscreen Zing! Illustration: David Squires/The Guardian

double quotation mark Prize o’ the day to Barry Glendenning, surely, for mentioning Johnny Crumplin (football genius) in Monday’s Football Daily. As an Ipswich fan marooned in Sussex, I spent much of my teenage years at the Goldstone which, despite being a dump (I stood on the crumbling South Stand), held a certain magic for me. It still does, actually. Haven’t been to the Amex yet – hopeless nostalgia is undoubtedly a factor. The team weren’t much better than the ground for most of that time, but the 1987-88 promotion season was memorable. Garry Nelson was a bit special, Doug Rougvie had played under Fergie at Aberdeen and Gerry Armstrong had legendary status after *that* goal, but the rest of the team probably (and unfairly ) fall into the journeyman category. I loved them all. Keith Dublin dribbling his way into and then out of trouble, sleeves-up Kevin Bremner who grafted and worked the Albion into the promotion places, Deano (one of the Wilkins brothers) classy and, of course, Barry Lloyd, who never brought a sub on until the last four or five minutes, frustrating us beyond belief. And into this pantheon came teenage Johnny C who, to start with, was utterly hapless, hence the nickname football genius. Somehow, despite this, we took to him from the off and it was lovely to see how he grew into becoming an Albion legend in what were fallow years. Blimey, not sure where that all came from – you can probably tell I’m stuck out in the middle of the Fens on a slow-moving train. But thank you for bringing it all back to me!” – Jonathan Foulkes.

double quotation mark I know the powers that be have listened to Football Daily’s ‘Stop Football’ pleas and given us very little to do for the next three weeks but, as we are just five games in to the Premier League season, can everyone stop going on about the race for the Golden Boot and which team are going to bloody champions” – Nigel Sanders.

double quotation mark Judging by the photo of him sitting behind their ‘Life’s Good’ logo in yesterday’s Quote of the Day, LG could do a lot worse than appoint José Mourinho as a brand ambassador for their campaign. As football watchers have long known, he exudes the spirit of that exclamation from every single pore” – Andrew Parker.

double quotation mark So, Jonathan Wilson has a new book, about football in Eastern Europe, Behind the Curtain, while his take on Zidane as the new France manager will reveal the ‘wizard behind the curtain’. Brilliant effort from the subeditor and marketing team working in harmony” – Paul Vickers.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day prize goes to … Jonathan Foulkes, who wins a copy of Behind the Curtain by Big Website’s Jonathan Wilson. Sports.title: Branthwaite reveals brain study helped him conquer injuries and earn England call
Sports.content:
Jarrad Branthwaite has credited a “complex” rehabilitation programme in Germany, which analysed links between his injuries and his brain and movement, with his return to the England squad.

The Everton defender’s fine start to the season has been rewarded with a place in Thomas Tuchel’s squad for the Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia. If selected, it will be Branthwaite’s second appearance for the England senior side having been blighted by hamstring and groin problems in recent years.

The centre-half has been ever-present in the Premier League after being restricted to 10 appearances last season by repeated hamstring issues. In the search for a solution to his injury problems, Everton sent the 24-year-old to the MYOS sports and health clinic in Munich at the start of the summer. Branthwaite believes that was a turning point.

“I sat down with the club after the three or four times where I was picking up the injuries,” he said. “It was to look at the wider picture, look at the holistic approach of the body essentially. I went over there for three or four weeks working with a team alongside the club, just to assess different things, and hopefully that has helped. There were a lot of different things looked at like movement patterns, the brain; it was quite complex, but fingers crossed it has worked.”

Branthwaite was carried off in tears after sustaining another hamstring injury in the Merseyside derby defeat by Liverpool in April. The setback ended his season and his prospects of making a late play for the World Cup squad, and Everton’s form also plummeted in his absence.

“It is probably the worst thing as a footballer not to be on the pitch and I think when it keeps happening it is mentally tough because you are sort of doubting your body and going on the pitch wary of what is going to happen. I think now I am in a position where I got managed throughout the pre-season, managed my load well and hopefully I can stay on the pitch this season.”

Branthwaite made his England debut as a substitute in a win against Bosnia and Herzegovina in June 2024, and a recall was a target this season alongside a return to full fitness.

“I found out when I was having breakfast – it was a good start to the day,” the Everton defender said of his call-up last week. “It is a proud moment. Over the last season or so it has been a target of mine. When I have been out and not on the pitch, I wanted to get back playing and give myself the best possible chance to be in and around the England squad after missing such a lot of time.
