Brazilian diplomat Carlos Márcio Cozendey confirmed on September 16 that neither side had requested one, though an informal encounter of the kind held in September 2025 remains possible. Lula had said last week he intended to tell Trump directly not to interfere in the vote.

Trade tensions remain unresolved. Since July 22, certain Brazilian goods have paid an additional 25% under Section 301 of the US trade act, with exemptions including aircraft, coffee, beef and orange juice; a separate 12.5% forced-labour duty has applied since July 24, covering dozens of other economies as well. Brazil's trade ministry calculates that 23.1% of exports to the United States face the new duties, mostly cumulatively, for 37.5%. Brazil has held off on retaliation while negotiations continue, though Lula told CNN on Monday it could still invoke its reciprocity law if talks fail.

On the multilateral front, Lula said the UN is going through one of its most critical moments and that it “is failing” in its mission to prevent wars. “The feeling that moves me today is indignation,” he said, attributing the paralysis to the Security Council and the use of the veto by its permanent members, a practice Brazil has objected to since the first General Assembly in 1946. On the Middle East he said generations of Palestinians will carry the pain of the “genocide of women and children”, a characterisation contested in international legal debate, and criticised the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank. On Ukraine he said there would be “no winners on the battlefield”. He also called for regulation of large technology companies and artificial intelligence, and defended scientific evidence against climate disinformation.

World.title: Burnham says he raised the Falklands with Trump at their first meeting
World.content:
Burnham says he raised the Falklands with Trump at their first meeting

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 19:45 UTC Full article

“I think he's going to be a great prime minister. I think he's got a lot of assets on his side,” Trump said, adding that the United Kingdom “is a really special country”

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Tuesday that he raised the question of the Falklands with US President Donald Trump during their first meeting, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. “The Falklands we mentioned. And you were good enough to listen to us on those issues,” he told reporters. Trump made no public response on the archipelago.

The approach comes eleven days after the US president sidestepped, in Dublin, a question on whether the United States would come to Britain's aid in any future conflict over the islands, and after he told the BBC that he reviews every position. Several outlets have noted that those remarks, along with his comments favouring Irish unification, unsettled the British government.

The tone of the meeting was warm. “I think he's going to be a great prime minister. I think he's got a lot of assets on his side,” Trump said, adding that the United Kingdom “is a really special country” and that Washington is “with you all the way”. Burnham replied that the relationship “matters so much” to his country and that the two had established “a good connection” in earlier discussions. He also reminded Trump that Manchester, where he was mayor before entering Downing Street in July, is not a “town” as the president had described it, but “a great city”. “I don't hold it against you as the former mayor,” he joked.

It is their first face-to-face meeting; the two had spoken twice by telephone since Burnham took office. Trump had described him as “a nice guy”. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham had said Trump was not welcome in the city and that he would refuse to meet him.

The agenda covered Ukraine, the Middle East, trade, energy, immigration and Rolls-Royce, as Trump himself set out. Burnham was seeking interceptor missiles to bolster Ukraine's air defences ahead of winter, and ways to restore the movement of ships through the Strait of Hormuz, largely blocked since the start of the war with Iran in February, a closure that has driven up crude prices. “We're still ready to play our part in the Middle East in terms of helping you stop the conflict, open the strait,” the prime minister said, mentioning a request from Saudi Arabia and adding: “obviously, we're with you that Iran must never be a nuclear power”.

The United States has never taken a formal position on sovereignty over the archipelago, though it recognises British de facto administration and supported the 1982 military campaign. Argentina claims sovereignty over the islands; in the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Over 40 items and £60,000: the Friends of the Falklands Museum launch their website
World.content:
Over 40 items and £60,000: the Friends of the Falklands Museum launch their website

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 11:26 UTC Full article

FIMA Friends has been a registered charity in the UK since July 2016 and directs its funds to research into the archipelago's maritime history and the preservation of artefacts and archives

De Martino painting of Stanley

The UK charity that acquires and sends Falklands heritage items to the archipelago has launched a new website after securing more than 40 objects, documents and books for Stanley's historical institutions over the past decade.

The Friends of the Falkland Islands Museum and the Jane Cameron National Archives, known as FIMA Friends, has been a registered charity in the United Kingdom since July 2016 and directs its funds to research into the archipelago's maritime history and the preservation of artefacts and archives. Its acquisitions, obtained through auctions, direct purchases and donations, go to the Historic Dockyard Museum, the Jane Cameron National Archives and the library in Stanley. The most recent is an original oil painting depicting the action in San Carlos Water during the 1982 war. The website is fimafriends.co.uk

“We have spent over £60,000 in the last 14 years, contributing to historically important collections and helping the institutions share them with the public,” said the charity's chair, Graham Bound, who founded Penguin News in 1979, the only newspaper produced in the archipelago. “We have ensured that many valuable items are now where they belong: in the Falkland Islands.”

Among the items returned is the first known image of Stanley, a painting of the town shortly after its founding by the Italian artist Edoardo De Martino, whose works are also held in the Royal Collection in London. The charity also located and purchased the memorabilia of Louis Baillon, the only islander to win an Olympic gold medal, as a member of England's hockey team at the 1908 London Games.

Secretary and trustee Karen Clapp, who led the website's development, said it will be the charity's principal means of recruiting supporters. “It is important to have a digital footprint that allows people to see what we do and, just as importantly, join us with just a few clicks of a button,” she said, adding that trustees will be more easily contactable, particularly by anyone who learns of an item of historical value to the archipelago.

The site also carries details of forthcoming online talks and access to recordings of past lectures on the region's history. The charity has additionally funded exhibitions, publications, training and specialist equipment for the museum and archives.

World.title: Replica of the flag shown by Argentina's football team unfurled at Darwin cemetery
World.content:
Replica of the flag shown by Argentina's football team unfurled at Darwin cemetery

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

The delegation spent a week in the islands and visited Stanley, the Darwin cemetery and various sites of the 1982 fighting

A group of Argentine veterans of the 1982 war and relatives of fallen soldiers unfurled at the Darwin cemetery in the Falklands a flag bearing the inscription “The Malvinas are Argentine”, a design the Argentine press describes as a reproduction of the one displayed by Argentina's national football team after defeating England at the 2026 World Cup. It is the first time the emblem has been displayed in the archipelago.

The delegation spent a week in the islands and visited Stanley, the Darwin cemetery and various sites of the 1982 fighting. The two Argentine outlets that covered the trip differ on its composition: one describes a group of eleven veterans and relatives from the Agrupación 2 de Abril, based in Avellaneda, while the other mentions participants from La Matanza, La Plata and Córdoba. For several of them it was the first time they had set foot in the archipelago since the conflict. During the tribute they sang the national anthem before the graves and left letters, flowers, football shirts and rosaries.

The Darwin cemetery holds 230 graves. Of these, 121 plots contained 122 unidentified bodies, marked with the inscription “Argentine soldier known only to God”. In December 2016, Argentina and the United Kingdom tasked the International Committee of the Red Cross, together with the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team, with identifying them. Exhumations took place between June and August 2017, and the first report, in December that year, identified 88 bodies; the plaques were installed in March 2018. As of April 2025, 117 had been identified and five remained outstanding.

Among the relatives travelling was Gramisci, sister of Donato, killed in combat days before Argentina's surrender and whose remains were identified in 2018. “I think this is his place. Even though he is far from his family, far from what was his home, it is the place where he, without choosing it, chose to be,” she said. Argentina rejected repatriations at the time, arguing the soldiers were already buried on its own territory, which has made the cemetery a recurring destination for family visits over the past two decades.

Ramón Robles, who leads the group and fought near the cemetery's present location, described the trip as “humanitarian, to close chapters”. He said he applies for a new passport after each visit so as not to retain the stamp of the archipelago's authorities, which he regards as recognition of British administration. According to EFE's coverage, members of the group agreed in dismissing President Javier Milei's recent sovereignty measures as inconsequential; that assessment appears as the reporter's summary rather than a quote attributed to any individual.

The 1982 war left 649 Argentine dead, 255 British and three residents of the archipelago.

World.title: UK public debt nears £3 trillion, equivalent to 93.8% of GDP
World.content:
UK public debt nears £3 trillion, equivalent to 93.8% of GDP

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:40 UTC Full article

The figure is £78.5 billion higher than a year earlier, though its weight on the economy was 1.3 percentage points lower than in August 2025, reflecting a growing nominal GDP

The United Kingdom's public sector net debt reached £2,985.5 billion — close to £3 trillion, some US$4 trillion — at the end of August, equivalent to 93.8% of gross domestic product, according to figures published on Tuesday by the Office for National Statistics. The agency noted these are levels last seen in the early 1960s.

The figure is £78.5 billion higher than a year earlier, though its weight on the economy was 1.3 percentage points lower than in August 2025, reflecting a growing nominal GDP.

From the start of the financial year in April through August, the public sector borrowed £77.3 billion, 2.7% less than in the same period last year, but £8.1 billion above the Office for Budget Responsibility's forecast. That gap widened sharply: a month earlier it stood at £2.3 billion. The comparison comes five weeks before the UK budget, due on October 28.

In August alone, borrowing reached £18.3 billion, 19% more than a year earlier and £3.5 billion above the OBR's estimate. According to the ONS, the increase occurred because spending grew faster than revenue from taxes and other sources, partly because of inflation.

The government also paid £8.8 billion in debt interest in August, the highest figure on record for that month. Of that total, some £2.1 billion reflects the capital uplift on index-linked gilts, whose return moves with the Retail Prices Index, a mechanism that adds volatility to interest costs.

Not all indicators point the same way. Borrowing in the financial year to August equates to 2.5% of GDP, 0.2 percentage points lower than a year earlier, and is the tenth-lowest April to August period since comparable monthly records began in 1993.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds reaffirmed the Labour government's commitment to “maintaining fiscal discipline” while pursuing economic growth.

The figures frame the public spending debate running through Westminster. On September 9, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons his government would meet NATO's target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035, with an interim 3% goal, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch questioned the cost of the Chagos Islands agreement and argued a decade was too long to wait.

World.title: De la Espriella skips the UN and delegates Colombia's address to his vice president
World.content:
De la Espriella skips the UN and delegates Colombia's address to his vice president

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:30 UTC Full article

“You know I promised not to leave Colombia and I am going to keep that,” the president said in a video

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella will not attend the United Nations General Assembly and has delegated the country's address to his vice president, José Manuel Restrepo, scheduled for Thursday afternoon, September 24. It is the first time in recent history that a Colombian vice president has taken on that role.

The decision stems from a campaign pledge. “You know I promised not to leave Colombia and I am going to keep that,” the president said in a video released on Friday, adding that Restrepo “will read before the UN plenary words that will surely make a great impact”. Opposition congressman Alejandro Ocampo said on X that this is the first vice president to deliver Colombia's address to the body since 1946, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.

Security will be the central theme, as agreed by the president and vice president at a meeting in Barranquilla, with the presentation of the new government's national security strategy. The foreign ministry also flagged investment and “strategic alliances” as priorities. Restrepo will speak immediately before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The vice president arrived in New York on Sunday leading a delegation markedly smaller than those of previous governments, comprising Foreign Minister Ómar Bula, UN Ambassador Mauricio Gaona and Ambassador to Washington María Consuelo Araújo. He travelled on a commercial flight, in economy class and in a middle seat, according to a photograph he circulated himself. On Monday he held meetings with the World Economic Forum, the Inter-American Development Bank, energy sector executives and Dominican President Luis Abinader. “We have a clear agenda: attract investment, train the talent artificial intelligence demands and modernise the state,” he said.

Lists of planned meetings differ by source. Ambassador Gaona mentioned the United States, United Kingdom, France, Peru, United Arab Emirates, Chile and Ecuador; other coverage adds Saudi Arabia, Estonia and Switzerland, and explicitly includes strengthening ties with Israel. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau welcomed him on X.

De la Espriella, in office since August 7, has softened his position on the organisation. During the campaign he called it “a political directorate of the left” and threatened to withdraw Colombia's delegation. Once in government, Bula confirmed before Congress that Colombia will remain on the Security Council, to which it was elected in 2025 and where its term runs to December 2027.

The new government's foreign policy has aligned with the United States and Israel. Last week, Colombia was one of four countries to abstain in the vote allowing Palestine to address the assembly remotely, after Washington denied visas to its representatives: 152 countries voted in favour, with the United States, Israel and Paraguay against. Washington last week kept Colombia on its list of countries it deems to have failed demonstrably to combat drug trafficking, though with explicit praise for the new president.

Last year's address, the final one by then president Gustavo Petro, led to the revocation of his US visa and his subsequent inclusion on the OFAC sanctions list. Petro referred to the episode on X on Monday: “Now that I will no longer give a speech at the United Nations Assembly, the last one put me on OFAC.”

World.title: UN general debate opens with wars, artificial intelligence and the Guterres succession
World.content:
UN general debate opens with wars, artificial intelligence and the Guterres succession

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:24 UTC Full article

The organisation expects 73 heads of state, 45 heads of government, 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince

The high-level general debate of the United Nations General Assembly opened on Tuesday in New York with the wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar at the centre of the agenda, alongside concern over the advance of artificial intelligence without global controls and the race to succeed Secretary-General António Guterres.

The organisation expects 73 heads of state, 45 heads of government, 49 ministers, 11 vice presidents and one crown prince. The 81st session formally opened on September 8, presided over by Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh, under the theme “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva opened the list of speakers, in line with the tradition assigning Brazil the first address. Following Guterres's opening remarks, US President Donald Trump and France's Emmanuel Macron also spoke. Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will not travel for a second consecutive year because the United States denied him a visa, and will address the assembly by video that same Thursday. The headquarters agreement requires Washington to allow access for diplomats from all member states. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani had called for Netanyahu's arrest over the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza; city authorities have no such power.

Who is absent is also notable. China's President Xi Jinping is sending a vice president and will meet Trump in Washington on Wednesday; the US president will spend only two days in New York. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not attending either, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi withdrew.

The succession to Guterres, whose second term ends on December 31, dominates corridor talk. The race narrowed to seven candidates after Chilean former president Michelle Bachelet withdrew on Saturday, a day after the Security Council's third informal consultation. According to sources cited by Reuters, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, secretary-general of UNCTAD, leads that straw poll by a narrow margin. The United States has not formally backed any candidate; a State Department spokesperson said candidates must publicly commit to the changes Washington requires and criticised what it described as a politicised ideology that had undermined the institution's effectiveness. The appointment will not be settled this week.

Artificial intelligence has pushed onto the agenda. Days before the gathering, executives from three major companies in the sector warned about the risk of the technology escaping human control and called for a pause; Trump dismissed those warnings as “a hoax” and urged continued advances to keep the United States ahead of China. The Security Council added a high-level meeting on the subject for Wednesday afternoon. Guterres said “the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety”.

The organisation's finances remain fragile. The United States paid US$725 million towards this year's regular budget, enough to avoid losing its General Assembly vote, but still owes more than US$1 billion. Richard Gowan, of the International Crisis Group, said the UN is no longer “in freefall”, though it is “stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis”.

World.title: Your LLC Name Is Available. Is Your Brand? The Three Checks Founders Often Confuse
World.content:
Your LLC Name Is Available. Is Your Brand? The Three Checks Founders Often Confuse

22nd Tuesday, September 2026 - 00:51 UTC Full article

Photo: Magnific

A business name can pass one check and fail another. State approval, trademark risk, and domain availability answer different questions. Yet founders often treat them as one test. That can create an awkward launch. The LLC may exist, while the preferred web address is gone or the chosen brand is too close to a mark already used in the same market.

Before spending heavily on signs, packaging, or promotion, using a free LLC registration service can remove the formation service cost while connecting the new company with a .com domain, business email, shared hosting, and marketing tools for the first year, while the state filing fee still applies. This makes the naming stage a good time to line up the legal entity with the identity customers will see online.

The safer approach is not to search for a name once and assume the result settles everything. Each check has a different job. The order matters too, because changing a brand after launch is usually harder than changing it while the business is still being set up.

Three Checks That Answer Different Questions

State Name Availability Is an Entity Check

A state business name search asks whether the proposed LLC name can be accepted under that state's naming rules. States may require the designation to be different enough from business names already on record. They may also restrict certain words or require an LLC designator.

Approval matters, but it does not create a nationwide brand right. A company can receive approval for its legal name and still face a separate branding problem elsewhere. State availability is therefore one check, not full clearance of the brand.

Trademark Search Looks at Marketplace Conflict

A trademark check asks a different question. It looks at whether a name, logo, or other sign that identifies a source may conflict with existing trademark rights for related goods or services. Two marks do not need to be identical before there can be a problem.

The USPTO Trademark Basics hub, updated August 4, 2026, includes guidance on searching for similar marks and preparing for federal registration. USPTO process guidance also makes an important distinction between trademarks, business name registrations, and domain names. Registering a domain name does not by itself create trademark rights.

A federal search is useful, but founders should know its limits. The important question is not simply whether an identical name appears. Similarity, the goods or services involved, and how a mark functions in the market can all matter. The more central the chosen brand is to the business, the more carefully this check should be handled.

Domain Availability Is a Digital Identity Check

The domain question is simpler, but it can change quickly. A .com may be free today and taken later. Founders should check the web address near the time they are choosing the business name, rather than waiting until formation and branding work are finished.

Domain availability also should not override the trademark check. Finding an attractive domain does not mean the matching brand is clear to use. A domain is a web address. Trademark law deals with signs that identify the source of goods or services and can raise concerns when similar marks create confusion.

Choose the Name in a Better Order



Photo: Magnific





Search Before You Spend on the Brand

A sound naming process begins with a shortlist rather than one favorite. For each candidate, check state availability, review trademark risk, and then check the domain. If one option has a serious problem, compare the next choice before spending money on design, printing, ads, or packaging.

This order also makes the formation package more useful. Once a workable choice has passed the main checks, the legal entity, domain, email, and website can be built around the same identity. That is easier than fixing mismatched branding after launch.

When the Exact Dot Com Is Unavailable

An unavailable exact-match .com does not always mean the business name must be dropped. A clear variation may still work if it is easy to remember and fits the company. However, adding a location, product term, or other word should be a branding choice, not a way to copy another business.

The same caution applies when the exact domain is listed for resale. Before paying a premium, founders should confirm that the brand still makes sense from the state and trademark angles. A costly domain cannot solve a legal naming conflict.

Keep the Legal and Digital Identity Aligned

The strongest result is not simply getting an LLC approved or securing a memorable .com. It is creating an identity that works across state records, customer contact, and the market.

That does not mean every public-facing brand must always match the LLC's legal name. Businesses can use trade names where allowed, subject to registration and other rules that may apply. Still, founders should know why each designation exists and make sure customers can tell which company they are dealing with.

Checking state availability, trademark risk, and domain availability before launch cuts avoidable rework. Those checks make the final choice easier to build around.

World.title: SENER: Wind power expected to grow 80% by 2030
World.content:
Mexico is doubling down on its renewable energy ambitions, with wind energy generation expected to increase 80% by 2030 to reach 15 gigawatts, the Energy Ministry (SENER) reported in September.

Mexico is expected to increase its renewable energy generation from 24.6% of its total portfolio in 2025 to over 38% in 2030, said Jorge Islas Samperio, SENER’s Deputy Minister of Planning and Energy Transition, at a forum of the Mexican Wind Energy Association (AMDEE) and the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC) earlier this month. He said renewable sources will account for more than 74% of new capacity additions, including solar, wind and hydroelectric power.

The SENER plan includes 6.86 gigawatts of capacity additions, of which 4.7 gigawatts have already been allocated to 17 wind farms.

At the same Sept. 10 forum, CFE announced the awarding of eight wind energy projects under mixed-ownership schemes, with a total capacity of 2.9 gigawatts.

The projects, which include 890 megawatts of battery storage, are expected to be operational in Nuevo León and Tamaulipas by 2030, supplying clean power to the industrial hubs of northeastern Mexico.

Energy Minister Luz Elena González previously presented the government’s plan to add almost 32.5 gigawatts of generation capacity to the national grid by 2030, with around 22 gigawatts — roughly 70% — coming from renewable sources, predominantly solar (55%) and wind (30%). González said that total investment across CFE, joint ventures, and private projects was expected to reach 739 billion pesos (US$ 41.9 billion).

In the September forum, Samperio highlighted opportunities for Mexico to develop across the wind energy value chain, including parts manufacturing and construction, and operation of wind farms.

The deputy minister said that expanding Mexico’s renewable energy capacity would be key to meeting growing electricity demand, supporting industrial development and achieving the country’s energy transition goals.

Meanwhile, AMDEE President Gerardo Pérez Guerra acknowledged that legal certainty, public-private collaboration and the expansion of transmission networks are needed to encourage new investments in infrastructure and storage.

With reports from La Jornada

World.title: MND Local San Miguel de Allende: Art passport, charity events and celebrity sightings
World.content:
A new passport guide focuses on the city’s lesser-known artists and art studios; a cow-sorting benefit event is coming up; an athletic challenge will help feed local schoolchildren, and a celebrity sighting is reported at a local bar and restaurant. Read on about some of the community activities going on in and around San Miguel de Allende.

Art passport draws attention to SMA’s ‘hidden studios’

San Miguel jewelry maker Mariana Díaz started thinking about her Hidden Studios Art Passport project in January after a period of feeling invisible as an artist and realizing others were in a similar situation.

“I just thought about everybody having so much talent, but no one knows about it,” she said. “People keep on the same route in Centro, and they really don’t walk around and see all the good stuff that’s out there.”

Her idea led to a Sept. 12 launch of the initial project, which included 14 local artists plus members of the public who can use her printed passport guide to find artists, studios and creative spaces around the city and collect stamps for each one they visit.

“The event was great,” Díaz said. “There were 70 people there. It was wonderful to see everybody. My family was there, all the artists were there and they brought a little piece of themselves — a sample of their art, a painting or a sculpture or something.”

How it works

Artists pay her a fee to participate and send in pictures of their work to be put in the passport guide. She then gives them stamps that she designed to hand out to people who visit their studios. It works like a treasure hunt and can be done year-round, she said.

Since the art passport project just started, Díaz is currently highlighting the opportunity for participation for artists and local businesses such as hotels, cafes and restaurants.

“There are two options that help,” she said. “People can carry the passport in their restaurant or cafe or appear in the guide or put their business in the guide.”

Seven artists have already signed up for the second edition of the passport, she noted, and more hotels and other businesses may join in.

“There are some big names interested, and I feel it could become really big at some point,” Díaz said. “I’m waiting to have the guide with me and go deliver it everywhere. The majority are really interested in it. It’s something for their guests to do.”

For more information, she can be reached on Instagram, Facebook or WhatsApp.

Upcoming cow-sorting event will benefit local NGO

The Billy Boots Cup cow-sorting event will be held Saturday, Oct. 10, at Rancho Sol Dorado, a 120-acre private ranch community and club about 6 miles north of San Miguel at Km 5.5, Marroquín de Abajo. Doors open at 10 a.m., and the action starts at 11 a.m. Admission is free.

Cow sorting (also known as ranch sorting) involves teams of riders separating numbered cows from a herd and putting them in pens in numerical order within specific time limits. The event will benefit Feed the Hungry San Miguel, a nonprofit organization that distributes meals to local schoolchildren.

Besides the equestrian action, there will be food and drinks, a raffle and 20 local vendors on hand.

Walk, Run, Bike challenge to help feed local schoolchildren

Feed the Hungry San Miguel will hold its seventh Walk, Run, Bike for Food Challenge on Sunday, Oct. 25, from 8:30 a.m. to noon to benefit its food and nutrition programs. The goal is to provide more than 5,000 nutritious school lunches every day to local and rural communities.

The nonprofit organization, formed in 1984, invites participants to sign up now to walk, run or bike through the Viñedo Dos Búhos countryside east of San Miguel and stay afterward for live music, food and community spirit.

Another benefit for Feed the Hungry San Miguel is coming Sunday, Nov. 15. The annual Fashion Feeds runway brunch is scheduled from noon to 3 p.m. at Live Aqua, located at Calzada de la Presa 85 in Centro.

Another celebrity sighting reported

Spotting famous people in and around San Miguel isn’t uncommon to anyone who spends time out and about. Diego Luna, Karol G, Lorde and Bill Murray have recently been seen in the city, along with others who likely slipped in and out without being recognized.

The most recent celebrity sighting was Sept. 18, when Canadian actor and musician Ryan Gosling was spotted enjoying the ambiance at Sala de Despecho at Umarán 14 in El Centro. The venue offers a bar, restaurant and karaoke featuring Spanish-language “pop and heartbreak ballads.” No word yet on whether he joined in.

Gosling is known for his breakout role in “The Notebook” (2004), followed by starring roles in “La La Land” (2016) and “Barbie” (2023), among others. His latest project, “Star Wars: Starfighter,” has reportedly finished filming and is in post-production, with release scheduled for May 2027.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: Guanajuato has drawn US $630 million in data center investment as it evolves toward being a tech powerhouse
World.content:
Guanajuato is expanding its footprint in the digital economy with a portfolio of data centers that has drawn a combined investment of US $630 million and the creation of 200 jobs, as reported in a state government statement.

The Bajío state has currently two operational facilities and another in development, two of which belong to ODATA, a member of the Aligned Data Centers group located in San Miguel de Allende and Apaseo el Grande.

Centros de datos impulsan inversión y empleo tecnológico estatal

Guanajuato reporta 2 centros de datos en operación y uno en desarrollo, con inversión conjunta de 630 mdd y 200 empleos directos. Proyectos exigen energía, conectividad, seguridad y talento especializado.… pic.twitter.com/mCxUopjYFZ — Red Popular (@RedPopularMx) September 21, 2026

The third project is still under construction, also in San Miguel de Allende.

The development of these projects required a new substation at the San Miguel de Allende Business Park (PESMA)—featuring a 60 MVA capacity and an investment exceeding US $45 million— to ensure sufficient and reliable energy for new technological and industrial operations.

This electrical infrastructure is complemented by the Bajío region’s central location and by new investments in fiber-optic connectivity.

According to authorities, the data centers established in Guanajuato incorporate energy and water-efficiency technologies, including state-of-the-art cooling systems and reuse of treated water.

State Economy Minister Cristina Villaseñor explained that the inclusion of information technologies — including data centers, artificial intelligence, and semiconductors — is one of the strategic sectors within the Guanajuato Suma strategy, whose central objective is to evolve the economy from a traditional industrial base into a technological powerhouse.

According to the state government, Guanajuato has drawn over US $6.5 billion in investment — equivalent to 81.9% of the six-year target of $8 billion — across various sectors, including digital infrastructure and data centers.

Villaseñor explained that this strategy responds to changes in the global economy driven by the reconfiguration of supply chains and the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). In this context, the state’s vision is to boost digital infrastructure growth while protecting the region’s natural resources.

This vision dovetails with President Claudia Sheinbaum’s policy y regarding the technology industry.

Although she has said that Mexico needs data centers to develop AI and modernize its technological capabilities, she has warned that the country must not become a global hub for data storage and processing to meet external demand, given the high energy and water consumption involved.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Over 4,000 corrupt officials sanctioned since Sheinbaum took office: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🚨 Corruption crackdown continues: Anti-Corruption Minister Raquel Buenrostro said 4,193 public servants were sanctioned between Oct. 1, 2024 and June 30, 2026, mostly for improper payments, data theft and unjustified purchases. Sheinbaum said corruption prevention efforts have saved over 80 billion pesos in government contracts.

👶 Newborn deaths in Durango under investigation: Sheinbaum said authorities are investigating the deaths of five newborns last week at an IMSS hospital in Durango city. Parents alleged poor hygiene in the hospital’s neonatal unit.

🌀 Hurricane Polo not expected to make landfall in Mexico: Sheinbaum said the Category 5 storm will skirt the Pacific coast near Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán without directly hitting Mexico, though she urged residents to stay alert for updates.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The fight against corruption, the deaths of five babies in a hospital in Durango and the presence of Hurricane Polo off Mexico’s Pacific coast were among the issues discussed at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference.

The seriousness of each of the issues made today’s mañanera particularly consequential.

While progress in combating corruption can be celebrated by the government — even though there is still plenty of work to be done — the deaths of five newborns in a public hospital raise serious concerns about Mexico’s public health system.

More than 4,000 public servants sanctioned since Sheinbaum took office

Anti-Corruption and Good Governance Minister Raquel Buenrostro told reporters that 4,193 public servants received administrative sanctions between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and June 30, 2026.

She said that the main reasons why officials were sanctioned were for:

Making or authorizing “improper payments.”

Stealing government information, including personal data.

Approving payments for goods or services that were “never delivered.”

Approving “unnecessary, unjustified purchases.”

Forging documents.

Sexual harassment.

Buenrostro said that 3,528 of the public servants committed “non-serious offenses” and were sanctioned by the ministry she leads. She said that an additional 665 public servants committed “serious offenses” whose cases were referred to the Federal Administrative Justice Tribunal.

Sanctions can include dismissal or suspension from work. Officials accused of committing serious offenses, such as embezzlement and fraud, are investigated by the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

Buenrostro said that 53 officials accused of serious offenses have been ordered to stand trial during the term of the current government.

Sheinbaum: Prevention of corruption in government contracts has generated savings of more than 80 billion pesos

Sheinbaum said that Buenrostro and the ministry she leads dedicate a lot of their efforts to preventing “bad behavior” and corruption within government departments.

She said that the Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance “immediately” halts any government bidding process that “has problems” and takes action against any public official possibly involved in “an act of corruption.”

Sheinbaum said that bidding processes that are scrapped due to possible corruption are “repeated.”

“In two years, as Raquel says, it’s close to 83 billion pesos [US $4.8 billion] that we’ve managed to avoid [losing],” she said.

Sheinbaum: Deaths of newborns in IMSS hospital are under investigation

Sheinbaum said that the deaths of five newborn babies in a Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) hospital in Durango city are under investigation.

She said that the investigation is aimed at determining what caused the deaths of the babies, all of whom died last week in Durango’s IMSS Zone 1 General Hospital.

IMSS said in a statement on Monday that federal health authorities had arrived in Durango and that they, along with IMSS medical and epidemiological teams, were carrying out a “comprehensive review of clinical files, care protocols, epidemiological surveillance and measures for the prevention and control of infections.”

Parents of the deceased babies have denounced a lack of hygiene and other irregularities in the hospital’s neonatal intensive care unit. IMSS said that antibiotic-sensitive bacteria was detected in the hospital, but asserted that its presence didn’t in itself explain the deaths of the newborns.

Hurricane Polo not expected to make landfall in Mexico

Sheinbaum said that current information indicates that Hurricane Polo — a Category 5 storm — won’t make landfall in Mexico.

“Until now the information we have is that it won’t directly reach the coast,” she said.

“It’s going to be skirting the Pacific [coast], particularly along the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán,” Sheinbaum said.

She urged residents of Pacific coast states to be “very attentive” to announcements from Civil Protection authorities regarding the hurricane.

“So far there has been intense rain,” Sheinbaum said.

“… It doesn’t appear that [the hurricane] is going to make direct landfall. … If there is other information, it will be immediately announced,” she said.

World.title: In Mexico City’s ‘Little LA,’ deportees find work and a community
World.content:
Tabacalera, in Mexico City, is known for its wide streets, palm trees and colossal Monumento de la Revolución. Lately, the neighborhood has gained global recognition for its community of deportees, who have dubbed it “Little LA.”

A slew of recent articles — from the Guardian to Airmail Weekly — have celebrated the deportees finding new homes in Little LA after expulsion from the United States.

Yet, for most Tabacaleros, it’s just another day in the neighborhood.

“I didn’t even know they were calling it Little LA,” said David Jiménez, a Mexico City local, who laughed when I suggested the name.

David works at an English-language call center — one of five in the area — attracting some 2,000 deportees with decent wages and stable employment.

“Many (of the deportees) don’t actually live in Tabacalera,” Jiménez explained, “But because so many work here, Tabacalera is like their meeting place.”

For many of the 190,000 Mexican nationals deported since Trump’s re-election, deportation is just the start of building a new life. Often without Spanish skills, many struggle to find work, housing and the legal papers needed to establish themselves in Mexico.

Israel Concha was deported in 2014. After losing everything in the United States, he was violently kidnapped upon arrival in Mexico.

Eventually, he landed in Tabacalera, where he found work at a call center.

“Call centers,” Concha remembers realizing, “will hire anyone speaking English.” He shared the postings across his growing network of deportees in Mexico. Many of those joining him in Tabacalera were from Los Angeles.

“So we started calling it Little LA,” he told me over Zoom.

Though he now lives in Las Vegas, Concha today leads New Comienzos, an organization he started in Tabacalera to help deportees land in Mexico City.

Walking around Little LA, Concha’s story — of landing and leaving — seems common. Though Tabacalera’s call centers offer employment and stability, few settle permanently in Little LA.

The expected length of call center employment, Israel told me, is about eight months. Beyond this, Tabacalera’s handful of deportee-owned small businesses, like El Diablo and a giant burrito stand, have been sold or closed, per Shunaxi Estrada Guzman, New Comienzos’ Director of Volunteer Programs.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Comienzos (@newcomienzos)

Jesús Daniel Sandoval Gallardo runs Shelter Constitución de 1917, a shelter for migrants and returnees. “Arriving here is often traumatic for them,” he explained. “The work they do here in Little LA, in Tabacalera, is a platform for them to find better opportunities or move elsewhere.”

Still, Little LA’s transience doesn’t change the power of its name.

“Little LA is a community,” said Estrada. “(It’s) a name that is helping returnees to identify a place they can gather and find help and see that, yes, we do have a community here.”

This brought one recently self-deported woman, who preferred to remain unnamed, to a “Little LA Tour” hosted by New Comienzos. “I saw all these videos and came here to check out what Little LA is.”

Though we learned much about New Comienzos’ impactful work on our tour — helping, by their count, over 100,000 deportees through wide-ranging programs — the bilingual, binational Little LA I had read about wasn’t visible during the tour or my other visits.

Apart from the call centers, the clearest glimpse I caught was a 10-year-old sign, hanging in a mini-mart, run by a woman who seemed used to the press.

Outside of the call center, I asked David if the name “Little LA” bothers him. “Of course not. The name’s for their community here. The neighborhood is still Tabacalera.”

Though his colleague debated him — how different is it from Trump renaming the Gulf of Mexico? — they both agreed that there’s no real tension here about Little LA.

“It’s not like gentrification in La Roma.” David continued, “I mean, (the deportees) are vulnerable and came here in difficult circumstances.”

For deportees stuck between worlds, the degree to which CDMX’s Little LA exists — in Tabacalera, its call centers and the media — is, perhaps, not the point, after all.

Logan J. Gardner is a writer, photographer and filmmaker based in Mexico City. His coverage includes culture, food and travel, and geoeconomics. He earned degrees from Wharton and the University of Cape Town and formerly worked at L.E.K. Consulting and Netflix. Sign up to receive his newsletter, Half-Baked, or follow him on Instagram for more.

World.title: AmCham-IMSS deal pledges US $44 million to bring clinical trials to Mexican public hospitals
World.content:
The Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) and the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham) have signed an agreement to increase sponsored clinical research in public hospitals, with a projected investment exceeding 766 million pesos (US $44 million) during the 2026–2030 period.

The agreement aims to have more pharmaceutical industry clinical trials conducted within IMSS’s hospital network. The project involves the IMSS Foundation, AmCham, and the pharmaceutical companies Amgen, AstraZeneca, Bayer, Bristol Myers Squibb, Johnson & Johnson Innovative Medicine, MSD, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Roche, and Sanofi.

“This is a major step for Mexico, the Mexican people, and the implementation of Plan México,” AmCham Director General Pedro Casas wrote in a post on his official X account.

IMSS Director General Zoé Robledo highlighted the opportunity to expand the Mexican public sector’s participation in this type of research.

“Why should the IMSS lead clinical research in Mexico? Because today, 70% of clinical trials conducted by pharmaceutical companies in our country take place in private centers, even though no one else possesses what we have at the institution,” he said.

Robledo noted that this agreement does not entail displacing private hospitals; rather, it seeks to ensure that IMSS competes for projects that are currently channeled to other institutions or countries, “seeking to occupy the place that corresponds to its scale.”

Indeed, the strategy seeks to leverage IMSS’s infrastructure and reach, which has more than 1,800 medical and highly specialized care facilities that serve approximately 70 million beneficiaries. It also involves training of 729 IMSS researchers with the aim of strengthening capabilities and increasing the number of studies that can be conducted within the institution.

“With this potential investment of 767 million pesos, it is clearly the most ambitious public initiative of its kind,” Robledo said.

The strategy’s primary objective will be to translate scientific research findings into everyday patient care, particularly for diseases requiring a high level of medical services. Priorities include high-prevalence or complex conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, cancer, kidney disorders, neurological diseases, and rare diseases.

In fact, the newspaper Excélsior reported that IMSS is already working on a Phase 3 study for people with Sjögren’s syndrome, and that another Phase 3 trial related to irritable bowel syndrome is planned.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Brugada, Mamdani swap notes on housing, care systems at U20 mayors summit in New York
World.content:
Mexico City’s public care system and Mayor Clara Brugada’s community center initiative won praise from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during the 2026 Urban 20 Mayors Summit (U20), an annual gathering of mayors from major G20 cities and other metropolises around the world.

Speaking alongside Brugada in New York on Sunday, Mamdani said that Mexico City is a city “that many of us look to for inspiration, especially in how we answer the crisis of care in our economies.”

Gracias, @NYCMayor, por reconocer las #UTOPÍAS de la Ciudad de México como un proyecto para garantizar una vida plena. Una visión de ciudad que pone a las personas y a las comunidades al centro. ¡Es un gusto que este proyecto sea inspirador en las grandes ciudades del mundo! pic.twitter.com/gvZzhVLnF2 — Clara Brugada Molina (@ClaraBrugadaM) September 20, 2026

“When we’re talking about care blocks, we talk about these often within our own administration as an example of what it can look like to deliver for people in our own city,” he said.

Under Brugada’s leadership, the Mexico City government has set up a public care system, a central part of which is the provision of free childcare as well as services aimed at the well-being of seniors and people with disabilities.

Among the government-run centers that offer these services are Unidades de Transformación y Organización para la Inclusión y la Armonía Social (Units of Transformation and Organization for Inclusion and Social Harmony), known as Utopías. These community centers — which also offer cheap meals and a range of recreational, cultural, social and educational facilities — first opened in Iztapalapa when Bruagada was mayor of that Mexico City borough (2018-23) and are now being expanded to other parts of the capital as the city government seeks to offer greater support to primary caregivers, including working mothers.

Brugada is aiming to open 100 new Utopías during her 2024-30 mayorship, while solidifying caregiving as a “public responsibility” rather than a private one.

Mamdani said that “when we talk about Utopías, [there is] the understanding also that we have to be delivering dignity to working people … to ensure they can live lives that are full, lives that are flourishing.”

“And it is such a pleasure to have a fellow mayor here as we do with the mayors of Freetown and Rome who understand that the issues of the working class must be issues at the forefront of our politics,” he said. “And one day I will return to Mexico City, but I don’t know when that is.”

In separate remarks on Sunday, Mamdani said he would like to work with President Claudia Sheinbaum and “any other leaders from across Mexico” to address “global crises.”

“… The crises we face are global crises and that is true for Mexico City, for Rome, for Freetown, for New York City and so many others. And we’ve also watched in admiration of President Sheinbaum’s initiatives and the ways in which she is tackling the same issues of cost of living,” the mayor said.

Brugada draws inspiration from NYC

While Mamdani looks to Mexico City for inspiration, Brugada was herself inspired by New York, a city she said she visited as a young “social activist” in 1987.

In a social media post, the mayor noted that on Monday, she met with Mamdani and “repartidores paisanos” — i.e. Mexicans who work in the Big Apple as deliverymen and deliverywomen for companies such as Uber Eats and DoorDash.

“In Mexico City we will replicate some of New York’s good practices to support those who work in this activity,” Brugada wrote.

She said her government will create “spaces where [repartidores] can rest, recharge their bikes and access bathrooms.”

“We take care of our workers here and there!” Brugada wrote.

En #NuevaYork me reuní con el alcalde @NYCMayor y con repartidores paisanos. Replicaremos en la Ciudad de México algunas de las buenas prácticas de Nueva York para apoyar a quienes se dedican a esta actividad. Como espacios donde puedan descansar, recargar sus bicis y acceso a… pic.twitter.com/NBd5HeccBm — Clara Brugada Molina (@ClaraBrugadaM) September 21, 2026

On Monday morning, the mayor used the New York City Subway to get to her meeting with Mamdani.

“Hello. We’re going on the subway to City Hall where the Mayor Mamdani awaits us,” she said in a video message.

Above the video, Brugada wrote: “On the way to a meeting with the Mayor of New York. We’re continuing the exchange of ideas and experiences about the future of our cities. As in our beloved #CapitalDeLaTransformación [i.e. Mexico City] public transport is what connects and integrates major metropolises … and here we go.”

Brugada: ‘No (affordable) housing, no peace’

During an address at a U20 forum on affordable housing on Sunday, Brugada said that Mexico City would, “of course,” join a global “affordable housing coalition” proposed by Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni.

“I know that many cities present here will [also] join,” she said.

In a video posted to social media, Brugada said that Collboni had made a “very good proposal to build a coalition of cities in favor of affordable housing.”

In the same video, the mayor of Barcelona — a city with serious tourism-related housing problems — said that Mexico City is among the first cities to join “the defense of a fundamental right, as is the right to decent and affordable housing for everyone.”

“This is a fight that all the big cities of the world are in, and I’m very happy that Mexico City together with New York and Toronto … have joined the initiative in order to do big things,” Collboni said.

In her forum address on Sunday, Brugada declared that without affordable housing, there is “no peace,” and spoke about her government’s housing initiatives and the progress made during her mayorship and that of Sheinbaum, who governed Mexico City from December 2018 to June 2023.

“Between 2018 and 2025, nearly half a million people were lifted out of housing poverty in Mexico City. Despite these results, significant challenges remain. As in other cities around the world, the city continues to face a housing shortage, as well as gentrification and the displacement of communities due to speculative dynamics in the real estate market,” she said.

“To address this situation, in Mexico City we have developed the largest housing policy in our history — and one of the policies of greatest reach at an international level as well,” Brugada said.

“The three pillars of this housing policy are firstly, the large-scale construction of social housing; secondly, regulation of the real estate market; and thirdly, we carry this out in partnership with the people through a model of co-management,” she said.

“… We have the goal of building 200,000 … [affordable] homes by 2030,” the mayor said.

“I’m talking about new homes and improved homes. … This means unprecedented progress in reducing the housing shortage,” Brugada said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mass nesting event brings more than 100,000 olive ridley sea turtles to Oaxaca’s Playa Escobilla
World.content:
More than 100,000 olive ridley sea turtles came ashore at Oaxaca’s Playa Escobilla in a single mass nesting event last week, but the spectacle masks a fragile reproductive outlook: As few as 30% to 40% of the eggs may hatch.

According to the newspaper El Universal Oaxaca, 101,500 females emerged from the Pacific Ocean in Santa María Tonameca last Tuesday in a huge, synchronous nesting event known as an arribada.

The sixth arribada (literally “arrival” in Spanish) of the 2026-27 season lifted the season’s running total to more than 465,000 turtles as of last week, according to the paper.

The olive ridley turtle is among the smallest species of sea turtle in the world. They are found primarily in tropical regions, with a nesting season that generally runs from May through February or March.

Playa Escobilla is among the world’s leading nesting sites for the olive ridley, or Lepidochelys olivacea.

The species is listed as endangered in Mexico and faces risks from egg poaching, fishing, destruction of nesting habitat and climate-related events. Conservation efforts are abundant all over Mexico, and volunteer opportunities are many, as detailed this month in Mexico News Daily.

Despite the current large Escobilla tally, Rafael Villanueva Alcázar of the National Commission of Natural Protected Areas (Conanp) cautions that nesting totals do not guarantee a comparable increase in hatchlings.

“It sounds like a lot,” he said, “but it’s actually very low compared to other beaches that have a higher rate of hatchling production.”

Only about 30% to 40% of Escobilla nests hatch, Villanueva said. By comparison, Playa Ceuta in Sinaloa estimates an 85% hatch rate, but it has only about 500 olive ridley nests per season.

No global hatching rate for sea turtle nests could be found, but one widely cited statistic is that roughly one in every 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings worldwide survives to adulthood.

Rising sand temperatures, changes in sand composition, erosion, strong swells and low humidity are among the factors reducing hatching success. Egg theft and other human-caused damage also take a toll.

Conditions can vary sharply between seasons and sanctuaries.

At Morro Ayuta, another major olive ridley refuge on Oaxaca’s coast, a record 1.9 million olive ridley nests were protected and more than 34 million hatchlings were released into the sea during the 2025-26 season.

Guillermo González Padilla, the head of that turtle camp, said those numbers were “unprecedented” thanks to “the rains, the wetter beaches and the fact that the summer’s temperature [in 2025] was ideal for egg incubation.”

(For this season, Morro Ayuta had counted about 135,000 turtles through the start of its third arribada earlier this month, according to Conanp.)

Meanwhile, at Escobilla, conservation work over the past 35 years has helped. Officials set aside a 5-kilometer protected area for nesting during last week’s arribada, and Conanp is monitoring the nesting grounds along with other federal agencies and local communities.

Local participation is critical because available park rangers alone cannot protect the beach from poachers and other threats. Also, according to EDUCA, a Oaxacan community development NGO, locals help strategically relocate eggs — which average 100 per nest — after arribadas.

With reports from El Universal Oaxaca and MeganoticiasMx

World.title: Kast UN Speech Declares Chile Is Back and Faults the United Nations
World.content:
Chile · United Nations

Key Facts — What happened José Antonio Kast addressed the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday 22 September 2026, his first as president.

— His message Chile is back after years of stagnation, he said, and foreign investors should choose it.

— His complaint The United Nations has not risen to the challenges of our times, he told delegates from the podium.

— What he asked for Less bureaucracy, suspension of non-priority agendas, and reform of the Security Council designed in 1945.

— The catch He conceded that Chile’s economy has still not taken off and that unemployment remains high.

— Why foreigners should care A cautious trading nation is now grading the multilateral institutions it has long leaned on.

Chile’s new president used his first turn at the General Assembly to sell his country to investors. Then he told the United Nations, from its own podium, that it had fallen short.

File photograph of Chile’s President José Antonio Kast speaking at a lectern before a Chilean flag.

The Kast UN speech put Chile back on the General Assembly stage on Tuesday 22 September 2026. President José Antonio Kast told the assembled world leaders that his country was back.

“He venido hasta este foro a contarles que Chile está de vuelta”, he said. In English: I have come to this forum to tell you that Chile is back.

Then came the sting. He told the world body, from its own podium, that it had fallen short.

A conservative president marking six months in office

Kast is a conservative lawyer who took office on 11 March 2026. He won the runoff of 14 December 2025 with 58.2% of the vote.

He beat Jeannette Jara of the Communist Party, who took 41.8%. He succeeded Gabriel Boric, the leftist who had governed Chile since 2022.

The address ran 18 minutes, according to La Tercera, a Santiago daily. He spoke after Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, BioBioChile reported.

The numbers he put on the record

Kast said Chile is now “un país más seguro, un país más competitivo y un país con menos burocracia”. That is a safer country, a more competitive one, with less bureaucracy.

“Llevamos seis meses, y estamos ordenando la casa”, he said. We have been here six months, and we are putting the house in order.

He told delegates the homicide rate fell 11.5% in the first half of 2026. His border plan, Escudo Fronterizo, cut irregular entries by 86%, he said.

Expulsions rose 50% on the year before, he added. Those are his own government’s figures, delivered from the rostrum.

On the economy he cited a company tax cut from 27% to 23%. Applications worth more than US$44 billion entered the environmental permitting system in six months, he said.

More than US$33 billion of projects were approved, some after years of waiting, he told the hall. A further US$17 billion had been unblocked at the environmental stage, he said.

He also conceded the obvious. Chile’s economy “aún no despega”, he said, and unemployment “se mantiene alto”.

In English: the economy has still not taken off, and unemployment stays high. “El cambio va a llegar”, he added, promising that the change will come.

Unemployment was 9.5% in the May to July moving quarter. That figure comes from Chile’s National Statistics Institute, published on 28 August 2026.

File photograph of police lined across a tree-lined avenue in Chile. Security came first in the Kast UN speech. (Photo: Rjcastillo, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The uncomfortable part

Kast then turned on his hosts. “Esta organización no ha estado a la altura de los desafíos de nuestros tiempos”, he said.

In English: this organisation has not risen to the challenges of our times. He introduced the passage as the most uncomfortable thing he had come to say.

“No es posible mantener vigente el orden mundial del año 1945 en un mundo del 2026”, he added. The world order of 1945 cannot stay in force in 2026, he meant.

He put three proposals to the organisation. Cut the bureaucracy, suspend agendas that are not priorities, and reform the Security Council.

That council is the body of 15 states that can order sanctions and peacekeeping missions. Five of them hold permanent seats and a veto.

Wars, Venezuela and artificial intelligence

Kast asked the assembly to end the world’s wars, without naming a single one. “Las guerras deben cesar”, he said: the wars must cease.

Conflict raises the price of bread, transport and harvests far from the fighting, he argued. Chile imports practically all the oil it consumes, he reminded delegates.

Chile is resuming relations with Venezuela under its new leadership, he told the hall. On that change he offered a middle course.

Some would have Chile refuse to recognise it, he noted, and others would have it align unconditionally. “Chile no hace ni una cosa ni la otra”, he said: Chile does neither.

Venezuela has a historic chance to rejoin its democratic traditions, he said. He then turned to artificial intelligence, calling it an ethical and geopolitical question.

The most powerful technology humanity has built is appearing, and nobody is governing it, he told the hall. He proposed a Chilean approach he called “ritmo responsable”, a responsible pace.

The pitch to investors

El Mostrador, a Santiago news site, had written that morning that tariffs and an anti-crime pact would shape his agenda. Only the pact reached the podium, as the Acuerdo de Santiago, a South American security deal.

Trade reached the speech mainly as an invitation. “Elijan Chile para invertir”, Kast said, telling the assembled leaders to choose Chile to invest.

He promised rules that do not change overnight, courts that work and contracts that hold. He offered Chile’s minerals and the Strait of Magellan as assets for world trade.

Why it matters beyond Chile

Chile is a mid-sized trading economy that has long specialised in not making enemies. A Chilean president publicly grading the United Nations is a change of register.

The timing is delicate. Michelle Bachelet, a former Chilean president, quit the race to be UN secretary-general on 19 September 2026.

Kast told reporters in New York on Monday 21 September 2026 that he felt “el mayor respeto” for Bachelet. That is the greatest respect, for her as a person and as a former president.

He added that his government had never intended to back her bid and would support no other candidate. His speech the next day made no mention of her candidacy.

He closed on the region rather than on himself. “América Latina puede ser el continente de la próxima década”, he said: Latin America can be the continent of the next decade.

More: Chile coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is José Antonio Kast?

He is the president of Chile, sworn in on 11 March 2026. Born in Santiago on 18 January 1966, he is a lawyer and a former member of the Chamber of Deputies, where he sat from 2002 to 2018. He founded the Republican Party and ran for president three times, in 2017, in 2021 and in 2025. He belongs to the populist right and won the December 2025 runoff with 58.2% of the vote.

What did the Kast UN speech demand of the United Nations?

Three things. He asked the organisation to cut its bureaucracy and concentrate its budget where lives are at stake. He asked it to suspend agendas that are not priorities. And he asked for reform of the Security Council, which he said still mirrors the politics of 1945 rather than those of 2026.

Is Chile’s economy improving under Kast?

Not yet, on his own account. He told the General Assembly that the economy has still not taken off and that unemployment remains high, while arguing that his reforms are already under way. Chile’s National Statistics Institute put unemployment at 9.5% for the May to July moving quarter, in figures published on 28 August 2026.

What is the Acuerdo de Santiago?

It is the regional agreement Kast promoted to coordinate South American governments against transnational organised crime. He cited it at the United Nations as proof of closer regional coordination, alongside a border plan he says has cut irregular entries sharply. Chile is also bidding for Valparaíso to host the secretariat of the High Seas treaty.

World.title: Bruce Mac Master Snub: Gaviria Calls Colombia’s Government Arrogant
World.content:
Colombia · Politics

Key Facts — What happened Former minister Alejandro Gaviria said on X that the government orders ministers to shun independent business leaders, journalists and executives.

— What the veto is Vicky Dávila of Semana posted on X, citing unnamed government sources, that no minister may meet Mac Master.

— Who is targeted Bruce Mac Master has led ANDI, Colombia’s largest business association, since 2013; its board reconfirmed him on 8 September 2026.

— The catch The government has not confirmed the directive, and no official response to Gaviria has been reported.

— Who else objected Senators Andrés Forero of the Democratic Centre and Ariel Ávila of the opposition Green Alliance both criticised it.

— Why it matters The row comes as ANDI questions health funding in the 2027 budget now before Congress.

A reported order to keep ministers away from the head of Colombia’s main business lobby has drawn fire from a former minister and senators on left and right.

The Casa de Nariño, Colombia’s presidential palace in Bogotá, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Bruce Mac Master, head of Colombia’s biggest business association, is at the centre of a new political row. A reported order barring ministers from meeting him has drawn fire from former minister Alejandro Gaviria.

Without naming President Abelardo de la Espriella, Gaviria called the government “increasingly arrogant, isolated and ineffective”. He made the charge on X, in a post reported by Infobae on Tuesday 22 September 2026.

What the reported veto is

The veto is not about a board seat, a delegation or a commission. It concerns access to the government itself.

The claim came from Vicky Dávila, a former presidential candidate who manages publications at the news magazine Semana. She posted it on X on 21 September 2026.

“Government sources confirm that from now on, no minister can meet Bruce Mac Master, president of ANDI,” she wrote. She added that officials were weighing extending the veto to ANDI board members.

The political news site La Silla Vacía noted that Semana itself had not carried the report. It described Dávila as a kind of spokesperson for the new government.

The Presidency has not confirmed that any such order exists. No official response to Gaviria or to the senators who objected has been reported.

Mac Master has run the National Business Association of Colombia, known as ANDI, since 2013. It groups about 1,500 companies in industry, finance and commerce, according to the news site Las2orillas.

Gaviria’s words, and his stake

Gaviria served as health minister under Juan Manuel Santos and as education minister under Gustavo Petro. His post did not mention De la Espriella by name.

“The order is clear,” he wrote, in The Rio Times’ translation. “Do not talk to business associations, journalists or executives who show any independence.”

“The purpose is also evident: to end dissent, to build by force a kind of artificial consensus,” he continued.

He ended with the line quoted most widely. “The result is predictable: a government that is increasingly arrogant, isolated and ineffective.”

Gaviria has a personal interest in the dispute. His wife, the economist Carolina Soto, withdrew this month from the presidency of the Colombian Chamber of Infrastructure, a construction lobby.

“In view of the opposition my appointment generated, I have decided to decline,” Soto said, as quoted by the outlet Cambio. Infobae reported that she had faced pressure from the government.

The skyline of central Bogotá, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

A board that kept its president

The friction predates this week. Cambio reported on 8 September 2026 that the government had signalled, through various channels, that it preferred a new head at ANDI.

ANDI’s board confirmed Mac Master anyway at a meeting that day. Rodolfo Castillo became board chair and María del Rosario Gómez vice chair, according to Las2orillas.

Earlier, Dávila had written that Mac Master had “zero interactions” with the new president. La Silla Vacía reported that, officially, the two men have no quarrel.

Cambio also described a split over donations for reconstruction in Chocó, a Pacific coast department. Mac Master chose a trust and donors’ board rather than the fund run by first lady Ana Lucía Pineda.

Criticism from both sides of Congress

The reaction crossed party lines. Senator Andrés Forero of the Democratic Centre, the party of former president Álvaro Uribe, objected publicly.

“This is not right,” Forero said. “Business associations’ autonomy and independence is a democratic value that should not be lost.”

He urged the government to reconsider what he called an “inconvenient and alarming decision”.

Senator Ariel Ávila of the opposition Green Alliance went further. He said the president gives no press conferences or interviews and speaks only to “friendly” media.

Ávila also said officials call to demand the heads of journalists and business association managers. He likened the conduct to “any banana-republic authoritarian”.

The health budget in the background

The row lands as ANDI challenges the government on health spending. On 21 September 2026 the association warned about the per-patient payment that funds Colombia’s health insurers.

ANDI said this year’s adjustment of 12.94% would leave a gap of 3.7 trillion pesos (about US$1.16 billion). It had recommended an increase of 15.6%.

That conversion uses the official rate of 3,192.53 to the US dollar for 22 September 2026. The rate is published by Colombia’s Financial Superintendence.

Mac Master argued that the 2027 budget debate in Congress should rest on technical criteria. Infobae read that as criticism of Health Minister Ana María Vesga.

What comes next

For now the dispute rests on a reported directive the government has neither confirmed nor denied. No minister has said publicly whether they will meet the ANDI chief.

The first test will come as Congress debates the 2027 budget. ANDI has already asked for health spending to match the system’s real costs.

More: Colombia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Bruce Mac Master?

He is the executive president of ANDI, the National Business Association of Colombia, a post he has held since 2013. ANDI groups about 1,500 companies from industry, finance and commerce. He was a frequent critic of economic measures under former president Gustavo Petro. The ANDI board confirmed him again on 8 September 2026.

What exactly was vetoed?

Not a seat or appointment. On 21 September 2026 Vicky Dávila, a Semana executive, wrote on X that government sources said no minister may meet Mac Master. The government has not confirmed the directive, and no official response has been reported.

Who is Alejandro Gaviria?

He is a Colombian economist and former university rector. He was health minister under Juan Manuel Santos and education minister under Gustavo Petro. His wife, Carolina Soto, withdrew this month from the presidency of the Colombian Chamber of Infrastructure after what she called opposition to her appointment.

Has the government responded?

No response from the Presidency or any minister has been reported. The criticism has come from Gaviria and from senators Andrés Forero of the Democratic Centre and Ariel Ávila of the Green Alliance.

Sources: Infobae on Gaviria’s post and the reported veto, La Silla Vacía on Dávila’s post and the reaction, Cambio on the ANDI board vote, Las2orillas on the new ANDI board, La República on ANDI’s health funding warning, Colombian open data on the official exchange rate

World.title: Viracopos Power Outage Cancels 26 Azul Flights and Slows Security Checks
World.content:
Brazil · Travel

Key Facts — What happened Part of the passenger terminal at Viracopos, near Campinas, lost power at about 3:10 a.m. local time on Tuesday, 22 September 2026.

— Who was hit hardest Azul, which runs most flights at the airport, said it cancelled 26 flights because of the power failure.

— Why queues built up X-ray scanners at the entrance to the departure area went down, so security checks were done by hand.

— The catch The operator says the backup generator did not work, and knock-on effects on flights could last up to two days.

— What was not affected The runway, aircraft apron, access roads and cargo terminal kept working, according to the operator.

— What travellers should do Check the flight status with the airline before leaving for the airport, as both the operator and Azul advise.

A failed substation and a backup generator that never started left Azul’s main hub in the dark for hours. The airport warns that delays could last for up to two days.

An Azul turboprop near a runway in Brazil, file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

A Viracopos power outage threw Azul’s main hub into disarray on Tuesday 22 September 2026. Queues stretched to the terminal doors as X-ray scanners and flight boards went dark.

Azul, the airline that dominates the airport near Campinas, said it cancelled 26 flights because of the failure. The operator warned that knock-on delays could last up to two days.

Viracopos International Airport sits about 80 kilometres northwest of São Paulo. It is the main hub of Azul and one of Brazil’s leading air cargo gateways.

A substation fails before dawn

The trouble began at about 3:10 a.m. local time, which in Campinas is Brasília time. Aeroportos Brasil Viracopos, the private company that runs the airport under a federal concession, said one substation feeding the check-in hall failed.

What should have happened next did not. The airport has a generator for outages, but it did not work, the operator told g1, the Globo group’s news site.

The concession also said there are three redundancy points meant to prevent this kind of blackout. The link between the three substations was interrupted, and it is investigating why.

Power began to return to the check-in hall at about 6:30 a.m., the operator told the news agency Estadão Conteúdo. Even so, g1 reported that part of the terminal was still on emergency lighting at noon.

The departure boards were dark overnight and came back on at about nine in the morning. The operator had said it expected full power to be restored by 12:30 p.m. Brasília time.

Security checks done by hand

The outage hit the X-ray machines at the entrance to the departure area. Security screening had to be carried out manually, the operator said, slowing the flow of passengers and staff.

During the morning the line for the departure area ran the length of the hall and reached the terminal door. Check-in and baggage drop counters were also crowded, according to g1.

Some passengers were stuck on the other side. Clara Maia, a social media influencer with 3 million followers, said she spent about two hours stuck on board an aircraft.

“There was a blackout and nobody gets in, nobody gets out,” she wrote in a post quoted by g1. At 9:07 a.m. she posted that she had finally got off.

Check-in counters at the domestic terminal of Fortaleza Airport, file photograph. (Photo: Jcornelius, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)
