World.title: No evidence of a 'wage-price spiral' in Australia
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Iain Ross, a member of the Reserve Bank's monetary policy board, gave a very interesting speech last night.

He rejected the idea that Australia has almost experienced runaway wage growth in recent years that could have fed into damaging inflation.

Rate rise looking likely All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them during a speech in Sydney.

"I want to talk about wage-price spirals," he said.

"The 'threat' of rising wages has been a persistent theme in the financial press since inflation began rising sharply from mid-2021.

"A number of media commentators have raised the risk of a wage-price spiral — pointing to the 1970s when the oil price shock collided with large pay rises flowing through the economy.

"[But] the labour market framework of today is very different to that of the 1970s and 1980s.

"There is no evidence of the emergence of a wage-price spiral in the present circumstances and recent data suggest such an outcome is unlikely," he argued.

The formation of wage-price spirals

Dr Ross is a former President of the Fair Work Commission, a former judge of the Federal Court and Supreme Court of Victoria, and a former assistant secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU).

Iain Ross, RBA monetary policy board member, says the labour market framework of today is very different to that of the 1970s and 1980s. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Nobody on the RBA's nine-person monetary policy board has had as much practical experience with Australia's labour market and wage-setting institutions.

It was rare to hear a speech from an RBA board member (these days) that focused so heavily on the reality of Australia's modern wage-setting institutions, and the decline in workers' power, to challenge the idea that our economy could experience a "wage explosion" any time soon.

There's nothing wrong with lifting wages The national accounts are likely to show living standards as measured by GDP per person have gone backwards for four consecutive quarters for the first time in 40 years. So why are we talking about a wages explosion?

What is a "wage-price spiral"?

According to the idea, Ross explained, following an increase in aggregate demand or an external cost shock, businesses raise their prices, which pushes up inflation.

Workers then want higher wages to maintain their real wages, and if they think inflation will remain high, they may push for particularly large wage increases (so 'expectations' play an important role in the process).

Those higher wages then feed into higher costs, and prices, and so on, which amplifies the inflationary effects of the original shock, and round and round we go:

(Source: "A wage-price spiral: What are the chances"?, Iain Ross, Monetary Policy Board member, University of Melbourne Centre for Employment and Labour Relations Law, 22 September 2026 - Melbourne.)

Australia's economy experienced episodes of rapidly rising prices and wages in the 1970s and 1980s.

But Ross explained that those events occurred in a very different Australia.

If we're hit by stagflation, it will be different this time The World Bank has warned the global economy will soon experience stagflation, but that doesn't mean we're returning to the 1970s, writes Gareth Hutchens.

He said our modern labour and wage-setting institutions, our modern financial system, our extremely diminished union movement and much tougher sanctions for unlawful industrial action, and the broader industrial structure of our economy, were significantly different from 50 years ago.

He said our modern industrial relations system limited how frequently workers could revise their wage claims, and how easily higher wage claims could spread through the economy these days.

"These changes in Australia's wage-setting mechanisms have made the wage-price dynamics of the 1970s much less likely to recur," he said.

A 'substantially different' wage bargaining environment today

It's worth reading his entire speech, if you're interested in learning more about the big differences between the 1970s and today.

Iain Ross says the wage bargaining environment is "substantially different" in Australia today compared to the 1970s. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

He talked about the old concept of "comparative wage justice," which held that employees doing the same work for different employers or in different industries should receive the same amount of pay, irrespective of the capacity of their employers or industry.

He said that concept helped to spread large wage rises through Australia's economy 50 years ago.

Declining productivity needs bold reform Business used the collapse of unions to suppress wages and oligopoly power to increase prices. Expecting it now — using AI — to fix declining productivity, rising inequality, generational anger and political polarisation is fanciful.

And he discussed the old practice of indexing wages to the consumer price index every three months, which tied rising wages with rising prices in a rapid inflationary feedback loop in the 1970s.

"The situation is very different today," he said.

"Comparative wage justice no longer plays the pervasive role it once did, and quarterly indexation is not a feature of the current system.

"The current enterprise bargaining arrangements, in particular, effectively operate as a shock absorber by constraining the bargaining capacity of those who are the subject of enterprise agreements.

"Such employees are unable to pursue claims for increased wages until the enterprise agreement to which they are subject has passed its nominal expiry date," he said.

Does the RBA think the unemployment rate is still too low?

His speech was delivered at a fascinating time.

The RBA board will hold a highly-anticipated meeting on Monday and Tuesday next week to discuss what to do with interest rates.

Interest rates back at 'sensible level' If you are struggling with current interest rates, the Reserve Bank's leaders delivered the sobering message that they are only just getting back to a "more sensible level".

All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders expect the RBA to raise rates next week, given inflation and economic activity have been stronger than anticipated in Australia recently.

Inflation is still a global problem, and central banks in comparable countries have been lifting rates again.

RBA governor Michele Bullock also made a public appearance yesterday (a few hours before Dr Ross delivered his speech).

And she warned that Australia's jobs market was probably still a bit too tight at the moment and putting upwards pressure on wages, business costs, and inflation more generally.

Australia's unemployment rate is currently 4.5 per cent.

"I think between 4.5 and 5 [per cent unemployment] will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that it'll ease pressure on inflation," Bullock said.

Loading...

Will the RBA board members vote as one next week?

Whatever the RBA board does with interest rates next week, it will be interesting to see if its decision will be unanimous.

Under the board's new voting regime, which began in early 2025, there have been 12 meetings.

Of the 10 meetings where unattributed votes have been published, there have been split votes 30 per cent of the time:

And two of the three meetings in which the board's nine members have failed to vote as one have occurred this year.

Will next week's meeting record another split decision?

World.title: Federal government urged not to let fire ant eradication funding lapse
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Advocates are urging state and federal treasurers to fund the next step of fire ant eradication efforts, with a funding cliff looming in June next year.

State and federal agriculture ministers met last week to discuss the National Red Imported Fire Ant Eradication Program Response Plan 2027-32.

Queensland Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett presented the potential impacts and consequences of wider proliferation of fire ants.

Eradication of the pests was deemed to remain "technically feasible, cost beneficial and in the national interest".

Ministers "agreed to consult their respective governments on funding and come back together for a final decision" ahead of next year's budget.

Loading...

'Turning of the tide'

Invasive Species Council (ISC) advocacy director Reece Pianta said the program was beginning to see a "turning of the tide" in fighting the spread of fire ants.

"We've seen 208,000 hectares, an area almost the size of the ACT, transition from the suppression zone into active eradication," Mr Pianta said.

"Fire ants removed from the Murray-Darling Basin in northern New South Wales, no new nests detected in central Queensland."

Advocates say the program has been effective and have urged the federal government to commit to funding the next five years. (Supplied: Invasive Species Council)

Mr Pianta said if the ants got out of control they would cause more than $2 billion in economic damage each year. ISC modelling suggests the eradication program would cost $1 billion over five years.

He said the track record of funding for the program was "pretty scary", and that the last funding gap in 2023 saw efforts move backwards.

Fears Australia will lose war on fire ants As fire ants continue their relentless march across south-east Queensland, a biological control expert warns "one or two selfish individuals" could destroy Australia's eradication plan.

"What that resulted in was about a 40 per cent increase in the fire ant infestation zone. It grew from around 600,000 hectares to about 850,000," he said.

He said another funding gap in the program could see governments lose the chance to eradicate the pests completely.

The ISC urged governments to ensure funding for the next "really crucial" phase of the program.

"There's a responsible program in the field now, the community is backing it," Mr Pianta said.

"We need our governments to fund it to complete its work.

" For our treasurers and finance ministers around the country, the cost-benefit analysis is clearly in favour of paying to complete eradication right now. "

Reece Pianta says another funding gap could see the country lose its chance to eradicate the pests. (Supplied: Georgia Tech Ant Lab David Hu and Nathan Mlot)

Mr Perrett told state parliament in June that fire ants remained "one of Australia's most significant biosecurity threats" as he announced $10.5 million in state funding for suppression efforts in 2026-27.

"Primary producers have strongly supported the suppression efforts because they understand what is at stake … sugarcane, nursery, turf and hay know that fire ants threaten their industries, and more broadly agricultural production, regional economies, and our way of life," he said.

"Noting that a new response plan is being negotiated for the nationally cost-shared program, I again call on the federal government and cost share partners to include fire ant suppression within the next response plan."

The Invasive Species Council is calling on state and federal treasurers to fund the next tranche of fire ant eradication efforts. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins has been contacted for comment.

Program aims to strangle spread

Fire ant eradication works by mixing insect growth inhibitor with corn grit, which is then carried to the queen by worker ants.

The bait stunts the growth of the queen, who then cannot produce new worker ants, and the colony collapses.

The biosecurity zone map covers Brisbane, Logan, and Ipswich, and reaches as far north as the Sunshine Coast and south into northern New South Wales, with isolated hotspots across the south-east.

Any materials such as soil or hay being moved from these areas must go through strict biosecurity measures to ensure no fire ants are onboard.

Map of the fire ant eradication zone (orange) and surveillance zone (blue). (Supplied: National Fire Ant Eradication Program)

The National Fire Ant Eradication Program targets properties in a broad band known as an "eradication area" around a fire ant "suppression zone", which covers a large corner of south-east Queensland, including Brisbane.

The goal is to treat every property in the eradication area up to six times over a two-year period, before contracting the zone and targeting a new set of properties.

That band is intended to shift gradually toward Brisbane and the coast, strangling the ants' spread.

Properties not within the eradication zone will not be specifically targeted, but residents can contact the Fire Ant Suppression Taskforce and work with them to treat fire ants found on their properties.

Areas are monitored for five years following treatment to ensure fire ants do not return.

World.title: Taylor Swift announces first new song since her wedding
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Taylor Swift has announced a new song, the first since she tied the knot with NFL player Travis Kelce in what was dubbed America's royal wedding.

The song, titled Patient Zero, is due to be released on Friday, US Eastern time.

It was announced in true Swift fashion early Tuesday morning, local time, with the pop powerhouse launching a cryptic countdown clock on her website.

Loading Instagram content

Her dedicated fans, known as Swifties, quickly got to work trying to decode whatever news was coming, noting that her official Instagram bio changed to read, "And, baby, that's sh0w business f0r y0u," with each "o" replaced with a zero.

Now it seems clear the gesture referenced the new song's title.

Once the countdown timed out, her website updated to reveal three limited-edition CD variants of the new track: one with a double-sided cover, plus an acoustic and piano version, for $US3.99 ($5.60) each.

It is her first new song since marrying Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden in July.

Swift's last album, The Life of a Showgirl, was released last October, and she contributed a song to the Toy Story 5 soundtrack in June.

Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift married in July. (AP: John Locher)

News dropped ahead of Swift's history-making MTV VMAs

On Monday, it was announced that Swift will receive the inaugural Artist Director Honors at the MTV VMAs on Sunday, becoming the most awarded artist in VMA history.

Swift is tied with Beyoncé for the title. They have 30 each.

Swift songs removed from Trump social media posts Despite their long-running feud with the pop superstar, the Trump White House and campaign had used several Swift tracks in TikTok videos, including the 2020 song August for a video showing the US president and First Lady Melania Trump watching fireworks.

The new award aims to recognise artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling".

Swift has nine nominations at this year's award show, following only Madonna, who leads with 11.

Her appearance at Sunday's show raised the spectre of further announcements, as Swift has been known to make news onstage.

Announcement follows Swift's 2026 Emmys pre-taped skit

At the Emmys last week, Swift appeared in a pre-taped skit, playing a rookie in the Law & Order: Special Victims Unit office.

Mariska Hargitay's Olivia Benson went through two large crime boards to make connections between Swift's songs and the Emmy-nominated shows to see if she would attend the telecast.

One of the detectives called it a "rabbit hole." In reality, Swift was at Arrowhead Stadium during the award show, sitting alongside Tom Cruise to watch the Chiefs open the NFL season against the Denver Broncos.

In one pointed moment, Swift looked to the camera and appeared to utter a series of hints: "Saccharide. Ares. From the Vineyard. North or South," she said. Fans have been urgently trying to decode the message since.

AP

World.title: British backpacker left by Greyhound bus in outback roadhouse
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A British backpacker was left stranded at an outback toilet block in the middle of the night after her interstate coach service departed without her.

Emma had been travelling Australia since late August and on September 5 boarded a Greyhound bus at Alice Springs heading towards Adelaide.

She said the bus made a scheduled stop at Pimba around midnight, and the driver had increased the stop time to 25 minutes after the bathroom onboard the vehicle had a malfunction.

"[The driver] said he's going to ... add an extra five minutes onto what would have been a 20-minute stop at Pimba," Emma said.

"There's a queue to get into the loos, of course, so I queue, and I wait, and then I get in there, use the loo, brush my teeth."

Emma said about 15 minutes had passed from the time the bus had pulled in when she exited the toilet, leaving her about 10 minutes to return to her seat.

" I leave and the bus isn't there. "

Emma had been travelling around Australia. (Supplied: Wolf Cocklin)

Emma said she had been left alone at the truck stop toilets, near a service station, which was shut at that time of the night, in the remote locality surrounded by desert and scrub.

"It was four degrees that night, I found out later, I had my little rucksack, a little bit of water, no food, didn't have my passport, didn't have anything – most of my stuff was still on the bus," Emma said.

"So at that point I start sort of worrying a bit more, I call Greyhound, they don't answer."

Waiting for a lift

Emma said she rang Triple Zero (000) for help — eventually a police vehicle undertaking a custody transfer from Roxby Downs to Port Augusta picked her up at about 2:30am.

"It was so nice to be warm and safe, because by 2:30, I'd been out there for nearly three hours," she said.

"I'm standing in the toilet block because it's slightly sheltered and therefore about a couple of degrees warmer than the rest of the place."

Greyhound Australia has confirmed the passenger did not return to its bus in Pimba. (Supplied)

The tourist was able to collect most of her belongings, except for one bag, at Port Augusta after the local police liaised with Greyhound.

She then booked a regional bus through a different company to get to Adelaide.

"I went to considerable extra expense because I had to buy a hotel and breakfast and food, and another bus to Adelaide because they [Greyhound] didn't take me to Adelaide the way they were supposed to," she said.

"I'd probably want my ticket back and a bit of compensation as well because you don't endanger your passengers like that."

Emma's backpack was meant to be left for collection at Adelaide's Central Bus Station, however she said the bag was dropped off at another location outside of the CBD.

"Then started a lovely five-hour adventure trying to extract it [the backpack] from them," she said.

Greyhound investigating incident

In a statement, Greyhound Australia said its investigation into the incident was ongoing, but confirmed a passenger "did not return to the coach following a scheduled comfort stop at Pimba".

After receiving notification of the incident, Greyhound Australia said it "worked with police to locate the passenger and assist them to a place of safety".

The company said it provided "24/7 customer support" through 1300 GREYHOUND with "an out-of-hours emergency service available" for urgent travel-related matters.

It said customers could also reach out on the Greyhound website and its online chatbot.

"We have not identified any issues indicating the emergency service was unavailable during the period in question," the spokesperson said.

"The safety and wellbeing of our passengers remains our highest priority.

"While our review remains ongoing, it would be inappropriate for Greyhound to comment on individual allegations or unverified claims relating to operational matters that are still being investigated."

Greyhound said its Adelaide-based supervisor was at the depot for approximately 90 minutes with the passenger's luggage but when she did not arrive, the bag was arranged to be transferred on a subsequent service to be delivered to her final destination.

Emma said having backpacked on buses around the world, her experience in Australia left much to be desired.

"The quality and feel of safety is about the standard that I met in Bolivia, which had some pretty old and pretty knackered buses," she said.

World.title: Central Victorian council votes to keep divisive public holiday
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A Central Victorian council has been drawn into a local public holiday debate, backing a slim majority of locals who wanted to keep a controversial race-day holiday.

The City of Greater Bendigo council voted on Monday night to keep Bendigo Cup Day as the local public holiday for another five years.

The 4-1 vote to retain the current arrangement will see part of the shire taking a public holiday on Wednesday, October 28, a week prior to the Melbourne Cup.

Residents in the municipality east of the Campaspe River, including Heathcote, will continue to observe Melbourne Cup as its public holiday.

The decision followed a community survey that drew 2,672 responses, with mayor Thomas Prince calling it the council's "third most ever engaged survey".

The meeting saw councillors vote in line with the slim majority of respondents.

About 38 per cent of survey respondents said they wanted to keep Bendigo Cup Day holiday, while 36.5 per cent preferred Melbourne Cup Day and 24.7 per cent preferred the Friday of the Bendigo Show.

Meanwhile, just over half of businesses surveyed, making up 4 per cent of the responses, called for the date to be changed to Melbourne Cup Day, citing business operation concerns and alignment with the rest of the state as reasons to switch.

Thomas Prince says he was "challenged" by the survey. (Supplied: City of Greater Bendigo)

The mayor told the meeting he was "challenged" by the survey.

"It feels like a popularity contest around what the community want," Cr Prince said.

"Most of our contributors, I think, will be related to the sports racing industry and the jockey club and those at the Bendigo Show, and they're very self-invested ideas and opinions.

"The question is, 'What is most important for Bendigo?'

"What's best for Bendigo … is that we want our own holiday. We want a chance to celebrate who we are."

Eppalock Ward councillor Aaron Spong was the only councillor to vote against the motion, arguing the business feedback deserved more weight.

"Tradition does matter, but so does practicality," Cr Spong said.

" Local pride matters, but so does business certainty. "

Epsom Ward councillor Andrea Metcalf, who moved the motion, said analysis by consulting firm IER and council data put the 2025 Bendigo Cup's local economic activity at between $2.9 million and $3.2 million, with more than 6,500 people attending the cup.

The Bendigo Show draws about 20,000 people across its two days, five days before the cup.

"Both the show and the cup can be successful under the current arrangement," Cr Metcalf said.

Cr Prince told ABC Central Victoria Breakfast the alternative of moving the holiday to Show Day would have come at the Bendigo Cup's expense.

"To elevate that to probably potentially completely squash the Bendigo Cup day also just didn't make sense," he said.

The Bendigo Jockey Club welcomed the vote, with chief executive Paul Scullie saying the club had heard "the importance of ensuring our business community benefits from the public holiday" and wanted racegoers to "shop locally, stay locally, eat and drink locally".

The council will now apply to the state government, which makes the final decision on local public holiday arrangements.

World.title: NT mango farmers raise alarm on cuts to working holiday visa program
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Saramat "Tou" Ruchkaew says fruit could be left to rot on her 85,000-tree mango farm outside Darwin, following cuts to Australia's working holiday visa program.

The changes announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke last week mean backpackers will have to enter a ballot if they want to remain in Australia for more than 12 months.

The number of second-year visas will be capped at 45,000, while just 5,000 third-year visas will be issued and in total, Australia will welcome about 38,000 fewer second and third-year backpackers than it did in 2026.

Ms Ruchkaew said the reduced numbers would be devastating for the agriculture sector.

Saramat "Tou" Ruchkaew grows a variety of mangoes at her Top End farm. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"This is a big, big issue for the farming community," she said.

"The mango industry needs 2,500 people per season … [backpackers] work hard, make money, move on.

" Why fix something that's not broken? "

Under the current system, backpackers who complete 88 days of specified regional work during their first year in Australia can extend their visa.

And while the number of first-year working holiday visas is not being reduced, there are concerns backpackers could choose not to complete regional work if it will no longer guarantee them a second year in Australia.

Mango farmers in the NT say they rely on backpackers to fill the roles that keep their businesses afloat. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"They're just like 'No, if we work 88 days, then we don't get in the ballot, why would I? I'm here to have a good time'," Ms Ruchkaew said.

Ballot plan 'lunacy'

Rebecca Koivu is visiting from Finland, picking up work while exploring Australia, and is considering entering the ballot to stay for a second year.

"I feel like all the farms are going to suffer because so many of my friends are doing that right now," she said.

"They're only doing it for the opportunity for the second and third years."

Backpackers wanting to work regionally while travelling will now have to enter a ballot to stay in Australia. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

NT Mango Industry Association president Leo Skrilos said the ballot idea was "lunacy".

"Are we running a casino or a country?" he said.

" Are they picking names out of a hat? "

Mr Skrilos said the government's attempt to reduce backpacker numbers looked like a "knee-jerk reaction" to One Nation's recent surge in the polls on the back of the party's hard-line stance on immigration.

"I think One Nation's popularity is because they're looking to do something about … the people that are coming over on visas that are taking units and houses," he said.

Leo Skrilos says concerns about the effect of population growth on housing availability have "nothing to do with backpackers". (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's got nothing to do with backpackers."

Ms Ruchkaew, who immigrated to the NT from Thailand 35 years ago, said she was concerned by some of the public discourse around immigration.

"I contribute significantly to this country … we're not a liability," she said.

"The same as the backpackers, they come in, they work hard, they look around, they enjoy their life."

Visa changes add to tough season

Two hours south of Ms Ruchkaew's farm, at Marie Piccone's orchard near Katherine, 2026 has already been a difficult year.

"We had an extensive wet season with lots of flooding, significant flooding, significant erosion, significant road damage," she said.

Marie Piccone says the federal government has not considered the full impact of the new policy. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

"And then we've had really tough conditions with fire threats and wildfires once the flooding had finished."

Ms Piccone said the visa cuts suggested the federal government was "out of touch" with business owners and regional Australia.

"I'm not convinced that there's any consideration of what we [are dealing with] out here in what I call the engine room — people who are in business and are trying to have an economic outcome," she said.

Farmers say mangoes could be left to rot without enough workers to pick them. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"I think it's very clear to anyone watching that they're just worried about the votes in the next election and we're not a big vote base."

Territory and federal Labor at odds

NT Opposition Leader Selena Uibo said the Northern Territory relied "heavily" on working holiday visa holders and called on her federal Labor colleagues to offer the territory a carve-out from the rest of the country.

"The federal Labor government will show a complete lack of regard for the Northern Territory if they do not give us a carve-out," she said.

Selena Uibo says the NT should be treated differently when it comes to working holiday visas. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I'm very happy to openly say that to my federal Labor colleagues and to our federal Labor government.

World.title: Diana's brother 'sorry' for factual error amid calls to 'pulp' new book
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Princess Diana's brother Charles Spencer has told 7.30 that the controversial book he wrote about his late sister contains one factual error, but he will not pull it from shelves.

The novel, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, was released in the United Kingdom after a week of disagreement over its contents and questions about its accuracy. It's due to go on sale in Australia today.

Broadcaster Piers Morgan is demanding Earl Spencer "pulp" the memoir because it contains claims about him that are "all bulls**t".

Morgan says his lawyers have sent letters to the peer and the book's publisher, Penguin, threatening legal action if it remains in stores.

The media personality has bristled at suggestions in the book he was involved in a decision to print "stolen" images of Diana while he was editor of London's Daily Mirror, pointing out he had not started working at the newspaper until almost two years after the story in question hit the presses.

Morgan also disputes Earl Spencer's recollection of a phone call the pair had, where the aristocrat revoked his invitation to Diana's funeral. Earl Spencer claimed Morgan "snarled with annoyance".

Earl Spencer's book has hit the shelves in the United Kingdom. (Reuters: Jack Taylor)

Speaking with 7.30 at his family's home north of London on Tuesday, local time, Earl Spencer apologised for the error.

"I have got a date wrong, so there's been a public statement made on my behalf to state what I have done, and I apologise," he said, but said Morgan's "surly behaviour" on the phone was "true".

While the eBook and future printed editions will be updated to remove the claim about Morgan's time at the Daily Mirror, Earl Spencer does not plan to remove the first edition from sale.

In a video posted online, Morgan railed: "If Earl Spencer can be so incredibly, defamatorily wrong about basic facts involving me, why should we believe anything else he puts in this book?"

'Classic gaslighting': Spencer responds to Palace

Piers Morgan has threatened to sue Earl Spencer over claims made in the book. (Reuters: Belinda Jiao)

The aristocrat's new book has made allegations about Britain's royal family and their treatment of Diana, and dredged up damaging stories already in the public domain.

Several excerpts from the book, some particularly critical of King Charles III, who was married to Diana for 15 years, were published ahead of its release, sparking a fierce rebuke from Buckingham Palace.

The most disparaging allegations Earl Spencer has made relate to phone calls he says he had with Charles around the time of Diana's 1997 death in a car crash. Charles and Diana's acrimonious divorce had been finalised the previous year.

Earl Spencer accused Charles of sounding "giddily elated" during a conversation on the night Diana died, and also of saying "we'll forget her soon enough" several days after the crash.

He also claimed Charles had commented on Diana's weight after their engagement, which contributed to the well-documented eating disorder that she lived with, amid other details about his sister's deteriorating mental health.

Last week, after the first excerpts from the book were published in British newspapers, Buckingham Palace released this fiery statement: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

Earl Spencer told 7.30 Buckingham Palace's words amounted to "a classic bit of gaslighting" because they were suggesting his "brain isn't working correctly".

When asked why people should believe his account over King Charles', Earl Spencer said: "The king hasn't actually said anything. I've told the truth, and his spokesman or whatever has tried to cloud my truth — the truth — with a question mark."

Earl Spencer says he decided to write the book to coincide with the 30th anniversary of his sister's death, and because he — aged 62 — has become increasingly aware of his own mortality.

"Neither of my parents made it to 70," he told 7.30. "Why not do it while I still have what I laughingly call my brain active and give it a go?"

Princess Diana was killed in a car crash in 1997. (Reuters)

The earl, who has previously worked as a journalist and historian, has already written several books.

Some have accused him of trying to profit off his sister's death by releasing the memoir.

"Money has never been any part of my writing this book at all," Earl Spencer said, adding that he had received a "flood of applications for interviews" about the anniversary that he did not want to do.

"And then I thought, how about if people want to know what I had to say, why don't I say it myself?"

King Charles and Queen Camilla step out in London. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Diana 'loved Australia', despite turmoil

The book contains multiple references to time Diana spent in Australia.

It details her time at her mother and stepfather's property in country New South Wales in February 1981, shortly before her engagement to Charles was made public. Earl Spencer claimed his sister spent the trip mulling her options.

"Diana made her decision during her fortnight hidden away from the press on the other side of the world," a passage in the book reads.

Prince Charles and Princess Diana chat during a 1988 trip to Sydney. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Earl Spencer also references an infamous picture of a sobbing Diana snapped at the Sydney Opera House during her first royal tour to Australia in 1983.

Huge crowds turned out to see her in Sydney, Melbourne, and other cities, prompting some media at the time to describe the scenes as "Dianamania".

Earl Spencer claimed the amount of attention Diana had been getting had angered Charles and made him envious.

"Outside the Sydney Opera House, Diana was so upset at her husband's attitude towards her that she sobbed uncontrollably in public for two minutes," Earl Spencer wrote in his book.

He told 7.30 his sister "loved Australia" and while the 1983 tour had been "happy", it was a "pivotal point" in Diana's relationship with Charles for the wrong reasons.

"She was a young bride trying to do the right thing, and then feeling that somehow she's getting it wrong," Earl Spencer said.

People visit Althorp House, the home of the Spencer family, last month. (Reuters: Chris J. Ratcliffe )

The book includes a fresh claim the late billionaire Mohamed Al-Fayed groped Diana early in her romance with his son, Dodi. Dodi and Diana dated after her divorce with Charles was finalised.

Earl Spencer told 7.30 he had hosted Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children at the 550-acre Althorp Estate shortly after they relocated to the UK from California last month.

"One of the things I can give them [at Althorp] is privacy," he said.

The couple's return to Britain has sparked a flurry of interest, particularly as Harry, the king's second son, had said as recently as last year, he would not return to his home country.

"It's one thing to look at these people as princes and princesses, and it all sounds a bit Disney, but they're still humans, and they have relatives they've dropped by on," Earl Spencer said.

"And yes, this is a sort of absurd-looking house, but it's still a home when they need it."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Moree crime rates falling but residents say drone use is overreach
World.content:
For the past nine months, drones have been hovering over the skyline of Moree, in north-west NSW.

With an unwanted reputation as a hot spot for youth crime, the town was chosen as the site for a NSW Police drone trial.

Speaking in February when police went public with details of the trial, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon assured the community that "this is not about surveillance, it is about responding to crime".

But Gomeroi man Ian Brown was not convinced.

"To be able to see the drones at night, to see it happening, to see them hovering above, but they're meant to be responding to active incidents," he said.

" [If] there's no active incident occurring in your street, why is the drone hovering over here? "

Ian Brown says the Indigenous community of Moree should not be the "test cases" for drone footage being used as evidence in court. (ABC News: Max Tillman)

Mr Brown is the Head of Advocacy and Engagement for Just Reinvest NSW, an organisation that aims to reduce interactions with the criminal justice system for First Nations people.

He said some members of Moree's Indigenous community were feeling watched.

"They feel like they're being surveilled and, yes, they acknowledge that youth crime is an issue, but they don't want to feel like they can't walk out into their own backyard," Mr Brown said.

" At the end of the day we are the most researched, we're the most over-surveilled community in Australia and I think we shouldn't have to be that test case, especially our young people who are our most vulnerable in the community. "

Trial extended

The NSW government recently announced the trial would be extended from the initial six months to two years.

It said a community survey of 516 people found more than 80 per cent of respondents felt positive or very positive about the drone use and believed they enhanced public safety.

Figures from the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) showed crime was already on the decline in Moree when the drones were introduced and had continued to fall since.

The number of young people charged with a crime in Moree has fallen significantly in recent years — from 240 in 2022–23 to 113 in 2025–26.

In the past two years, break and enters into non-dwellings have fallen by 50 per cent and motor vehicle theft is down by 36 per cent.

BOCSAR executive director Jackie Fitzgerald said it was impossible to accurately assess the impact of the drones at this stage.

Jackie Fitzgerald doubts it is possible to attribute crime reduction in Moree to the drones alone. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

"In a small area like Moree there are so many factors that influence crime rates, even individuals being detained in custody or coming out of custody … as well as those more formal crime-control strategies," she said.

“I don't believe we can definitively say that the drones are responsible for the crime declines.

"In fact, a lot of the crime declines that we've been reporting in Moree have occurred prior to the implementation of the drones."

The ABC asked NSW Police for details about how often the drones had been deployed but was told that information would only be provided if a GIPA (Freedom of Information) request was approved.

NSW Police confirmed that in addition to being used for "operational purposes", footage captured from the drones would be used as evidence in court "if a criminal offence or public safety issue occurs".

Loading...

Principal solicitor at the Justice and Equity Centre, Jonathan Hall Spence, said that was starting to happen.

"This footage might be appearing in the brief of evidence, but there's not much chance for the court to test it or probe it because people plead guilty so that they can resolve the matter quickly," he said.

Jonathan Hall Spence says there is a lack in legislative framework for the drone trial. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

"There hasn't yet been [a] legal challenge to the use of drone footage in evidence, but I anticipate that we will probably see that before long."

A legal grey area

Police drones over troubled town Police will control drones from more than 600 kilometres away from a rural town battling high crime rates.

Mr Hall Spence said the drones were different to other forms of cameras used by police.

"Drones can get really up close and personal to people's properties and backyards, and they can also do that in a way that's not necessarily very noticeable," he said.

"You're definitely going to hear a helicopter that's flying over your backyard.

"As long as we're not understanding exactly how police are using these drones and in what circumstances, it's really not going to be clear whether there are sufficient safeguards or limitations on how the drones are used."

Mr Hall Spence said communities could be having their rights infringed without even knowing.

"It may only be when footage turns up in a brief of evidence in a court case that you realise that your property was under surveillance," he said.

Police say the drones are used for "preventing, disrupting and responding to criminal activity". (Supplied: NSW Police)

Lorraine Finlay, Australia's Human Rights Commissioner, has also expressed concerns about how the technology could fit into existing laws that were written long before drones existed.

"We need to make sure that if this technology is being used there is a clear foundation in law and there are clearly legislated safeguards and limits," she said.

Lorraine Finlay questions whether laws on surveillance and privacy are fit for purpose. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

"We know from past experience the potential for these types of policing tools to gradually expand over time in terms of the way they're used."

In a statement, a spokesperson for NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said the drones were operating under "established governance arrangements and standard operating procedures to ensure lawful, proportionate and transparent use".

Calls for evidence and evaluation

In August's budget estimates, Ms Catley said an evaluation of the trial was being completed by police, but it would not be made public.

Ms Finlay said the decision to extend the trial should not have been made before the evaluation was complete.

"We don't have all the evidence, and yet it feels as though the decision has already been made without explaining to the broader community how this works," she said.

Police drones have been installed on top of the Moree police station since January this year. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

"This isn't just a question about whether the technology works or doesn't work.

Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg says the Coalition are trying to better align the retirement and housing systems after he slated a proposal yesterday to allow superannuation to be used as collateral for a housing loan.

Bragg’s proposal was swiftly dismissed by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who said it was not a Coalition policy and that its formal policy position would be unveiled soon.

Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg. Alex Ellinghausen

“It’s not a policy, but it’s certainly an idea. Now, in relation to collateral, you could use some of your money to ultimately reduce the amount of money you need for a first home deposit, or you could use some of the money in cash and super to offset the amount of mortgage you might have to pay in terms of the interest,” Bragg told ABC’s 7.30 last night.

“So what we’re seeing now is high inflation, high interest rates, people paying a lot of interest on their mortgage. So I think a lot of people would be interested in these ideas being further considered.”

World.title: ASX set to advance, Wall Street steady; Oil prices slip
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance, Wall Street steady; Oil prices slip Stan Choe Updated September 23, 2026 — 6:16am ,first published 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street held near its record high in a relatively quiet day for markets worldwide. The S&P 500 closed flat and is sitting 0.4 per cent below its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 185 points, or 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite advanced 0.5 per cent. Energy and financial stocks fell on Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 5.58am AEST pointing to a rise of 27 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.12¢. US stocks had been higher in the morning, when the price for a barrel of Brent crude briefly fell below $US98. But oil prices later trimmed their losses, and Brent was most recently at $US99.66 per barrel.



That’s down from the nearly $US110 that it touched last week, but it’s still much more expensive than the $US72 it was fetching before the war with Iran began. It’s been swinging with uncertainty about when the war will allow crude to freely flow again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. On Wall Street, AutoZone rose 3.2 per cent after the retailer reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its revenue fell short. CEO Phil Daniele said the auto parts seller faced “a difficult selling environment” in the first two months of the quarter, but it improved afterward and “we feel we are well positioned for sales growth” in its upcoming fiscal year. Related Article Opinion

Oil ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At Thor Industries, which sells recreational vehicles, the mood was more muted. CEO Bob Martin said expensive fuel, high interest rates and still-high inflation are stretching its customers’ budgets, and business “never reached the inflection point many in the industry expected” in its latest fiscal year. Its stock rose 5.5 per cent, though, after it delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Such strong profit reports are one of the main reasons the US stock market has reached the brink of its all-time high despite high oil prices and jitters about whether stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry shot too high. Many companies are close to closing the books on their third quarter of the year, which ends with September. And analysts are forecasting companies in the S&P 500 will report overall growth of nearly 29 per cent for the quarter from a year earlier, according to FactSet. If they’re right, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25 per cent for the index. And stock prices tend to follow the track of corporate profits over the long term. On Holding’s stock that trades in the United States jumped 8.6 per cent after the Swiss sneaker and sportswear company unveiled its financial goals for upcoming years. It also approved a plan to buy back up to $US1 billion ($1.4 billion) of its stock through 2029. Such purchases send cash directly to investors and boost the company’s per-share performance. On the losing end of Wall Street were several stocks of companies in the oil and gas industry, which were hurt by the drop in crude prices. ConocoPhillips fell 1.8 per cent.



Banks also dropped, continuing their weak run since last week, when the Federal Reserve raised the overnight interest rate that it controls for the first time in three years. When the spread narrows between short-term interest rates and longer ones, banks come under pressure because they make profit off the difference. JPMorgan Chase fell 3.4 per cent and was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500. Related Article Aviation Jetstar staff to stop charging baggage and seat fees in union protest The gap between short- and long-term yields in the bond market did not move much, as the 10-year Treasury yield held steady at 4.96 per cent from late Monday. Like oil prices, it also remains far above where it was before the war with Iran began, when it was at 3.97 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher across much of Europe and Asia. London’s FTSE 100 was an outlier and dipped 0.3 per cent.



Stocks rose 0.2 per cent in Hong Kong and 0.1 per cent in Shanghai after Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies, including what it said was China’s most powerful AI chip. That comes just days ahead of a meeting between Chinese and US leaders at which competition to lead on AI technology is expected to be a major theme. World.title: Rape victims claim Swans sex assault case on the fast track while their complaints are dogged by delays
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Rape victims claim Swans sex assault case on the fast track while their complaints are dogged by delays Carla Jaeger and Cameron Houston September 23, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two rape victims have expressed fury over what they describe as a stark contrast between their cases and the intensive and rapid Victoria Police investigation into allegations of sexual assault involving Sydney Swans players. Despite having never met, both women detailed remarkably similar experiences, claiming they were treated with hostility while their cases were beset by unnecessary delays and police under-resourcing. Melbourne woman Sam says she has been failed by police investigating her alleged rape case. Simon Schluter One believes she may never see justice after the man accused of drugging and raping her in South Melbourne last month was able to flee home to Mexico after Victoria Police failed to place a border alert on him. The women’s decision to speak publicly come as Victoria’s unsolved sexual-crime case rate soars to record highs.



Sam, who waived her legal right to anonymity but asked that her surname not be used, now regrets notifying police after she was allegedly raped in May by a man she met on a dating site. Her frustration over the handling of the case turned to fury last month when she observed the police response to claims of sexual assault involving a group of Sydney Swans players at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. “Excuse my language, but it made me f---king livid. Clearly, they’ve got the resources when it comes to a high-profile case because they know that they’ll be under media scrutiny. But for a normal person like myself, the lack of care is just so evident,” Sam told this masthead. “They can fly detectives into New South Wales to question them within a couple of weeks, but they can’t go a suburb over to go and pull someone in for questioning.”



For 30-year-old Katie Arthur, the trauma from the police’s response to her complaint has, in some ways, eclipsed the alleged crime itself. Arthur felt a similar fury to Sam’s about the pace of the police response to her case. While pleading to come in and provide her statement sooner, she remembers asking – in a moment of exasperation – “What if I said I was raped by a football player?” “I can’t process what has happened to me because I’m too busy now trying to process the letdown of the police [response],” she said.



Arthur has also given permission for her full name to be published. “No one grows up dreaming of being the [rape victim in the paper]. But I now see the media as such a powerful outlet to speak on behalf of victims that have been let down by the one system supposed to protect them.” A Victoria Police spokesperson said the force had been in “constant contact” with both victims and detectives had referred them to support services. “Both [investigation] teams are progressing these matter as quickly as possible, noting the cases are complex, and we must ensure investigations are thorough,” the spokesperson said. “We also want to be clear that any report of sexual assault is not treated any differently because we have someone with a high profile involved.”



Arthur was allegedly drugged and raped on August 2 by a tenant staying at her midterm accommodation business. Grappling with shame and shock, she struggled to process the alleged attack before eventually reporting the incident to police on August 18. Arthur was forced to wait another 10 days to make a formal statement, despite pleading to come in earlier and repeatedly warning police via phone and email that her alleged attacker was a flight risk. “I am concerned the alleged rapist will leave the country as he is on a 5/6 month student visa,” she wrote in one email shared with this masthead. Detectives from Melbourne’s Sexual Offences and Child Abuse Investigations Team (SOCIT) informed her they were too busy, with one detective citing crippling understaffing, claiming their team of five was juggling 108 active cases.



Victoria Police said the delay in recording a statement was to ensure there was enough time to make a detailed report. Despite Arthur’s warnings, the accused fled the country on August 20 or 21 – but she didn’t find out until September 3 despite being terrified that a sexual predator was still residing at her property. “I needed to know if he was still in the country,” she said. “Not only for my safety, but he was living at the business I run. I have a duty of care to my other tenants.” After making her statement, Arthur said detectives stonewalled her requests for updates, and questioned why she took two weeks to make her complaint.



“You’re saying you will judge the severity of someone’s case by how quickly they come forward. It’s disgusting. You may as well say, ‘Don’t come forward unless you’ve been raped that day’,” Arthur said. Related Article Domestic violence Life sentences for rape, new charge for ‘slow femicide’ in Labor domestic violence pledge A detective outside of Melbourne SOCIT is now reviewing the unit’s handling of her case after Arthur lodged a complaint. Victoria Police said: “We take any allegations against the conduct of our members seriously and have strict procedures and policies in place. “No alert was issued for restrictions on international travel because police did not have evidence to meet the legal threshold required to prevent the person leaving the country.”



Arthur is now grappling with the reality that the man accused of attacking her may never face justice. “I can’t explain the trauma of not only experiencing assault ... but being forced to be your own advocate, and feeling like you are not believed. “It’s just as traumatising as being assaulted.” Sam agonised over whether to make a report to police. “I sat outside Oakleigh police station and tried to go in, and I was just numb and had no idea what to do. And I was afraid of not being believed,” she said.



Sam underwent a forensic examination at Monash Hospital the day after her alleged assault on May 18. She provided detectives with a statement on May 24, but claims to have been treated with a lack of empathy ever since. She says her concerns about the pace and rigour of the police investigation have been repeatedly dismissed. “There has been no empathy or understanding … the officer in charge of my investigation would keep saying: ‘Sam, you’re one of 30 cases that I have’,” she said. The Victoria Police spokesperson said the “safety of victims was at the forefront for police” and that unsolved cases continue to be investigated. They added that the timing of Sam’s report to police was of her choosing. “She first wanted to take some time to consider taking police action.”



The women’s complaints come after Victoria recorded 2962 unsolved sexual offence cases at the end of March 2026, a rolling figure that leapt by 1172 cases (66 per cent) in 12 months, Crime Statistics Victoria figures show. The rise follows a recorded 1790 unsolved cases in 2025, up 240 from the year prior. Meanwhile, 2024 recorded just 33 more unsolved cases than 2023’s total of 1517. Total sexual offences in Victoria dropped slightly between 2025 and 2026, recording 685 fewer offences at the end of March 2026. At the same time, unsolved cases spiked, arrests fell, and fewer complaints were withdrawn. An intent to summons, which indicates police intend to charge somebody but have not yet done so, more than doubled from 458 in 2025 to 1066 in 2026. Sam was told the officer responsible for her complaint had been forced to take stress leave because she was burnt out by her caseload. “Their workload should not be my problem. I said her, ‘What if this was your daughter, if this was your mother, this was your sister, a close friend? Would you accept that?’,” Sam said.



“The whole system has completely let me down, and it’s made me go. Why would I ever go to the police again,” she asked. Arthur feels similarly: “If you want to hold a perpetrator accountable, you need to be a lawyer. You need to be your own detective. You need to be your own everything. “You need to have everything written down and have zero trust that they’ll be able to actually do anything.” Victoria Police did not respond to a question about staffing of their SOCIT units. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Kids moving back home? Here’s what it could really cost you
World.content:
Analysis MoneyPlanning & budgetingSpending Kids moving back home? Here’s what it could really cost you Emily Chantiri September 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you have ever had an adult child leave home, you’ll understand that the chapter is never really closed, until they’re fully established or coupled. That said, many young couples also return to live with a parent to save money and buy a home. Fortune 500 financial services company Thrivent’s 2025 fourth annual Boomerang Kids Survey found parents are now more likely than ever to provide temporary financial support for adult children returning home after having moved out. About 46 per cent of parents report adult children aged between 18 and 35 moving back home, a trend continuing from previous surveys. When mum and dad are spending thousands subsidising an adult child’s lifestyle it’s not helping them become financially independent. Getty After a divorce, father of two Ivan* moved into a two-bedroom apartment close to the city. His daughter and son decided to rent elsewhere with their friends. Just as he was getting back on his feet and starting to enjoy single life, his son called and said he couldn’t continue renting and asked if he could move in with him.



“My grocery bills doubled overnight when my son moved back. I went from buying groceries as needed and picking up a handful here and there, to a full-blown grocery shop each week.” Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Want to learn how to invest? Here are three expert tricks and the rule of 72 Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor While his son was studying and getting a study allowance, Ivan was also helping him financially by giving him money each week. “He still needed extra money for bits and pieces.” Eight months later, his son landed a part-time job that was closer to his mother and moved in with her. Things were back to normal and bills gradually decreased, until his daughter was struggling with rent and asked to move in with him. “Here we go again. My daughter does have a part-time job and I don’t have to give her money, but I still help her out. I am back to buying more food, more electricity costs, and she uses my car. I feel that this will be ongoing and, why I feel I will always need a two-bedroom place. It’s tough for kids these days.”



Long showers and leaving lights on A 2025 study from online comparison service, iSelect, combined appliance energy use data, usage habits of Australians aged 18 to 29, and state electricity prices to uncover the cost of energy when living with an additional adult. The data revealed how frequently these young adults living at home use different devices and appliances, such as showers, lights, and kettles and the amount of energy use and costs involved Even a low-usage young adult uses around 1800 kWh per year, costing households approximately an extra $436 annually. At moderate usage, this rises to almost 3000 kWh per year, which equates to around $698 in extra costs. A high-usage young adult can add 4648 kWh per year or around $1061 annually. Mum and dad subsidising lifestyle



Chartered accountant Selina Kulkarni said it’s the long showers, extra loads of washing, lights and heating, food disappearing from the fridge, toilet paper, shampoo, washing powder and all those little household expenses increasing. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert I have two super funds with different strategies. Which should I choose? Paul Benson Money contributor For example, an extra $100 a week in groceries, $20 in utilities and $20 in household supplies is more than $7000 a year. The second big cost people approaching retirement forget about is what that money could have become. Supporting an adult child for several years can quietly mean tens of thousands of dollars less invested for retirement. “I don’t think the answer is trying to charge your kids market rent. If living at home allows a young person to save $15,000 or $20,000 a year towards a house deposit or investments, that can be a brilliant financial decision for the whole family.”



The problem she adds, is when mum and dad are spending thousands subsidising an adult child’s lifestyle, while the child is spending the money they’ve saved on eating out, travel and entertainment. Supporting an adult child for several years can quietly mean tens of thousands of dollars less invested for retirement. iStock “That’s not helping them become financially independent. It’s just transferring the cost of their lifestyle to their parents.” * Names have been changed. Emily Chantiri is a Sydney journalist, bestselling author and regular contributor to Business, Money and Career sections.



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: ‘An institution in the private school system’: The hidden reality of youth gambling
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation ‘An institution in the private school system’: The hidden reality of youth gambling Nicole Precel September 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Students are illegally gambling online, getting around supposed age limits with ease and using phones to place bets while at school. Social media gambling influencers, ads on games or streaming platforms, the ease of setting up betting accounts and the normalisation or parental facilitation of betting have contributed to a rise in teen gambling habits, experts say. Henry Brayshaw, a former Geelong Grammar student who started gambling at 16 and has now pulled himself out of a problem gambling habit. Jason South It’s illegal for anyone to gamble under the age of 18, yet 2025 Australia Institute research that analysed data from 2017, 2023 and 2024 found more than 902,000 Australians aged 12 to 19 gambled annually, enough to fill the MCG about nine times over. About 600,000 were aged between 12 and 17. Monash University associate professor Charles Livingstone, a gambling researcher, said it was easy for teens to set up betting accounts, especially if they already had money from a part-time job.



“If you beg, borrow or steal somebody’s ID, you can set up an account almost instantly,” Livingstone said. He called the online media presence of gambling promoters “extraordinary at the moment”, with social media influencers using gambling as “their schtick” to promote poker machines as well as illegal gambling sites, including offshore casinos that are unlicensed in Australia. Livingstone said there were also “weird little operators” taking bets on school-level football games and on club-level soccer in suburban Melbourne. “At every level you can think of, and a lot you can’t, there is somebody trying to sell kids on gambling.” Jack, 22, given a pseudonym as he asked to remain anonymous, went to a private school and said roughly 25 per cent of his year 12 peers were betting. He started gambling when he was about 16.



“A mate had a big win. [I was thinking] that seems easy. That’s when you start going along with it. You either win, and think it’s easy, and then you lose and you start chasing that loss,” he said. Social media gambling influencers have contributed to the problem. Artwork: Stephen Kiprillis “Boys punted at school – on our phones, in class, at lunchtime, just wherever.” His classmates weren’t allowed phones in class but snuck them in. They made fake accounts under their names using false ages and deposited money but never verified their accounts. “It sounds stupid – even if we won a lot of money, we couldn’t withdraw it. We were just young and dumb. Not making the right decisions.”



After he graduated, he put all of his money – $3500 – on one horse and lost it in one bet. That’s when he knew he had to stop. In June, a gambling website illegally soliciting bets on sporting clashes between Victoria’s most elite private schools was reported to state and federal authorities. How to talk to your children about gambling The state government’s Love the Game not the Odds campaign says attitudes to betting start developing well before someone is legally allowed to bet. It says it’s important to have open conversations about gambling with your kids early. It’s also important to tailor the message so it’s relevant to them, chat in small doses, choose humour, listen to them and practise what you preach. Here are a few conversation starters: Do you think sports betting seems risky?

Do you think people have to gamble to enjoy sports?

What do you think about gambling?

Have any of your friends ever gambled? The Love the Game not the Odds campaign also recommends these talking points: Gambling works on the rules of probability – the odds of winning don’t change.

There’s no such thing as a sure bet. While a gambler’s knowledge may increase, luck and other factors can always change the outcome more.

Gambling ads make betting look like a fun game that everyone wins. But they don’t show the risks. For more advice or support on how to talk to children about gambling, visit Love the Game. The Associated Public Schools group, which consists of 11 schools, including Geelong Grammar, Brighton Grammar and Scotch College, notified the state’s gaming authority and the federal communications watchdog to investigate the site. An Australian Communications and Media Authority spokesperson said it continued to investigate but had pulled the site down.



In 2023, the Victorian Gambling and Casino Control Commission banned betting on any sport in which all the participants are minors. Melbourne teachers Haydn Flanagan and Matthew Sekfy, who have been teaching for 25 years, said they had seen gambling become completely normalised among students in the past four or five years. They have both found students looking at odds in classrooms, sneaking off to bet and openly discussing their wins. One boy cheered in class because he had won $500; another lost $1000. Together Flanagan and Sekfy created Gambling Education Australia, and they deliver preventive sessions to schools and sports clubs in Melbourne and Queensland. “There’s no stigma whatsoever, no thought that it needs to be hidden,” Flanagan said. “Particularly as the weekend comes up, they’re talking about what they’re gambling on, who they’re backing.



“It’s a rite of passage almost in some segments of the community. I’d say particularly rife within the boys’ schools.” He said parent-supported gambling was adding to the problem. Related Article Exclusive

Online gambling Anti-gambling register firm defends industry ties amid debt and tax woes CQUniversity psychology lecturer Dr Cassy Dittman’s research, released in July, found parents were relatively unconcerned about gambling and that parental facilitation – where parents spoke positively about wins or placed bets on their children’s behalf – was the strongest predictor of both teen gambling and gambling problems. Alliance for Gambling Reform lived experience advocate Mark Kempster said that in the past 12 months the fastest rise in gambling he had seen was among teens rather than any other demographic.



“It is more of the private school kids who tend to fall into it quicker and put themselves in bigger holes because of the money they have access to,” he said. Kempster, who gives gambling harm talks in Tasmanian schools, said teachers called him at least monthly about problem gambling in their schools. “I think schools are unaware or naive as to how big a problem this is becoming across all schools,” he said. Government school internet services are filtered to block access to gambling, pornography and other age-inappropriate content. But Kempster said students were gambling at lunchtime, using VPNs or their own phones. He cited the example of a 17-year-old who had been left $20,000 by his late father, and gambled it all away.



“He was an emotional wreck.” Henry Brayshaw says his gambling addiction resulted in a debt of $180,000 at its worst. Jason South Former Geelong Grammar student Henry Brayshaw, now 29, said gambling was an “institution in the private school system”. Brayshaw’s gambling addiction, which started in a pub when he was 16, led to a $180,000 debt at its worst. “It’s like bread and butter for young men out of private school. Really parents with lots of money, kids with credit cards that have got no limits, no true understanding for the value of money,” he said.



“It [became] a deeply embedded, passed down through generations, cultural gambling problem from the moment I entered Geelong Grammar until I left in 2015.” Related Article Exclusive

Online gambling $6b betting giant had 500 problem-gambling breaches, but the regulator took too long to fine it He said some young gamblers didn’t understand the depth of their addiction until they left school. His father, James Brayshaw, a former host of The Footy Show and a sporting commentator, had voiced a 2021 Sportsbet campaign. Henry Brayshaw said they’d become estranged, but not because of gambling. “I would love him to be an advocate against [gambling],” he said. “He always told me ... don’t get hooked in or sucked in.”



In term 2 this year, Geelong Grammar vice principal Tom Hall communicated with secondary school parents about the growing prevalence of sports gambling among young people and to “make [them] aware of a range of measures designed to support students and parents” through education about gambling risks. Gambling harm posters are hung around the school, and students are encouraged to speak with a trusted adult or the school’s counselling team if they are concerned. Livingstone said the number of gambling promotions on social media and by influencers was overwhelming, and the Australian Communications and Media Authority needed more resources to tackle the problem. “It’s a major lapse in the regulatory system that this stuff just happens without anyone seemingly intervening in it,” he said. ACMA issued a warning against a social media influencer for breaching online gambling rules in July. ACMA member Carolyn Lidgerwood said it should also serve as a warning to others.



Australians are banned from promoting illegal gambling services and can face fines of up to $59,400, or up to $2,475,000 if facilitating access through hyperlinks. Related Article Updated

Education Private school sports betting site reported to gambling regulators In August, the federal government passed laws that will restrict advertising related to licensed gambling operators on TV and online from January 1. A Department of Education spokesperson said Victorian schools taught students about the risks of gambling by building an understanding of probability and chance, developing critical analysis skills of media such as gambling ads and promoting strategies for seeking help. Schools can also access Be Ahead of the Game to help young people understand the risks of gambling.
