World.title: ‘Nobody expects a veg dish to be this good’: Nat Thaipun’s crowd-pleasing Thai curry sauce
World.content:
This takes that same delicious idea and turns it into a drizzly, buttery sauce with a nice little kick. It’s built to sit over whatever looks best at the market that week – asparagus is the star today, but it’s just as good with spring beans, sugar snaps, or charred baby zucchini (or big ones – no judgment). Anything with a bit of snap and sweetness holds up to this sauce. Serve it as a killer side, a light main, or bring it to a barbecue – nobody ever expects a veg dish to be this good.

This is an absolute crowd-pleaser – less a strict “recipe” and more a technique you’ll be reaching for all through spring and well into summer. In Thailand, it’s super common to eat raw or lightly blanched veg dipped into rich, curry-style pastes – we call them “dips”.

Plate the vegies and generously drizzle with the curry butter sauce. Finish with sliced chilli, crushed nuts of your choice, and a fine grating of lemon zest.

Stir through the makrut lime leaves and lemon juice. Taste and adjust – it should be rich, a little sweet, salty and bright all at once.

Take off the heat. Using a whisk or hand blender, add the cold butter, a few cubes at a time, until the sauce is glossy and emulsified (see below). Don’t let it boil again or it will split.

Pour in the stock, fish sauce and brown sugar. Simmer gently for 5 minutes to let the flavours come together.

In a saucepan over medium heat, add the oil and coconut cream. Allow the cream to split – it will shift from a smooth, opaque white to a glistening, oily surface with tiny bubbles along the edges. As it cooks off, clear pools of oil will visibly separate and the aroma will become richly fragrant and nutty. Just as it splits, turn the heat down slightly to stop it from spitting, then add the Panang curry paste. Fry, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until deeply flavoursome, fragrant and the oil turns red.

Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Blanch the asparagus or your chosen vegie for 60-90 seconds until it’s bright green and just tender, then shock in iced water. Strain, pat dry, toss with a little oil and salt and set aside or char on a hot grill pan for extra colour just before serving.

Core technique: Emulsifying curry sauces

Emulsifying involves forcing two things that don’t naturally want to mix – such as oil and water – to create a smooth, glossy sauce. Instead of building a heavy curry, I let the coconut cream split first, then whisk in cold butter right at the end. If we don’t split the coconut cream properly at the start, it will split later in the sauce. That’s what gives the sauce its velvety mouthfeel, the kind that coats your tongue but never feels too greasy. (It’s important to note that not everything has to be emulsified. Curries are always split in Thailand and that is the beauty in those curries, however in some of my recipes I’ve purposefully emulsified the sauces, merging more traditional European techniques with Thai flavours.)

In the method, letting the coconut cream “split” means cooking out the water until the natural oil separates and starts to glisten. It’s a classic South-East Asian cooking technique, not a mistake. You “bloom” your curry paste in that rendered coconut oil to really unlock the flavour, then use what’s left of the coconut solids as the base you build your cold butter into.

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up

Because you are balancing heat and fat the whole time, there is always a small risk the sauce might split – but don’t panic.

The sauce should be smooth and emulsified. Dion Georgopoulos

How to fix a split emulsion

A split emulsion almost always comes down to temperature. Either the pan was too hot when the butter went in, or it went in too fast. Here’s how to bring it back.

Pull the pan off the heat completely. The residual heat will keep cooking the emulsion apart, so get it off the stove first. Always use a mat or trivet on your bench under your pan. Pour the split sauce into a jug or bowl. This stops it cooking any further and gives you full control when you rebuild it. (Alternatively, you can put your pan straight into a bowl of ice water, cooling it from the bottom.) When you rebuild it, you’re adding it back a little at a time rather than fighting the whole pan at once. Start a fresh base. In a clean pan or the same one wiped and cooled slightly, gently warm 40ml (2 tbsp) of cream, coconut cream or even just water over low heat. For this Panang curry butter sauce, use coconut cream, but this trick is worth remembering for any butter or cream sauce you’ve split, curry or not. (Note: Sometimes all it takes is to cool the entire base down, and re-whisk it with a whisk or an immersion blender. This solution depends on how much time you’ve got.) Remove the pan from the heat, and gradually whisk the split sauce back into the fresh base, a spoonful at a time, whisking or blending constantly. You are rebuilding the emulsion around a small, stable amount of liquid rather than fighting the whole batch at once. If it starts seizing up or cooling too fast to loosen, put the pan back over the lowest possible heat for a few seconds, whisk, then pull it off again. Once it comes back together and looks glossy, you can slowly stream in the remaining sauce if there’s more to incorporate.

World.title: Since my husband left me, no one thinks I can do my job. I hate it!
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Since my husband left me, no one thinks I can do my job. I hate it! Kirstin Ferguson September 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: unfair assumptions following a divorce, a manager sending AI slop and what to do when your go-to references pass away. Your relationship status should not change your chances of promotion. Dionne Gain Last year, my husband left me after 20 years of marriage. For a few weeks, I’ll admit I was operating on one cylinder at work because of the fallout, but I soon returned to working as hard and capably as ever. Recently, I was overlooked for two opportunities that seemed ideally suited to me. A colleague then confided that she heard a male manager say, “Nah, she hasn’t been any good since her hubby cleared out.” I am deeply offended. Should I confront management or find another job? Related Article Got a Minute? My daughter’s ex-boyfriend is interning in my office. Can I tell HR he’s a creep? I am offended too – on behalf of all women! That comment is insulting, demeaning and breathtakingly unprofessional. It reduces a capable woman’s career to her relationship status and turns a brief, understandable response into a permanent judgment about her competence. Your husband may have left, but he certainly did not take your competence, ambition or professional future with him.



But now for deep breaths. The reality is that you heard this second-hand, so don’t storm into your boss quoting it as fact. What I would do is ask for very specific feedback about why you were overlooked and what criteria were applied. Listen carefully and make notes. You need to establish whether there are legitimate reasons that you didn’t get the role. If you still feel there were no valid reasons other than a misguided perception, you might like to think about whether you want to raise it with someone senior in the organisation. I think your best approach, though, will be to show your managers through your actions how ready you are for the next opportunity. Your future is now in your hands, and I reckon you will knock their socks off. My manager, who put the boss into verbosity, has lately discovered AI on Outlook. So, on top of our endless and time-wasting conversations, I now get spammed by emails full of corporate jargon when all I needed was a yes or no to a simple inquiry. As a frontline worker, I simply don’t have the time for all of this. How do I approach a request for more efficient communication? Sounds like your boss is feeling terribly clever sending out long emails full of big words. It is definitely a good idea to try and nip this in the bud. I am tempted to tell you to reply with a long AI-generated email to see how they enjoy finding a simple yes or no answer in among the slop, but that would be childish ... I think you probably need to tackle this head-on. Explain how busy you are and that in a frontline role you need to be able to make quick decisions. I wouldn’t accuse your boss of outsourcing to AI, but rather say that it is something you are noticing more generally. I would ask if your team could establish a communication protocol – a simple agreement about how you speak to each other by email – and suggest that longer messages be saved for those that really need them. If you point out to your boss that they are most likely to get a quicker reply from a shorter email, that may help, too. Good luck!



I am 58 and work in a specialised field. Although happy in my current role, after five years I have been approached about changing employers. My previous two roles lasted six and five years, but within the past six months, both former managers who acted as my referees have died. Both had direct knowledge of my work and were contacted before I secured my current position. What is the accepted recruitment etiquette now? Must I nominate people with less direct knowledge, or simply explain why my longstanding referees are unavailable? Related Article Got a Minute? I was accused of intimidating my boss. How can I keep working with them? As terribly sad as this is, I don’t think this will have any impact on your recruitment process. If you just explain what has happened, I would expect any recruiter to understand. It is hardly a situation that can be held against you when applying for a new role. In terms of who you should ask to be a referee now, I would choose the strongest alternatives. Ask people who can credibly speak to different aspects of your working like, such as another senior manager, an external stakeholder, a project leader or even a board member. They don’t need to have been your direct supervisor, as long as they can explain the professional relationship and what they observed about your work. If you still have concerns, you can supplement such referees with performance reviews written by your now deceased former managers, as well as any written commendations or significant achievements.

World.title: ASX set to advance, Wall Street steady; Oil prices slip
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance, Wall Street steady; Oil prices slip Stan Choe Updated September 23, 2026 — 6:16am ,first published 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street held near its record high in a relatively quiet day for markets worldwide. The S&P 500 closed flat and is sitting 0.4 per cent below its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 185 points, or 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite advanced 0.5 per cent. Energy and financial stocks fell on Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 5.58am AEST pointing to a rise of 27 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.12¢. US stocks had been higher in the morning, when the price for a barrel of Brent crude briefly fell below $US98. But oil prices later trimmed their losses, and Brent was most recently at $US99.66 per barrel.



That’s down from the nearly $US110 that it touched last week, but it’s still much more expensive than the $US72 it was fetching before the war with Iran began. It’s been swinging with uncertainty about when the war will allow crude to freely flow again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. On Wall Street, AutoZone rose 3.2 per cent after the retailer reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its revenue fell short. CEO Phil Daniele said the auto parts seller faced “a difficult selling environment” in the first two months of the quarter, but it improved afterward and “we feel we are well positioned for sales growth” in its upcoming fiscal year. Related Article Opinion

Oil ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At Thor Industries, which sells recreational vehicles, the mood was more muted. CEO Bob Martin said expensive fuel, high interest rates and still-high inflation are stretching its customers’ budgets, and business “never reached the inflection point many in the industry expected” in its latest fiscal year. Its stock rose 5.5 per cent, though, after it delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Such strong profit reports are one of the main reasons the US stock market has reached the brink of its all-time high despite high oil prices and jitters about whether stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry shot too high. Many companies are close to closing the books on their third quarter of the year, which ends with September. And analysts are forecasting companies in the S&P 500 will report overall growth of nearly 29 per cent for the quarter from a year earlier, according to FactSet. If they’re right, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25 per cent for the index. And stock prices tend to follow the track of corporate profits over the long term. On Holding’s stock that trades in the United States jumped 8.6 per cent after the Swiss sneaker and sportswear company unveiled its financial goals for upcoming years. It also approved a plan to buy back up to $US1 billion ($1.4 billion) of its stock through 2029. Such purchases send cash directly to investors and boost the company’s per-share performance. On the losing end of Wall Street were several stocks of companies in the oil and gas industry, which were hurt by the drop in crude prices. ConocoPhillips fell 1.8 per cent.



Banks also dropped, continuing their weak run since last week, when the Federal Reserve raised the overnight interest rate that it controls for the first time in three years. When the spread narrows between short-term interest rates and longer ones, banks come under pressure because they make profit off the difference. JPMorgan Chase fell 3.4 per cent and was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500. Related Article Aviation Jetstar staff to stop charging baggage and seat fees in union protest The gap between short- and long-term yields in the bond market did not move much, as the 10-year Treasury yield held steady at 4.96 per cent from late Monday. Like oil prices, it also remains far above where it was before the war with Iran began, when it was at 3.97 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher across much of Europe and Asia. World.title: Rape victims claim Swans sex assault case on the fast track while their complaints are dogged by delays
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Rape victims claim Swans sex assault case on the fast track while their complaints are dogged by delays Carla Jaeger and Cameron Houston September 23, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two rape victims have expressed fury over what they describe as a stark contrast between their cases and the intensive and rapid Victoria Police investigation into allegations of sexual assault involving Sydney Swans players. Despite having never met, both women detailed remarkably similar experiences, claiming they were treated with hostility while their cases were beset by unnecessary delays and police under-resourcing. Melbourne woman Sam says she has been failed by police investigating her alleged rape case. Simon Schluter One believes she may never see justice after the man accused of drugging and raping her in South Melbourne last month was able to flee home to Mexico after Victoria Police failed to place a border alert on him. The women’s decision to speak publicly come as Victoria’s unsolved sexual-crime case rate soars to record highs.



Sam, who waived her legal right to anonymity but asked that her surname not be used, now regrets notifying police after she was allegedly raped in May by a man she met on a dating site. Her frustration over the handling of the case turned to fury last month when she observed the police response to claims of sexual assault involving a group of Sydney Swans players at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. “Excuse my language, but it made me f---king livid. Clearly, they’ve got the resources when it comes to a high-profile case because they know that they’ll be under media scrutiny. But for a normal person like myself, the lack of care is just so evident,” Sam told this masthead. “They can fly detectives into New South Wales to question them within a couple of weeks, but they can’t go a suburb over to go and pull someone in for questioning.”



For 30-year-old Katie Arthur, the trauma from the police’s response to her complaint has, in some ways, eclipsed the alleged crime itself. Arthur felt a similar fury to Sam’s about the pace of the police response to her case. While pleading to come in and provide her statement sooner, she remembers asking – in a moment of exasperation – “What if I said I was raped by a football player?” “I can’t process what has happened to me because I’m too busy now trying to process the letdown of the police [response],” she said.



Arthur has also given permission for her full name to be published. “No one grows up dreaming of being the [rape victim in the paper]. But I now see the media as such a powerful outlet to speak on behalf of victims that have been let down by the one system supposed to protect them.” A Victoria Police spokesperson said the force had been in “constant contact” with both victims and detectives had referred them to support services. “Both [investigation] teams are progressing these matter as quickly as possible, noting the cases are complex, and we must ensure investigations are thorough,” the spokesperson said. “We also want to be clear that any report of sexual assault is not treated any differently because we have someone with a high profile involved.”



Arthur was allegedly drugged and raped on August 2 by a tenant staying at her midterm accommodation business. Grappling with shame and shock, she struggled to process the alleged attack before eventually reporting the incident to police on August 18. Arthur was forced to wait another 10 days to make a formal statement, despite pleading to come in earlier and repeatedly warning police via phone and email that her alleged attacker was a flight risk. “I am concerned the alleged rapist will leave the country as he is on a 5/6 month student visa,” she wrote in one email shared with this masthead. Detectives from Melbourne’s Sexual Offences and Child Abuse Investigations Team (SOCIT) informed her they were too busy, with one detective citing crippling understaffing, claiming their team of five was juggling 108 active cases.



Victoria Police said the delay in recording a statement was to ensure there was enough time to make a detailed report. Despite Arthur’s warnings, the accused fled the country on August 20 or 21 – but she didn’t find out until September 3 despite being terrified that a sexual predator was still residing at her property. “I needed to know if he was still in the country,” she said. “Not only for my safety, but he was living at the business I run. I have a duty of care to my other tenants.” After making her statement, Arthur said detectives stonewalled her requests for updates, and questioned why she took two weeks to make her complaint.



“You’re saying you will judge the severity of someone’s case by how quickly they come forward. It’s disgusting. You may as well say, ‘Don’t come forward unless you’ve been raped that day’,” Arthur said. Related Article Domestic violence Life sentences for rape, new charge for ‘slow femicide’ in Labor domestic violence pledge A detective outside of Melbourne SOCIT is now reviewing the unit’s handling of her case after Arthur lodged a complaint. Victoria Police said: “We take any allegations against the conduct of our members seriously and have strict procedures and policies in place. “No alert was issued for restrictions on international travel because police did not have evidence to meet the legal threshold required to prevent the person leaving the country.”



Arthur is now grappling with the reality that the man accused of attacking her may never face justice. “I can’t explain the trauma of not only experiencing assault ... but being forced to be your own advocate, and feeling like you are not believed. “It’s just as traumatising as being assaulted.” Sam agonised over whether to make a report to police. “I sat outside Oakleigh police station and tried to go in, and I was just numb and had no idea what to do. And I was afraid of not being believed,” she said.



Sam underwent a forensic examination at Monash Hospital the day after her alleged assault on May 18. She provided detectives with a statement on May 24, but claims to have been treated with a lack of empathy ever since. She says her concerns about the pace and rigour of the police investigation have been repeatedly dismissed. “There has been no empathy or understanding … the officer in charge of my investigation would keep saying: ‘Sam, you’re one of 30 cases that I have’,” she said. The Victoria Police spokesperson said the “safety of victims was at the forefront for police” and that unsolved cases continue to be investigated. They added that the timing of Sam’s report to police was of her choosing. “She first wanted to take some time to consider taking police action.”



The women’s complaints come after Victoria recorded 2962 unsolved sexual offence cases at the end of March 2026, a rolling figure that leapt by 1172 cases (66 per cent) in 12 months, Crime Statistics Victoria figures show. The rise follows a recorded 1790 unsolved cases in 2025, up 240 from the year prior. Meanwhile, 2024 recorded just 33 more unsolved cases than 2023’s total of 1517. Total sexual offences in Victoria dropped slightly between 2025 and 2026, recording 685 fewer offences at the end of March 2026. At the same time, unsolved cases spiked, arrests fell, and fewer complaints were withdrawn. An intent to summons, which indicates police intend to charge somebody but have not yet done so, more than doubled from 458 in 2025 to 1066 in 2026. Sam was told the officer responsible for her complaint had been forced to take stress leave because she was burnt out by her caseload. “Their workload should not be my problem. I said her, ‘What if this was your daughter, if this was your mother, this was your sister, a close friend? Would you accept that?’,” Sam said.



“The whole system has completely let me down, and it’s made me go. Why would I ever go to the police again,” she asked. Arthur feels similarly: “If you want to hold a perpetrator accountable, you need to be a lawyer. You need to be your own detective. You need to be your own everything. “You need to have everything written down and have zero trust that they’ll be able to actually do anything.” Victoria Police did not respond to a question about staffing of their SOCIT units. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Kids moving back home? Here’s what it could really cost you
World.content:
Analysis MoneyPlanning & budgetingSpending Kids moving back home? Here’s what it could really cost you Emily Chantiri September 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you have ever had an adult child leave home, you’ll understand that the chapter is never really closed, until they’re fully established or coupled. That said, many young couples also return to live with a parent to save money and buy a home. Fortune 500 financial services company Thrivent’s 2025 fourth annual Boomerang Kids Survey found parents are now more likely than ever to provide temporary financial support for adult children returning home after having moved out. About 46 per cent of parents report adult children aged between 18 and 35 moving back home, a trend continuing from previous surveys. When mum and dad are spending thousands subsidising an adult child’s lifestyle it’s not helping them become financially independent. Getty After a divorce, father of two Ivan* moved into a two-bedroom apartment close to the city. His daughter and son decided to rent elsewhere with their friends. Just as he was getting back on his feet and starting to enjoy single life, his son called and said he couldn’t continue renting and asked if he could move in with him.



“My grocery bills doubled overnight when my son moved back. I went from buying groceries as needed and picking up a handful here and there, to a full-blown grocery shop each week.” Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Want to learn how to invest? Here are three expert tricks and the rule of 72 Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor While his son was studying and getting a study allowance, Ivan was also helping him financially by giving him money each week. “He still needed extra money for bits and pieces.” Eight months later, his son landed a part-time job that was closer to his mother and moved in with her. Things were back to normal and bills gradually decreased, until his daughter was struggling with rent and asked to move in with him. “Here we go again. My daughter does have a part-time job and I don’t have to give her money, but I still help her out. I am back to buying more food, more electricity costs, and she uses my car. I feel that this will be ongoing and, why I feel I will always need a two-bedroom place. It’s tough for kids these days.”



Long showers and leaving lights on A 2025 study from online comparison service, iSelect, combined appliance energy use data, usage habits of Australians aged 18 to 29, and state electricity prices to uncover the cost of energy when living with an additional adult. The data revealed how frequently these young adults living at home use different devices and appliances, such as showers, lights, and kettles and the amount of energy use and costs involved Even a low-usage young adult uses around 1800 kWh per year, costing households approximately an extra $436 annually. At moderate usage, this rises to almost 3000 kWh per year, which equates to around $698 in extra costs. A high-usage young adult can add 4648 kWh per year or around $1061 annually. Mum and dad subsidising lifestyle



Chartered accountant Selina Kulkarni said it’s the long showers, extra loads of washing, lights and heating, food disappearing from the fridge, toilet paper, shampoo, washing powder and all those little household expenses increasing. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert I have two super funds with different strategies. Which should I choose? Paul Benson Money contributor For example, an extra $100 a week in groceries, $20 in utilities and $20 in household supplies is more than $7000 a year. The second big cost people approaching retirement forget about is what that money could have become. Supporting an adult child for several years can quietly mean tens of thousands of dollars less invested for retirement. “I don’t think the answer is trying to charge your kids market rent. If living at home allows a young person to save $15,000 or $20,000 a year towards a house deposit or investments, that can be a brilliant financial decision for the whole family.”



The problem she adds, is when mum and dad are spending thousands subsidising an adult child’s lifestyle, while the child is spending the money they’ve saved on eating out, travel and entertainment. Supporting an adult child for several years can quietly mean tens of thousands of dollars less invested for retirement. iStock “That’s not helping them become financially independent. It’s just transferring the cost of their lifestyle to their parents.” * Names have been changed. Emily Chantiri is a Sydney journalist, bestselling author and regular contributor to Business, Money and Career sections.



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: ‘An institution in the private school system’: The hidden reality of youth gambling
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation ‘An institution in the private school system’: The hidden reality of youth gambling Nicole Precel September 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Students are illegally gambling online, getting around supposed age limits with ease and using phones to place bets while at school. Social media gambling influencers, ads on games or streaming platforms, the ease of setting up betting accounts and the normalisation or parental facilitation of betting have contributed to a rise in teen gambling habits, experts say. Henry Brayshaw, a former Geelong Grammar student who started gambling at 16 and has now pulled himself out of a problem gambling habit. Jason South It’s illegal for anyone to gamble under the age of 18, yet 2025 Australia Institute research that analysed data from 2017, 2023 and 2024 found more than 902,000 Australians aged 12 to 19 gambled annually, enough to fill the MCG about nine times over. About 600,000 were aged between 12 and 17. Monash University associate professor Charles Livingstone, a gambling researcher, said it was easy for teens to set up betting accounts, especially if they already had money from a part-time job.



“If you beg, borrow or steal somebody’s ID, you can set up an account almost instantly,” Livingstone said. He called the online media presence of gambling promoters “extraordinary at the moment”, with social media influencers using gambling as “their schtick” to promote poker machines as well as illegal gambling sites, including offshore casinos that are unlicensed in Australia. Livingstone said there were also “weird little operators” taking bets on school-level football games and on club-level soccer in suburban Melbourne. “At every level you can think of, and a lot you can’t, there is somebody trying to sell kids on gambling.” Jack, 22, given a pseudonym as he asked to remain anonymous, went to a private school and said roughly 25 per cent of his year 12 peers were betting. He started gambling when he was about 16.



“A mate had a big win. [I was thinking] that seems easy. That’s when you start going along with it. You either win, and think it’s easy, and then you lose and you start chasing that loss,” he said. Social media gambling influencers have contributed to the problem. Artwork: Stephen Kiprillis “Boys punted at school – on our phones, in class, at lunchtime, just wherever.” His classmates weren’t allowed phones in class but snuck them in. They made fake accounts under their names using false ages and deposited money but never verified their accounts. “It sounds stupid – even if we won a lot of money, we couldn’t withdraw it. We were just young and dumb. Not making the right decisions.”



After he graduated, he put all of his money – $3500 – on one horse and lost it in one bet. That’s when he knew he had to stop. In June, a gambling website illegally soliciting bets on sporting clashes between Victoria’s most elite private schools was reported to state and federal authorities. How to talk to your children about gambling The state government’s Love the Game not the Odds campaign says attitudes to betting start developing well before someone is legally allowed to bet. It says it’s important to have open conversations about gambling with your kids early. It’s also important to tailor the message so it’s relevant to them, chat in small doses, choose humour, listen to them and practise what you preach. Here are a few conversation starters: Do you think sports betting seems risky?

Do you think people have to gamble to enjoy sports?

What do you think about gambling?

Have any of your friends ever gambled? The Love the Game not the Odds campaign also recommends these talking points: Gambling works on the rules of probability – the odds of winning don’t change.

There’s no such thing as a sure bet. While a gambler’s knowledge may increase, luck and other factors can always change the outcome more.

Gambling ads make betting look like a fun game that everyone wins. But they don’t show the risks. For more advice or support on how to talk to children about gambling, visit Love the Game. The Associated Public Schools group, which consists of 11 schools, including Geelong Grammar, Brighton Grammar and Scotch College, notified the state’s gaming authority and the federal communications watchdog to investigate the site. An Australian Communications and Media Authority spokesperson said it continued to investigate but had pulled the site down.



In 2023, the Victorian Gambling and Casino Control Commission banned betting on any sport in which all the participants are minors. Melbourne teachers Haydn Flanagan and Matthew Sekfy, who have been teaching for 25 years, said they had seen gambling become completely normalised among students in the past four or five years. They have both found students looking at odds in classrooms, sneaking off to bet and openly discussing their wins. One boy cheered in class because he had won $500; another lost $1000. Together Flanagan and Sekfy created Gambling Education Australia, and they deliver preventive sessions to schools and sports clubs in Melbourne and Queensland. “There’s no stigma whatsoever, no thought that it needs to be hidden,” Flanagan said. “Particularly as the weekend comes up, they’re talking about what they’re gambling on, who they’re backing.



“It’s a rite of passage almost in some segments of the community. I’d say particularly rife within the boys’ schools.” He said parent-supported gambling was adding to the problem. Related Article Exclusive

Online gambling Anti-gambling register firm defends industry ties amid debt and tax woes CQUniversity psychology lecturer Dr Cassy Dittman’s research, released in July, found parents were relatively unconcerned about gambling and that parental facilitation – where parents spoke positively about wins or placed bets on their children’s behalf – was the strongest predictor of both teen gambling and gambling problems. Alliance for Gambling Reform lived experience advocate Mark Kempster said that in the past 12 months the fastest rise in gambling he had seen was among teens rather than any other demographic.



“It is more of the private school kids who tend to fall into it quicker and put themselves in bigger holes because of the money they have access to,” he said. Kempster, who gives gambling harm talks in Tasmanian schools, said teachers called him at least monthly about problem gambling in their schools. “I think schools are unaware or naive as to how big a problem this is becoming across all schools,” he said. Government school internet services are filtered to block access to gambling, pornography and other age-inappropriate content. But Kempster said students were gambling at lunchtime, using VPNs or their own phones. He cited the example of a 17-year-old who had been left $20,000 by his late father, and gambled it all away.



“He was an emotional wreck.” Henry Brayshaw says his gambling addiction resulted in a debt of $180,000 at its worst. Jason South Former Geelong Grammar student Henry Brayshaw, now 29, said gambling was an “institution in the private school system”. Brayshaw’s gambling addiction, which started in a pub when he was 16, led to a $180,000 debt at its worst. “It’s like bread and butter for young men out of private school. Really parents with lots of money, kids with credit cards that have got no limits, no true understanding for the value of money,” he said.



“It [became] a deeply embedded, passed down through generations, cultural gambling problem from the moment I entered Geelong Grammar until I left in 2015.” Related Article Exclusive

Online gambling $6b betting giant had 500 problem-gambling breaches, but the regulator took too long to fine it He said some young gamblers didn’t understand the depth of their addiction until they left school. His father, James Brayshaw, a former host of The Footy Show and a sporting commentator, had voiced a 2021 Sportsbet campaign. Henry Brayshaw said they’d become estranged, but not because of gambling. “I would love him to be an advocate against [gambling],” he said. “He always told me ... don’t get hooked in or sucked in.”



In term 2 this year, Geelong Grammar vice principal Tom Hall communicated with secondary school parents about the growing prevalence of sports gambling among young people and to “make [them] aware of a range of measures designed to support students and parents” through education about gambling risks. Gambling harm posters are hung around the school, and students are encouraged to speak with a trusted adult or the school’s counselling team if they are concerned. Livingstone said the number of gambling promotions on social media and by influencers was overwhelming, and the Australian Communications and Media Authority needed more resources to tackle the problem. “It’s a major lapse in the regulatory system that this stuff just happens without anyone seemingly intervening in it,” he said. ACMA issued a warning against a social media influencer for breaching online gambling rules in July. ACMA member Carolyn Lidgerwood said it should also serve as a warning to others.



Australians are banned from promoting illegal gambling services and can face fines of up to $59,400, or up to $2,475,000 if facilitating access through hyperlinks. Related Article Updated

Education Private school sports betting site reported to gambling regulators In August, the federal government passed laws that will restrict advertising related to licensed gambling operators on TV and online from January 1. A Department of Education spokesperson said Victorian schools taught students about the risks of gambling by building an understanding of probability and chance, developing critical analysis skills of media such as gambling ads and promoting strategies for seeking help. Schools can also access Be Ahead of the Game to help young people understand the risks of gambling.

World.title: ‘Nobody expects a veg dish to be this good’: Nat Thaipun’s crowd-pleasing Thai curry sauce
World.content:
This takes that same delicious idea and turns it into a drizzly, buttery sauce with a nice little kick. It’s built to sit over whatever looks best at the market that week – asparagus is the star today, but it’s just as good with spring beans, sugar snaps, or charred baby zucchini (or big ones – no judgment). Anything with a bit of snap and sweetness holds up to this sauce. Serve it as a killer side, a light main, or bring it to a barbecue – nobody ever expects a veg dish to be this good.

This is an absolute crowd-pleaser – less a strict “recipe” and more a technique you’ll be reaching for all through spring and well into summer. In Thailand, it’s super common to eat raw or lightly blanched veg dipped into rich, curry-style pastes – we call them “dips”.

Plate the vegies and generously drizzle with the curry butter sauce. Finish with sliced chilli, crushed nuts of your choice, and a fine grating of lemon zest.

Stir through the makrut lime leaves and lemon juice. Taste and adjust – it should be rich, a little sweet, salty and bright all at once.

Take off the heat. Using a whisk or hand blender, add the cold butter, a few cubes at a time, until the sauce is glossy and emulsified (see below). Don’t let it boil again or it will split.

Pour in the stock, fish sauce and brown sugar. Simmer gently for 5 minutes to let the flavours come together.

In a saucepan over medium heat, add the oil and coconut cream. Allow the cream to split – it will shift from a smooth, opaque white to a glistening, oily surface with tiny bubbles along the edges. As it cooks off, clear pools of oil will visibly separate and the aroma will become richly fragrant and nutty. Just as it splits, turn the heat down slightly to stop it from spitting, then add the Panang curry paste. Fry, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until deeply flavoursome, fragrant and the oil turns red.

Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Blanch the asparagus or your chosen vegie for 60-90 seconds until it’s bright green and just tender, then shock in iced water. Strain, pat dry, toss with a little oil and salt and set aside or char on a hot grill pan for extra colour just before serving.

Core technique: Emulsifying curry sauces

Emulsifying involves forcing two things that don’t naturally want to mix – such as oil and water – to create a smooth, glossy sauce. Instead of building a heavy curry, I let the coconut cream split first, then whisk in cold butter right at the end. If we don’t split the coconut cream properly at the start, it will split later in the sauce. That’s what gives the sauce its velvety mouthfeel, the kind that coats your tongue but never feels too greasy. (It’s important to note that not everything has to be emulsified. Curries are always split in Thailand and that is the beauty in those curries, however in some of my recipes I’ve purposefully emulsified the sauces, merging more traditional European techniques with Thai flavours.)

In the method, letting the coconut cream “split” means cooking out the water until the natural oil separates and starts to glisten. It’s a classic South-East Asian cooking technique, not a mistake. You “bloom” your curry paste in that rendered coconut oil to really unlock the flavour, then use what’s left of the coconut solids as the base you build your cold butter into.

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up

Because you are balancing heat and fat the whole time, there is always a small risk the sauce might split – but don’t panic.

The sauce should be smooth and emulsified. Dion Georgopoulos

How to fix a split emulsion

A split emulsion almost always comes down to temperature. Either the pan was too hot when the butter went in, or it went in too fast. Here’s how to bring it back.

Pull the pan off the heat completely. The residual heat will keep cooking the emulsion apart, so get it off the stove first. Always use a mat or trivet on your bench under your pan. Pour the split sauce into a jug or bowl. This stops it cooking any further and gives you full control when you rebuild it. (Alternatively, you can put your pan straight into a bowl of ice water, cooling it from the bottom.) When you rebuild it, you’re adding it back a little at a time rather than fighting the whole pan at once. Start a fresh base. In a clean pan or the same one wiped and cooled slightly, gently warm 40ml (2 tbsp) of cream, coconut cream or even just water over low heat. For this Panang curry butter sauce, use coconut cream, but this trick is worth remembering for any butter or cream sauce you’ve split, curry or not. (Note: Sometimes all it takes is to cool the entire base down, and re-whisk it with a whisk or an immersion blender. This solution depends on how much time you’ve got.) Remove the pan from the heat, and gradually whisk the split sauce back into the fresh base, a spoonful at a time, whisking or blending constantly. You are rebuilding the emulsion around a small, stable amount of liquid rather than fighting the whole batch at once. If it starts seizing up or cooling too fast to loosen, put the pan back over the lowest possible heat for a few seconds, whisk, then pull it off again. Once it comes back together and looks glossy, you can slowly stream in the remaining sauce if there’s more to incorporate.

World.title: Since my husband left me, no one thinks I can do my job. I hate it!
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Since my husband left me, no one thinks I can do my job. I hate it! Kirstin Ferguson September 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: unfair assumptions following a divorce, a manager sending AI slop and what to do when your go-to references pass away. Your relationship status should not change your chances of promotion. Dionne Gain Last year, my husband left me after 20 years of marriage. For a few weeks, I’ll admit I was operating on one cylinder at work because of the fallout, but I soon returned to working as hard and capably as ever. Recently, I was overlooked for two opportunities that seemed ideally suited to me. A colleague then confided that she heard a male manager say, “Nah, she hasn’t been any good since her hubby cleared out.” I am deeply offended. Should I confront management or find another job? Related Article Got a Minute? My daughter’s ex-boyfriend is interning in my office. Can I tell HR he’s a creep? I am offended too – on behalf of all women! That comment is insulting, demeaning and breathtakingly unprofessional. It reduces a capable woman’s career to her relationship status and turns a brief, understandable response into a permanent judgment about her competence. Your husband may have left, but he certainly did not take your competence, ambition or professional future with him.



But now for deep breaths. The reality is that you heard this second-hand, so don’t storm into your boss quoting it as fact. What I would do is ask for very specific feedback about why you were overlooked and what criteria were applied. Listen carefully and make notes. You need to establish whether there are legitimate reasons that you didn’t get the role. If you still feel there were no valid reasons other than a misguided perception, you might like to think about whether you want to raise it with someone senior in the organisation. I think your best approach, though, will be to show your managers through your actions how ready you are for the next opportunity. Your future is now in your hands, and I reckon you will knock their socks off. My manager, who put the boss into verbosity, has lately discovered AI on Outlook. So, on top of our endless and time-wasting conversations, I now get spammed by emails full of corporate jargon when all I needed was a yes or no to a simple inquiry. As a frontline worker, I simply don’t have the time for all of this. How do I approach a request for more efficient communication? Sounds like your boss is feeling terribly clever sending out long emails full of big words. It is definitely a good idea to try and nip this in the bud. I am tempted to tell you to reply with a long AI-generated email to see how they enjoy finding a simple yes or no answer in among the slop, but that would be childish ... I think you probably need to tackle this head-on. Explain how busy you are and that in a frontline role you need to be able to make quick decisions. I wouldn’t accuse your boss of outsourcing to AI, but rather say that it is something you are noticing more generally. I would ask if your team could establish a communication protocol – a simple agreement about how you speak to each other by email – and suggest that longer messages be saved for those that really need them. If you point out to your boss that they are most likely to get a quicker reply from a shorter email, that may help, too. Good luck!



I am 58 and work in a specialised field. Although happy in my current role, after five years I have been approached about changing employers. My previous two roles lasted six and five years, but within the past six months, both former managers who acted as my referees have died. Both had direct knowledge of my work and were contacted before I secured my current position. What is the accepted recruitment etiquette now? Must I nominate people with less direct knowledge, or simply explain why my longstanding referees are unavailable? Related Article Got a Minute? I was accused of intimidating my boss. How can I keep working with them? As terribly sad as this is, I don’t think this will have any impact on your recruitment process. If you just explain what has happened, I would expect any recruiter to understand. It is hardly a situation that can be held against you when applying for a new role. In terms of who you should ask to be a referee now, I would choose the strongest alternatives. Ask people who can credibly speak to different aspects of your working like, such as another senior manager, an external stakeholder, a project leader or even a board member. They don’t need to have been your direct supervisor, as long as they can explain the professional relationship and what they observed about your work. If you still have concerns, you can supplement such referees with performance reviews written by your now deceased former managers, as well as any written commendations or significant achievements.

World.title: MBIE confirms botched biometric projects costs blown out to $50.7 million
World.content:
A botched Immigration New Zealand project that has subsequently been abandoned has racked up costs of more than $50 million.

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakely appeared before MPs at select committee on Wednesday morning, the final sitting day of this parliamentary term, and confirmed $50.7 million of taxpayers' money has now been wasted on the biometric capability upgrades.

Blakely was found in contempt of parliament last month for deliberately misleading MPs about the failed I.T projects.

He told the committee on Wednesday he deeply regrets the position MBIE has found itself in, and "I recognise that we have a mountain to climb to rebuild the trust and confidence of this committee and of the Parliament."

"As chief executive, I take responsibility for the failures and I'm taking accountability by making the changes needed to strengthen the organisation. And I know that I will be judged on the results."

"In response to these deeply concerning failures, I've set up a structured programme of assurance work. Since we were last before you, we've now completed a stocktake of 70 active technology projects," Blakely told the committee.

"Going forward, we will report publicly on a quarterly basis on our technology portfolio, so there is open movement on whether our changes are improving performance.

"I'll consider the Public Service Commission's hearing report, findings, and take any necessary action, including employment actions where appropriate," Blakely said.

The privileges committee ruling that found Blakely in contempt prompted him at the time to offer his resignation to Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche, but it was turned down.

Roche said he took several factors into account when weighing that decision, including that Blakeley had been fresh into his job and had unreservedly apologised for his actions.

During a select committee appearance in March, Blakeley was asked about the progress of a biometric upgrade programme but failed to disclose that the project had already been cancelled.

In its findings, the Privileges Committee said officials would have known their incomplete answers would leave MPs with a false impression.

"The limited manner in which the ministry answered questions... was intentional," it said.

"We find that the ministry deliberately misled the Education and Workforce Committee and, in doing so, committed a contempt."

The report said it was "alarming" that neither of the senior public servants were aware they could have requested to provide evidence in private or secret.

"We wish to be very clear: officials appearing before select committees have an absolute obligation to tell the truth. Being truthful, responsible, and acting in good faith is the very essence of public service.

"To fail to meet these obligations is an insult to the entire public service."
