Tech.title: San Francisco sues Trump Media for selling early access to Trump posts
Tech.content:
is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

San Francisco is suing the Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company behind Truth Social, for selling early access to President Donald Trump’s posts on the social media site. The lawsuit, filed today in California state court, alleges that the Truth API feed is a “corrupt business scheme” that violates both California’s Unfair Competition Law and federal ethics and anti-corruption laws that prohibit insider trading.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle recently called Truth Social the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” While the latter part of that statement is objectively untrue based on any credible estimates — in fact, Truth Social traffic has declined over the last year — Trump often makes high-stakes announcements in his capacity as president on the platform, and his posts there have a clear effect on the global economy. To capitalize on this, Trump Media recently launched Truth API, a service that charges select customers $100,000 a month for early access to the 10 most influential accounts on Truth Social, including Trump’s and those of other White House officials. Trump Media’s interim CEO, Kevin McGurn, acknowledged as much in his announcement of Truth API, saying that “markets already move on Truth Social posts.”

The San Francisco lawsuit cites several examples of this, some of which took place after the launch of Truth API. On August 21st, for example, Trump posted that the federal government was going to “lower the price of ground beef for working families” by exempting some ground beef imports from tariffs. When the market opened a few hours later, cattle futures declined significantly, according to the complaint.

In today’s markets, early access means millions of dollars. This business scheme has turned public trust into private property.

“Trump Media has unlawfully created, priced, marketed, and operated a commercial mechanism that knowingly and willfully facilitates Trump’s use of nonpublic information for private profit,” the complaint alleges. The San Francisco suit alleges that Truth API is a way of making the floundering Trump Media — which reported a net loss of more than $238 million earlier this year — profitable.

Per his agreement with Trump Media, Truth Social has a six-hour exclusivity window on Trump’s posts, meaning he can’t post the same material elsewhere in that time frame. Even before the launch of Truth API, Trump’s Truth Social profile was extremely valuable for investors — so valuable that the company has sought to capitalize on it. The San Francisco complaint cites reports of hedge fund executives who say they feel pressured to buy the service even though they think it’s legally risky. “It’s a pay-to-play scheme for early access to the president’s market-moving government statements,” San Francisco city attorney David Chiu said in a Tuesday press conference. “In today’s markets, early access means millions of dollars. This business scheme has turned public trust into private property.” Beyond violating insider trading laws, the suit claims, Truth API disadvantages everyday investors by paywalling financially valuable information.

Trump Media hasn’t disclosed its list of Truth API clients, but the company has said it plans on marketing the product to AI companies and large news organizations.

The city has asked a judge to forbid Trump Media from offering Truth API or similar services, and to impose a fine of $2,500 per violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law.

This isn’t the first time Trump has been sued over Truth API. In August, The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a joint lawsuit in a New York federal court over the product, which it called “extraordinary, corrupt, and unconstitutional.”

Tech.title: Apple is reportedly working on a Whoop-like fitness tracker
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is working on a new fitness tracker with a screenless design, similar to the one made by Whoop, according to a report from Bloomberg. A prototype of the device reportedly has “a thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module.”

The device is in an early stage of development and likely wouldn’t arrive before 2028 if Apple decides to release it, Bloomberg reports. In addition to Whoop’s lineup of 5.0 bands, the company also sells MG — or “medical grade” — variants with a built-in EKG feature. The bands are designed to be worn continuously, as they offer more than 14 days of battery life.

As pointed out by Bloomberg, Apple has added several features already offered by Whoop to its new Apple Watch Series 12, including continuous heart rate tracking. Apple’s Health app also now has a “readiness score” used by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop, which is supposed to tell you how “ready” you are to work out based on several factors, along with an estimate of your biological age.

Tech.title: Qualcomm launches two new smartphone chips with emphasis on AI
Tech.content:
Qualcomm today announced two flagship smartphone processors, called Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with a focus on facilitating better AI-focused features.

At its annual Snapdragon Summit, Qualcomm said that the new chips can aid in improved personalization for AI agents. The chips have new sensing hubs that can run small models of up to 200 million parameters. With the new sensing hub, smartphones can run a personal scribe locally and differentiate between speakers. Plus, it can build memory based on your usage for better suggestions for automating tasks. The company said that it can run a complete voice-in and voice-out agent through the new chip

The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 has a new accelerator element that’s designed to run models in a more efficient way. The high-end Extreme version can run a 30 billion parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally. This means that while the overall model size is 30B, the model only activates a certain number of parameters for a particular task.

For comparison, at its Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple released a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, the most advanced of its third generation of foundation models.

The new Qualcomm CPU also provides pixel-level control for cameras to facilitate more pro-level experiences, along with improved stabilization and motion understanding. The Extreme version can support video recording at 8k60fps and at 4K240 for ultra HD slow-motion. It also enables the new Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec for pro-level recording.

What’s more, both chips can use AI to boost vocals and reduce noise. Plus, it has Qualcomm’s new voice bubble tech, which isolates users’ noise during calls.

At the event, Motorola announced its Motorola Signature 27 smartphone, powered by the Snapdragon Gen 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with general availability sometime this year.

Qualcomm has been working on more than 40 AI devices, but there is still a belief that a lot of people will use their phones for AI rather than other dedicated devices. Nothing co-founder Carl Pei has hinted at this trend in the past, and more recently, new Apple CEO John Ternus reinforced the same line of thought during the iPhone Duo launch earlier this month.

Tech.title: Apple could take on Whoop with a new fitness tracker, report says
Tech.content:
In Brief

Apple is in the process of developing a new screen-less fitness tracker that would put it into competition with Whoop — the fitness tech firm whose valuation recently crested $10 billion.

Bloomberg reports that the iPhone maker is currently engaged in a “technology investigation” — which, just as it sounds, is an exploratory effort to decide whether it will fully develop a product and release it. A number of prototypes have been developed around the item, the outlet notes.

The device — which is described as “a thin fabric band with a sensor-equipped computing module” — would not be released until at least 2028, Bloomberg said.

It’s worth noting that Apple already sells a fitness tracker in the form of its Apple Watch (the wearable records workouts, heart rate, sleep, and other categories). However, the new form factor sounds relatively similar to Whoop, which sells simple fitness bands that the company says can track a variety of health metrics.

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information.

The report arrives at a time when Apple is in a period of transition. Tim Cook stepped down from his position as CEO in August to now act as executive chairman, as new CEO John Ternus took the wheel. The company has also faced headwinds due to rising costs from a memory shortage. Despite this, it has promised a slate of new devices, including a new foldable phone, new tablets, and a new MacBook Pro. Meanwhile, it’s engaged in litigation against OpenAI, which it has accused of trade theft, as the battle to build the best hardware for the AI age continues.

Tech.title: Meta admits Muse’s likeness to OpenClaw isn’t a coincidence
Tech.content:
Early adopters of Meta’s Muse have been speculating that the reason the AI works so well is because it’s OpenClaw under the hood, wrapped in a more consumer-friendly package. Meta now says those comparisons aren’t entirely off-base. According to an X post by Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs (MSL), Muse was “definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw.”

However, he clarified that Muse itself was “built from scratch.”

Friedman, the former GitHub CEO who joined Meta last year alongside Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang, said that the team at Meta had fallen in love with OpenClaw and wanted Muse to be “something like OpenClaw” that could be scaled to billions of people.

Because OpenClaw is an open source project, it wouldn’t be surprising that Meta looked to it for inspiration, especially given its breakout success, which prompted OpenAI to snatch up its creator earlier this year. However, it speaks to Meta’s well-known playbook that involves taking promising products, then copying their best features — something it did most notoriously with Snapchat’s invention of the stories format.

Friedman’s statement on X was made in response to a post that had gone viral among the AI crowd, where Ansh Nanda, an AI app co-founder, claimed that “Muse is LITERALLY OpenClaw for normies.”

Nanda’s X post had included a conversation with Muse, where the AI agent said that the similarity between its own system files and those belonging to OpenClaw was not just “a coincidence” but rather “a match.”

Soon, this thread (and X more broadly) began blowing up as others shared their own comparisons and findings. For instance, one person pointed out that Muse also had a SOUL.md file, the plain text configuration file (written in a simple formatting language called Markdown) that defines an AI agent’s personality, communication style and tone, values, behavioral boundaries, and expertise.

A third noted that the files weren’t just named the same between the two assistants; their content was almost entirely the same.

Following his X post, Friedman also responded to a question about why Muse had copied the exact file names that made up the AI agent’s workspace and had “nearly identical content” for the SOUL.md file. Instead of disputing these claims, Friedman simply replied that “we thought that Peter [Steinberger, OpenClaw’s creator] got those things exactly right.”

“We built Muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw. After I used OpenClaw in January, I bought hundreds of Mac minis for the MSL team, and lots of us fell in love with using OpenClaw (and other personal agents), Friedman said on X. (TechCrunch has corrected Friedman’s punctuation for readability.)

“@steipete [Peter Steinberger] is a genius, and his harness was pioneering from the jump. I think a lot of people were inspired by it. Our goal with Muse was to build something like OpenClaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people,” he wrote.

The Muse app has been something of a hit so far, having recently hit No. 1 on the U.S. App Store. Data indicates that it’s now outpacing ChatGPT’s launch when the platforms and market availability are compared directly.

Reached for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed to Friedman’s statement, saying the company had nothing more to add beyond that.

Tech.title: Hacking group ShinyHunters claims it breached the FBI, stole agents’ and applicants’ data
Tech.content:
ShinyHunters, a prolific cybercriminal group known for large-scale data theft and extortion, says it has breached the FBI and stolen data on thousands of agents and applicants. The hackers made the claim on their dark web leak site, which TechCrunch reviewed, saying they had stolen “sensitive data on almost all FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job.”

404 Media first reported on the breach after receiving a sample of the stolen names, home addresses, and phone numbers of FBI agents and their spouses, and verifying a portion of the stolen data against public records. The hackers say their hack is “not financially motivated,” and are demanding that the FBI remove a report that they say contains false allegations about the group.

The independent publication said the hackers breached an Oracle PeopleSoft server, often used by human resources and recruiters to store job applicants’ personal information, then pivoted to breach an Amazon-hosted government cloud storing the agents and applicants’ data.

ShinyHunters told the publication that they took terabytes of data but did not say what they would do with the information if the FBI does not take down its published report. The stolen data could present a major counterintelligence threat, in which hackers and overseas spies use the information to coerce or extort FBI agents and their families into cooperating with a foreign government.

The hackers reportedly defaced the FBI’s jobs site, which showed at the time of publication that the portal was “currently down for maintenance.” The site also said that the FBI’s special agent applicant portal was also down.

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the incident on Tuesday, and neither did the ShinyHunters hackers.

This is the second known breach of an FBI system this year after unidentified hackers broke into one of the agency’s systems for managing real-time wiretaps and foreign intelligence-gathering warrants, which could have identified targets of the agency’s surveillance. Separately, FBI director Kash Patel also had his personal email account hacked and leaked by an Iran-backed hacking group called Handala in retaliation for U.S.-led strikes against Iran.

Tech.title: a16z is challenging Silicon Valley’s love for drop-outs by launching a school
Tech.content:
Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz is launching a school called The Horowitz Andreessen Academy aimed at aspiring founders who have just graduated high school and have not yet attended college.

The academy is aiming to train these high school grads with hands-on coursework on a variety of topics ranging from the technical (such as “AI Research and Models”) to life philosophy (such as “The Geometry of Luck,” which promises to teach students “about arranging a life so good fortune flows through it.”) Students will also work on personal projects. The school’s main pitch is that it promises to provide students with mentors who are big names in tech.

The school is currently accepting applications for its first year, which will be a one-year program that charges no tuition, and is open to about 50 students, “chosen on proof of work: what they have built, shipped, or earned,” according to the school’s FAQ. The academy is located in San Francisco and students will be responsible for their own housing (although the school is working to help them find it and match them with other student roommates).

One item to note: The academy is currently not an accredited school, so participants will not earn a degree, or college credits that transfer elsewhere.

In 2028, The Horowitz Andreessen Academy — which is a for-profit venture that has raised $42 million — hopes to offer a two-year program. At that point, it plans to charge tuition “similar in cost to an elite private university,” the school’s CEO Gagan Biyani said in a post on X. The schools, which is open to high school graduates, even if they are younger than 18, may also expand beyond 50 students in the future, an a16z spokesperson tells TechCrunch.

In exchange for that elite-tuition price tag, students will gain access to 200 speakers and mentors, including people from 10 founding corporate partners: Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe. Those companies and dozens of others hope to hire from the grads of this school, Biyani said.

So, this is like if Y Combinator (the most famed startup school) and Peter Thiel’s Fellowship Program (a famed program for young people who opt to build companies instead of attend college) had a baby. The difference is, instead of a short-term experience ending with funding for a company, these students will pay tuition, earn tech-trade skills, and have an inside track at tech industry jobs. Or they may also have a startup in the works, built with access to a lot of mentorship.

As the founders of the academy describe, it’s meant to be a new, middle ground between obtaining a full degree before entering the tech industry and dropping out to start a company. In this era when AI has been hampering the entry-level job market, gaining access to jobs may be enough reason for some young people to try this new trade school-like approach.

Tech.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Sol and Luna, boasting lower cost and fewer mistakes
Tech.content:
Earlier this month, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, which it heralded as its most powerful and capable model yet, and the “world’s best model” for a variety of activities, including computer work and coding. Now, the lab is expanding the GPT-6 generation with updated versions of the smaller Sol and Luna models.

“GPT-6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence; these models extend its benefits by making that intelligence more efficient and accessible,” the company writes.

The first models in the Sol and Luna series were introduced earlier this year, representing different tiers in OpenAI’s hierarchy of models. Sol is designed for complex tasks like coding, while OpenAI says Luna is more appropriate for clerical work — “high-volume tasks with a clear goal, like summarizing documents, extracting information, or answering quick questions.”

OpenAI is also emphasizing big improvements in efficiency and affordability — most notably, via a substantial price drop for API access. The 6 series models will be available at half the cost of the 5.6 series of Sol and Luna, a price drop that OpenAI attributes to improvements in caching and inference.

OpenAI also claims that its newest models are better at producing answers that are factually accurate, and notes that they have a lower error rate when it comes to coding.

“On our internal factuality evaluation, which is based on de-identified real-world conversations where users flagged mistakes by our models, GPT-6 Sol makes about half as many mistakes as its predecessor, reaching Astra-level reliability at much lower cost,” the announcement reads.

As is typical with OpenAI’s new model releases, the company is claiming that its newest offerings outshine those of its primary competitor, Anthropic. The company repeatedly claims that GPT-6 Sol and Luna handle tasks substantially better than Anthropic’s top models — like Fable and Opus.

Notably, Anthropic released a new version of Opus 5.5 just 90 minutes before OpenAI’s release, reflecting the intense competition between the two companies.

The new versions of Sol and Luna are now available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for most paid accounts, and in the ChatGPT API, while Luna will be available in the desktop app and for Free and Go users. OpenAI expects to roll out the models to ChatGPT (the app and website) gradually throughout the day.

Tech.title: Waymo’s latest expansion strategy: teenagers
Tech.content:
Waymo will allow teenagers as young as 13 to use its robotaxi service in Nashville as the Alphabet-owned company looks to scale its business by reaching a new group of riders.

Nashville is the second city to offer Waymo teen accounts; the company kicked off its teen account program in Phoenix last year. And more cities are likely to follow, according to the company.

A Waymo spokesperson told TechCrunch that its expansion to Nashville will be the “first of many” teen launches across multiple markets that use the Waymo app in the coming months. The spokesperson said it will offer teen accounts in cities where its operations are mature and local regulations allow it.

Nashville is a relatively new market for Waymo, although it has support from local leaders to offer the service to teens. The company launched its service in a 50-square-mile area of Nashville in April 2026, and earlier this month, its robotaxis became available on the Lyft app.

Waymo’s ridership has skyrocketed over the past two years — a trajectory largely driven by the rapid succession of new markets. Paid robotaxi trips grew tenfold from 50,000 per week in May 2024 to more than half-a-million per week earlier this year. Over that same time span, Waymo has launched robotaxi services in a dozen cities. In the past month alone, the company opened robotaxi services in Denver, Las Vegas, San Diego, and Tampa.

The company’s introduction of teen accounts provides another means of growth — this one targeted at a demographic that relies on parents or public transit to get to school, work, or activities.

There are few limits to the service. The teen account must be connected to a parent or guardian, but once activated, teens can hail autonomous rides anywhere in Waymo’s service area in Nashville — and bring their friends along. Waymo told TechCrunch that teen account holders can bring up to three guests ages 13 to 17. The company didn’t share how these ages would be verified.

That kind of access could certainly invite chaos — it’s not hard to imagine four 16-year-old kids unleashed in a robotaxi. But it may also be part of the appeal for parents who would rather their kids pile into a Waymo than in a vehicle driven by a teenager.

Tech.title: Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 with lower prices and Fable-level performance
Tech.content:
Anthropic’s newest model, Opus 5.5, was released on Tuesday, setting a new state-of-the-art in coding and knowledge work performance, according to the company. Opus is the most capable and expensive tier in Anthropic’s three-tier Claude lineup; Sonnet sits in the middle, while Haiku is the fastest and cheapest. Notably, Anthropic says, the release outpaces the larger Fable model in many benchmarks and succeeded in a number of informal tasks that Fable failed to complete.

The new model is also significantly cheaper than its predecessor. Output tokens will be charged at $20 per million tokens for Opus 5.5, compared to $25 for the previous model. Other metrics have similar price drops. The model is also faster to run, reflecting an overall drop in the compute required to serve it.

The new version also makes significant changes to how Opus communicates, with the Opus 5.5 less likely to use jargon and more likely to put important information at the start of its messages.

The launch comes just two months after the release of Opus 5 on July 24. According to the announcement, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, which are the next tiers in the lineup, will be released “in the coming weeks,” with similar performance improvements.

Anthropic says that Opus 5.5 is comparable to Mythos in its biology and cybersecurity capabilities, so its release is subject to the same safeguards as the company’s Fable model. Those safeguards limit how much the models can be used to discover exploits in compiled programs or developing recognizable biological weapons, among other tasks.

Opus 5.5 is Anthropic’s first model release since CEO Dario Amodei embraced calls to pace the frontier, deliberately slowing down progress on AI capabilities to match the rate of progress on alignment.

“I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence,” Amodei wrote in a post earlier this month, “not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.”

Opus 5.5’s safety training was broadly similar to its predecessors, with alignment testing and pre-release evaluation by outside organizations like METR and Frontier Design. But Anthropic emphasized that more advanced training and evaluation systems were already being prepared for future models, including improved security and monitoring systems.

“As AI becomes more capable, public policy should play a larger role in making sure the systems people rely on are safe. That capacity takes time to build, and we’ve started to put the infrastructure in place to support it,” the blog post reads. “We expect to share more details on these efforts soon.”

Tech.title: How to Claim Your Cut of Apple’s $250 Million Siri Settlement
Tech.content:
In May, Apple agreed to pay out $250 million as part of a class action lawsuit over claims the company overhyped its Apple Intelligence tools, specifically the long-delayed Siri AI overhaul.

Although the revamped Siri AI voice assistant is now available for owners of newer iPhones via iOS 27, you may still be eligible to claim cash back for past purchases. This settlement covers customers in the US who made their purchases from June 10, 2024 to March 29, 2025, and bought certain iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 models from Apple. If you qualify, you might receive up to $95 for each phone.

This settlement revolves around Apple’s promotion of Siri features to sell iPhones. “I expected to receive a Siri Apple Intelligence feature and did not receive it,” reads part of the statement you have to sign when filling out the claim form. As part of the settlement, Apple denies any wrongdoing.

“We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” read part of Apple’s statement from May about the settlement.

To file a claim, visit the dedicated website: smartphoneaisettlement.com. Click the blue button in the top-right corner of the page labeled File A Claim. First, you’ll be asked whether you have a Claim ID and PIN to enter. It’s not required for you to already have this info on hand. On the final page, you’ll need either your iPhone’s serial number or Apple Account ID on hand to file the claim.

Not sure where your serial number is located? Open the Settings app, tap General, then choose About. Your serial number will be a string of letters and numbers near the top of the screen.

You can choose to receive the settlement money through PayPal, Venmo, an electronic bank transfer, or a paper check. If you have multiple devices and want to make claims for all of them, then you’ll need to fill out the form again for every eligible device. iPhone owners have until December 21 to make their claims.

Tech.title: Rabbit Is Back, This Time With an AI Agent App
Tech.content:
Jesse Lyu doesn't think the Rabbit R1 was a flop.

Lyu's gadget was among the first in the gold rush to create dedicated AI hardware that acted as a virtual assistant. You could speak into the R1 and ask it to complete tasks for you—book an Uber; order food on DoorDash. After a buzzy launch at CES 2024, it earned scathing reviews. All the agentic stuff on the R1 just didn't work that well. WIRED gave it a 3/10.

Since those early days, the capabilities of AI assistants have vastly improved, and now the tech is all the rage. So Rabbit is banging the drum again.

On Tuesday, Rabbit announced OS3, a standalone “agentic operating system” designed to run across multiple screens. It also arrives as a software update for the company's R1 gadget, though you don't need an R1 to use it. Instead, you can access OS3 through a desktop browser, Telegram on your phone, or even iMessage.

It’s a striking pivot for a company that once championed the handheld hardware over smartphone apps, but the environment for this type of software has ripened.

Agents that handle tasks for you are all anyone in Silicon Valley talks about. Meta's new Muse agent was just banned from crawling Amazon to shop on a user's behalf using a virtual machine. Lyu smirks as he brings it up, saying, “We've been through all of this a year and a half ago,” calling back to the R1's controversial use of a virtual machine to execute app actions on your behalf. So was Rabbit just too ahead of the curve?

Tech.title: Adobe Premiere, One of the iPhone’s Best Video-Editing Apps, Is Now on Android
Tech.content:
Nearly a year after releasing Premiere for iPhone, Adobe is finally bringing its redesigned video-editing app to Android. The app has been in beta for several weeks but is now available as the official successor to Premiere Rush, which the company will stop supporting on September 30.

Eric Snowden, senior vice president of design at Adobe, tells WIRED the feedback for the iOS app has been “incredibly positive” (to his credit, it has a 4.8-star rating out of 5 on the App Store with more than 25,000 ratings). The goal with the Android version wasn't just to port the iPhone app experience, but to make it feel really native to Google's platform.

That includes making sure the app works just as well on every kind of Android device out there, whether it's a Samsung foldable or a candy bar Google Pixel. Yes, when you open up a folding phone with the Adobe Premiere app, you can view your footage on the left and see the multi-track timeline on the right, maximizing space. Snowden suggests optimizing the app for Android foldables will help the company with the iPhone app for the upcoming iPhone Duo.

Courtesy of Adobe

And if you're wondering whether this app will work well on Google's new Googlebook laptop platform, Adobe says its apps—Acrobat, Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere—are optimized for the new laptops, meaning they'll take advantage of the larger screen, but can’t quite deliver the “desktop-grade” experience you’ll find on Windows or macOS.

Equally important is ensuring the app runs on lower-power devices, though Premiere has a minimum requirement of 5 GB of RAM (phones will also need to run Android 13 or later).

“We wanted this to run on as many devices as possible, so the team spent a ton of time making sure that this is not just for flagship phones,” Snowden says. “This is for a really broad range of Android devices.”

Launch the Adobe Premiere app and you will see all your footage from your camera roll on the home screen. From there, you can choose creator-made templates—ranging from lifestyle to beauty to templates for foodies—to get started on an edit, or start from scratch if you'd like.

It's easy to add your footage, then opt for the mini editor or the full editor. The former lets you easily trim or replace your footage, and even choose a filter to apply a specific color style to all of your clips. You can export directly to YouTube Shorts without leaving Premiere. The full editor gives you a multitrack timeline for more granular edits, like layering text, music, and effects.

Tech.title: Viture’s Vonder Glasses Are Meant to Map Your Mind
Tech.content:
David Jiang, cofounder and CEO of smart glasses company Viture, tells me about how he used to yell at his kid.

His 10-year-old son played tennis. During tournaments, Jiang says he had a habit of shouting and criticizing his son’s mistakes as he played. He wanted to apply pressure to make him succeed—it was the way he’d been taught to raise kids, after all. It made sense.

But then, unprompted, his smart glasses sent him a message. The AI assistant in his company’s newest wearable had picked up on what he was doing, recognized that his behavior wasn’t helpful, and messaged him about what he should do differently. Stop shouting. Stop criticizing. Just be there, be present, and show that you support your son. That worked, Jiang says, and being called out like that has supposedly made him a better father and improved the relationship with his kid, all thanks to his yet-to-be-released Vonder AI glasses.

Tech.title: AI Models Built From Rat Brains Just Got Closer to Reality
Tech.content:
A biological computing startup that uses neural patterns from rat brain cells to build artificial intelligence just got a major boost from Amazon.

Starting Tuesday, select Amazon Web Services customers will gain access to The Biological Computing Company’s “rat brain” AI model as part of a limited preview. The startup’s technology is specifically designed to improve AI for generating videos. Both Amazon and The Biological Computing Company, which goes by the acronym TBC, says they expect the tech to roll out to all AWS enterprise customers soon.

“We figured out a way to code information, like images for example, to the biological material,” says TBC cofounder Alexander Ksendzovsky. “We then observe how the biology processes that information, and then we build a tool that mimics that process.”

This is not the first biologically-derived computing platform that Amazon has made available in its marketplace, says Deap Ubhi, global director of technology for startups at Amazon Web Services. Ubhi says the cloud-computing giant also works with Cortical Labs, an Australia-based company that combines lab-grown neurons with silicon chips to help companies process data. (It calls its products WAAS, or “wetware as a service.”) Cortical Labs also sells a multi-thousand dollar “biological computer,” a low-power device designed for use in laboratories that can supposedly keep neurons alive for six months.

TBC takes a “pragmatic approach,” says Ubhi, which is part of why the company appealed to Amazon. Rather than taking big swings or trying to reinvent the transformer, the core architectural unit of large language models, “they’re working within existing standards of the generative AI space and saying, ‘How can we make the current visual models more efficient?’” he explains.

A multi-electrode array, which TBC uses to record the activity of rat brain cells. Courtesy of The Biological Computing Co

As AI companies race to find ways to make their models more efficient, a once-fringe field known as biological computing has begun gaining traction. Researchers have long envisioned a world where computer software performs more like the neural networks inside human brains instead of relying solely on math-based algorithms.

But biological computing comes with unique challenges. The field requires running actual biology labs, not just computer labs, in which brain cells, stem cells, or synthetic biomaterials must be kept alive or preserved, carefully monitored, and somehow translated into meaningful digital information. While some startups have made progress in the field, bridging the divide between nature and code remains complicated.

The Biological Computing Company was founded in Baltimore, Maryland four years ago by two neuroscientists and neurosurgeons: Ksendzovsky, now the company’s CEO, and Jon Pomeraniec, who serves as president and COO. Earlier this year, TBC raised $25 million from a group of investors led by Primary Venture Partners, its first significant round of funding.

Tech.title: GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS Review (2026): Cinema-Quality Action Cam
Tech.content:
Don't let the GoPro in the name fool you, but its new Mission 1 Pro ILS (short for interchangeable lens system) isn't really an action camera. It's not even waterproof, and it uses potentially fragile interchangeable lenses. It's really a cinema camera crammed into the form factor of a GoPro.

While the average action camera user probably won't want the ILS version of the Mission 1 (the standard Mission 1 Pro serves that need), professional filmmakers, creators, and camera nerds have been clamoring for something like this for years, and it's finally here. It isn't perfect—in fact, it has some serious shortcomings—but this initial ILS camera does what it is meant to do quite well and, with incremental improvements, could become a truly great, tiny 8K video powerhouse.

What Is the Mission 1 Pro ILS?

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

The Mission 1 Pro ILS joins the Mission 1 and Mission 1 Pro to round out GoPro's high-end line of cinema-quality action cameras aimed at professionals. The major advantage over more consumer-oriented cameras like the GoPro Hero 13 or similar offerings from DJI and Insta360 is the large 1-inch (Type 1) sensor, which produces clearer, sharper video. The Mission 1 and Mission 1 Pro are still traditional action cameras, though, with a fixed ultrawide lens and rugged, waterproof bodies. Both deliver outstanding image quality, and the Mission 1 Pro is our favorite action camera on the market.

Tech.title: The UK Government Faces a Reckoning Over Palantir
Tech.content:
When Andy Burnham sat in his office in Manchester as the regional mayor, building an unrivaled power base on Britain’s left that ultimately catapulted him into the prime minister’s office, he did so in the only region of England that refused Palantir access to its data.

Now, as Burnham enters his first parliamentary session as British leader, Palantir could prove to be his first major test in office, as sources in Westminster tell WIRED the prime minister is under significant pressure from his new colleagues to break the company’s contentious contract with the National Health Service. The dispute could become the first major crisis of Burnham’s premiership, with those sources saying pressure is mounting on him to decide the future of Palantir’s growing role across the British state in the coming weeks.

Palantir currently holds contracts worth around £670m in the public sector, including major deals in health, defence, and policing. The largest—a £330m contract to manage healthcare data on the NHS Federated Data Platform—is the one Palantir opponents have opted to focus on. Reports circulated during Labour’s leadership election that Burnham would block Palantir, but they were swiftly cut down in follow-up reporting. Campaigners are now pushing for Burnham to use a break clause in Palantir’s contract with the NHS, which would see the deal end in 2027.

Burnham’s government and the Labour Party he leads are fractiously split on the issue. On one side, leading officials and parliamentary veterans argue cautiously in favor of the provider. On the other, Labour’s left-leaning grassroots and influential backbench MPs are pressuring the government to end the relationship, and in the process begin a huge schism with the company.

The government has so far obfuscated in response to an official petition asking for people to be able to opt out of Palantir’s FDP, after it got 10,000 signatures, saying only that the government would consider it in future policy making. A similar, non-official petition calls for Palantir to be removed from the NHS entirely and has already reached 177,000 signatures.

Growing public opposition to the company has put the government under real pressure to reduce Palantir’s role in the British state. WIRED spoke to three Whitehall sources who believe that, if the deal is to be broken, a decision to do so would need to be made in the next few weeks.

“Given the need to hire an alternate provider or make a decision to move the contract in house, any decision to tear up the contract would need to be done by the Autumn,” one Whitehall source tells WIRED. “Otherwise the government would risk botching any changeover.”

Many of the supporters who secured Burnham’s position in Downing Street are natural Palantir skeptics who come from the soft left. Intrinsically wary of privatisation, they want to see the firm’s role reduced or removed entirely from British politics.

Beyond the inner circle, opposition to Palantir is organised and loud, including many members of the Socialist Campaign Group, a faction within the Labour Party, who are on the whole more experienced MPs. Burnham supporters like Rachael Maskell have vocally opposed Palantir.

Maskell has highlighted her own work as an NHS clinician to justify her opposition to the company in a parliamentary debate in April. During a debate on Palantir’s FDP in February, she said: “This US spytech company is now deep into the data of our NHS and of course patients across the country. I know as a former clinician in the NHS, trust is key. If you do not have the confidence and trust of your patients, that results in people having worse health outcomes. So in the interest of our constituents' health, I urge the government to end this contract.”

Tech.title: Everything You Know About Political Violence Is Probably Wrong
Tech.content:
It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.

In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”

Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.

But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”

What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.

What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.

Courtesy of The New Press Buy This Book At: Amazon

Bookshop.org

Books-A-Million If you buy something using links in our stories, we may earn a commission. This helps support our journalism. Learn more.

Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?

America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.

Tech.title: Apple’s MLB Dodgers Live Broadcast Was Shot With iPhone 18 Pro Max
Tech.content:
iPhone 18 Pro Max units were spread strategically around the field of Dodger Stadium for the first Apple TV broadcast shot with iPhones that didn’t have sports lenses.

It was a beautiful night for a ballgame last Friday at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles — and some of the footage seen by viewers at home came right out of the phone in their pockets.

That’s the iPhone 18 Pro Max in their pockets, if they happened to be one of the serious fans who bought one when it went on sale Friday. Apple’s latest iPhones have video upgrades with physical aperture blades and new modes, which fans watching the Dodgers take on the San Francisco Giants saw for themselves: Out of the 30 cameras shooting footage of the game, 14 were iPhone 18 Pro Max units.

Several iPhone 18 Pro Max units were tucked into custom-made protective cushions to catch the game — and hopefully survive any unlucky foul balls rocketing their way. David Lumb/CNET

Ahead of the game, Apple brought members of the media, including me, to Dodger Stadium to see the setup, which would record footage for Apple TV’s final broadcast of the Friday Night Baseball game. As soon as I stepped from the stands out onto the field, I found the first of these iPhones on a tripod just inside the dugout, pointed at the field. Considering the phone had only been released to the public that morning, it didn’t surprise me that the phone case for mounting it on the tripod read “iPhone 17 Pro Max.”

A total of three iPhone 18 Pro Max units were arranged behind the plate — two on either side slid into protective padding and one atop the pitch speedometer cameras.

Our tour continued behind the home plate, where iPhones were slotted into custom-made, heavy padding on the backstop and perched above the tower of pitch clock cameras. Others were placed in the visitors’ dugout, posted on the right-field foul pole and positioned toward the field from either team’s bullpens.

One perched on the wall above right-center field was on a gimbal, nicknamed “the robo” and manually controlled from the broadcast center, was positioned to capture outfielders rushing to the wall and reaching over to rob home runs. And one was carried out in the stands to get live fan reactions during the game.

The Ronin gimbal-mounted iPhone 18 Pro Max setup, seen in profile, perched just in front of right-center field, ready to catch game-making plays at the wall — and the crowd reaction behind it. David Lumb/CNET

Apple had its first live iPhone-shot broadcast of a Major League Soccer game back in May, but around half of the fifteen iPhone 17 Pro Max units were bolted onto large, professional-grade telephoto lenses. At Dodger stadium, all the iPhone 18 Pro Max units are shooting from their lenses alone. It’s a way to show off the differences in video capabilities on the premium phones, especially under the challenging conditions of night-time baseball games that start in daylight and end under stadium lights, explained Dylan Ashbrook, director of content and brand development for Apple Sports.

“The new 48MP Fusion Main camera gives us even more versatile video capabilities, and the variable aperture on the Main camera gives us another tool for managing exposure in-camera, giving us more control over the look of the game as conditions change,” Ashbrook said.

Apple didn’t go into detail on the sixteen other cameras that shot the game, but presumably, they were conventional cameras with powerful telephoto lenses to capture plays up close. But the iPhones were chosen to capture angles that those hefty cameras couldn’t — because unlike them, nine of the iPhone 18 Pro Max units weren’t connected by cable wire to pipe in their live footage to the broadcast center. They sent it over wireless 5G — in the middle of the game.

An iPhone 18 Pro Max was positioned in visitor and home bullpens to capture close plays near the edge of the outfield. David Lumb/CNET

Live-streaming footage over 5G for a professional MLB broadcast

While five of the iPhones sent their footage through fiber cable to the broadcast center, nine sent theirs over a private 5G network, which T-Mobile set up ahead of the game. Apple tested the network and was confident there wouldn’t be any latency — in theory, it would be able to switch to any of the 14 iPhones around the stadium at any time.

Not needing a bulky cable to send broadcast footage freed up Apple to place the iPhones in many more locations. That behind-the-plate setup only required Apple to get specially made backstop cushions (which met MLB safety standards) with small slots to slide an iPhone 18 Pro Max into, rather than arduously rebuilding the whole setup with wire connections. Not needing wires also enabled the free 360-degree movement of the gimbaled setup on the outfield wall.

It also means most of Apple’s setup for the game is intentionally temporary. When I asked the company’s representatives touring us around the field why they hadn’t put up an iPhone on the left-field foul pole, they noted that they could easily switch around the layout for the next game — including adding more gimbaled iPhones on the outfield wall, which they’re particularly excited about.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max mounted above the speedometer — and cameras to capture spatial video. David Lumb/CNET

There’s one downside to the freedom of wireless iPhones: They won’t be plugged in to charge while they’re shooting video, which often drains the battery quickly. Since the iPhone 18 Pro Max units were shooting in 4K (which was later scaled down to 1080p in the broadcast center), and were streaming their footage to the broadcast center over 5G wireless, I was concerned about whether they’d last a whole game. While recent rule changes have shortened baseball games (last year’s average was around 2 hours and 40 minutes, according to MLB.com), that’s still a long stretch of continuous video.

Yet when I asked, Apple wasn’t worried. It was confident the iPhone 18 Pro Max units would last the whole game, no problem. (That’s also confidence that the phones wouldn’t overheat while recording video; temperatures topped out around 82 degrees F the day of the mid-September game).

This iPhone 18 Pro Max unit is mounted inside the home team’s dugout, sitting alongside the World Series Champion players of the Dodgers. David Lumb/CNET

Apple’s likely right to feel secure that the iPhone 18 Pro Max wouldn’t run out of battery while shooting the games. The company never gives out exact capacities for the batteries on its iPhones, but has said that its latest and biggest phone should get last 30 hours on a full charge. In his review, CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland got about a day and a half of casual use before hitting 0% on the battery, and on a more intensive day of use, had 14% charge left just before midnight.

I caught some of the game’s broadcast on Apple TV, and while most of the broadcast stuck with the views that most viewers are familiar with (and were likely shot by conventional cameras) like looking over the pitcher’s shoulder toward the batter and bleacher-positioned zoom-ins on big plays, I did notice some iPhone footage snuck in there.

Some of these were vantages at the field level of players and pitchers locked in to the game, but the biggest screentime came from the iPhone wandering around the stands getting the true fan experience. For viewers at home, this was definitely a new vantage from the seats they wished to be in, surrounded by jovial comrades adorned in Dodger blue.

Tech.title: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro vs. 17 Pro: What the Extra $100 Brings to the Newer Pro iPhone
Tech.content:
Though the new iPhone Duo might’ve captured a lot of headlines for its foldable design, the iPhone 18 Pro remains Apple’s standard-bearer due to its top-of-the-line camera, superb features and excellent battery life. One of the more impressive new features this year is the camera’s variable aperture, which lets you control exposure.

But while the iPhone 18 Pro has a lot going for it, it really isn’t too different from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro. The design, features and internal specs have very minor differences. If you really care about having variable aperture, perhaps the iPhone 18 Pro is the better choice. But if you care more about saving money, the 17 Pro, which retails for about $100 less, might be the wiser option.

Here’s a closer look at how last year’s flagship compares to this year’s.

The Dynamic Island is smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (right) than on last year’s 17 Pro Max. Patrick Holland/CNET

Design and display

When you look at the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 17 Pro side-by-side, there really isn’t a whole lot to differentiate them. They have the exact same dimensions of 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches, and both have 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR LTPO OLED displays. You can even use the same phone cases for the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro.

The iPhone 18 Pro is ever so slightly heavier — 7.44 ounces compared to the iPhone 17 Pro’s 7.27 ounces — likely due to the variable aperture’s polymer blades. Another change is that the Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro is slightly smaller, plus it supports up to three Live Activities at a time. On the inside, the 18 Pro has a redesigned vapor cooling chamber, which could be important if you intend to use the phone for more intensive tasks like gaming or lengthy video capture — the newer phone should be able to stay cooler for longer than the 17 Pro.

Unfortunately for those who love the color orange, you won’t find an iPhone 18 Pro in that shade. Still, the colors for the 18 Pro are quite lovely. The iPhone 18 Pro ships in glacier blue, burgundy red, black and silver. The iPhone 17 Pro comes in cosmic orange, deep blue and silver.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is able to show three Live Activities at once. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Camera features

Both the iPhone 17 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro feature a triple 48-megapixel rear camera array. The key difference, however, is that the iPhone 18 Pro has variable aperture, which allows you to control light exposure at the hardware level. You can switch between four aperture presets (f1.48, f1.8, f2.8, and f4.0 f-stops) to adjust the amount of light that hits the sensor. This allows for greater depth of field in close-up shots and improved low-light photography, among other things.

Aside from that, the front-facing camera remains largely unchanged. Both have an 18-megapixel selfie camera with a Center Stage feature that automatically frames the people in the shot, plus it can switch between horizontal and vertical orientations without having to rotate the phone.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available in black (pictured) along with burgandy, glacier and silver. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Performance and battery life

The iPhone 18 Pro ships with the brand-new A20 Pro chip, which is an upgrade over the 17 Pro’s A19 Pro chip. The processor is Apple’s first to use a 2-nanometer process, which means the chip is denser — possibly allowing Apple to make room for a bigger battery. We still have more testing to do, but in our initial tests, we’ve found that the A20 chip is quite the beast, never stumbling on videos or games.

If you still want an orange iPhone, the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max are currently your only option. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

As for battery life, we have so far found it to be the same on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro, with both phones lasting for close to 24 hours before needing to be recharged. The 18 Pro is one of the fastest-charging phones we’ve tested, with it charging from 0% to 82% in 30 minutes. That’s substantially faster than the 17 Pro, which recharged to 69% in the same test.

Check out more comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 17 Pro in the below specs chart.
